docs.title: Home
docs.text:
py-simple-wrap is a beginner-friendly Python package that wraps common, everyday tasks — file handling, date formatting, unit conversion, and more — into simple, readable functions. No boilerplate, no memorizing syntax you'll forget in a week.

pip install py-simple-wrap

This installs the lightweight core; a few modules need extra packages — see the Quickstart Tutorial below for the full list.

docs.title: Why py-simple-wrap?
docs.text:
Most everyday Python tasks — reading a file, converting units, validating an email — take a few lines of boilerplate every single time. py-simple-wrap wraps that boilerplate into one-line function calls, so you can focus on what you're actually building instead of re-deriving the same five lines of code for the hundredth time.

It's built by and for beginners, with contributions welcome from anyone who wants to help make Python a little less intimidating.

docs.title: 🐍 Python Compatibility
docs.text:
py-simple-wrap v0.9.0+ requires Python 3.11 or newer.

Supported versions: Python 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14.

⚠️ Python 3.10 support has been discontinued due to security vulnerabilities affecting Pillow, a dependency used by the image utilities.

If you're using Python 3.10, please upgrade to a supported version before installing v0.9.0 or later.

For more details, see our Security Policy.

pip install py-simple-wrap

This installs the lightweight core; a few modules need extra packages — see Installation in the Quickstart for the full list.

from py_simple import make_blank_file, miles_to_km, is_valid_email

make_blank_file("notes","txt")
print(miles_to_km(26.2))  # 42.16...
print(is_valid_email("hello@example.com"))  # True

Full walkthrough in QUICKSTART.md, or browse the documentation site.

docs.title: 😰 → 😎 See the difference
docs.text:
The traditional way 

import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

try:
    response = requests.get("https://github.com", timeout=10)
    response.raise_for_status()
    page = BeautifulSoup(response.content, "html.parser")
    title = page.title.string
except Exception as e:
    print("The site is down or address is invalid.")

The py-simple-wrap way

Needs the [web] extra: pip install py-simple-wrap[web]

from py_simple import get_page_title

print(get_page_title("https://github.com"))

docs.title: Contributor Hub
docs.text:
New here, or making your first contribution to an open-source project ever? You're in the right place. Nobody expects you to already know how this project formats things — that's what this page is for.

Pick whatever's stressing you out below, and go straight to it. You don't need to read all of it, and you don't need to read it in order.

docs.title: What do you need help with?
docs.text:
📝 "I need to write a docstring and I don't know what that even means." The Docstring Template has a copy-paste block — just fill in the blanks. It also explains why the format looks the way it does, in case you're curious, but you don't have to read that part to use it.

📖 "I added a new module and need to write a tutorial page, but I've never written docs before." The Tutorial Template walks through the exact structure every tutorial page in this project uses, with a real example to copy from. You're not writing from a blank page.

🧩 "The issue asks for a project that uses two modules, not one module page." The Project-Based Tutorial Template is the fill-in-the-blanks page for that build, plus where it goes in mkdocs.yml.

🚨 "My function needs to raise an error, and I don't know how this project wants errors to look." The Custom Exception Template has a fill-in-the-blanks class definition, plus a worked example showing both raising and catching it. Errors sound intimidating, but the pattern here is always the same one — once you've seen it once, you'll recognize it everywhere in this codebase.

🏗️ "I want to add a brand-new module from scratch, from file creation to tests." The Adding a New Module Guide walks through the complete checklist, file locations, docstring requirements, and testing steps.

✏️ "The issue asks me to add one function to a module that already exists." The Adding a Function to an Existing Module guide lists the files to touch, where the tests go, and how to export the helper without creating a new module.

🪢 "Rebase stopped on __init__.py or mkdocs.yml. What do I keep?" The Rebase Conflicts on Shared Files guide shows how to keep main's new lines and your addition, then continue the rebase.

📦 "My helper works in its module, but I cannot import it from py_simple." The Public API Export Template shows where to expose a helper, how to check both import paths, and how to avoid name collisions.

🌐 "My test calls a website. How do I test it without going online?" The Network Test Template gives you a working example with fake responses and request failures, then shows which parts to change for your own helper.

🧪 "My test changes files, environment variables or the working directory. How do I keep the next test safe?" The Keeping Tests Isolated guide starts with runnable tmp_path and monkeypatch examples, then shows what gets restored and what stays on disk.

🧹 "A pre-commit check failed, or changed my files. What do I do next?" The Pre-commit Guide shows how to run the repository's hooks, review their fixes, and stage and check your files again.

🔀 "I wrote my changes, but what are the exact steps to test, commit, and open a PR?" The Pull Request Workflow Guide breaks down the complete lifecycle: branch naming, running local pytest and ruff checks, formatting commit messages, opening the pull request, and addressing review feedback.

🎲 "My helper uses randomness. How can its tests pass reliably?" The Testing Random Helpers guide shows controlled draws, boundary cases, and shuffle checks that accept every valid ordering.

📊 "Codecov says my PR dropped coverage, or I want to know which lines my tests missed." The Code Coverage Guide shows how to run pytest-cov locally, read the Missing lines report, and write tests to hit uncovered branches before you push.

docs.title: Still stuck, or something's not covered here?
docs.text: That's okay too. Open an issue, or mention it in your pull request, and it'll get sorted out together — see CONTRIBUTING.md for how to reach out. Nobody's expected to figure this out alone.

docs.title: Code Coverage Guide
docs.text: Every pull request in py-simple-wrap automatically runs test coverage checks in GitHub Actions, and the repository maintains a 94%+ overall test coverage target. In addition to overall project coverage, Codecov tracks patch coverage—measuring whether the specific new or modified lines in your pull request are exercised by tests. This guide shows how to measure coverage locally, read the Missing lines report, and write tests to cover missing branches before pushing.

docs.title: Copy this workflow
docs.text:
Start in the repository's main folder with your virtual environment activated. Install pytest-cov using your environment tool:

Using uvUsing pip 
uv pip install pytest-cov

python -m pip install pytest-cov

Run coverage targeting the specific module you modified (substitute easy_<module> with your module name, e.g. easy_bytes):

pytest --cov=py_simple.easy_<module> --cov-report=term-missing tests/test_<module>.py

Example output:

---------- coverage: platform win32, python 3.13.4 -----------
Name                                                Stmts   Miss  Cover   Missing
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
py_simple_package/src/py_simple/easy_bytes.py         120      4    97%   45-46, 112, 185
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TOTAL                                                 120      4    97%

Cover shows your current test coverage percentage, and Missing lists the exact lines that your tests did not execute.

docs.title: How to read the results
docs.text:
Look at the columns in the summary table:

  • Stmts (Statements): Total executable statements in your Python file (excluding comments and blank lines).
  • Miss (Missed): Number of statements that never executed during your test suite.
  • Cover: The percentage of executed lines: (Stmts - Miss) / Stmts.
  • Missing: The exact line numbers in your file that were not reached during any test.

In the example above, Missing: 45-46, 112, 185 tells you: - Lines 45 and 46 were skipped (typically an if condition error guard). - Line 112 was never called (often an edge-case branch). - Line 185 was not hit (such as an except block).

Open py_simple_package/src/py_simple/easy_<module>.py, scroll to those line numbers, and see which branch needs a test.

docs.title: Covering missing lines
docs.text: Uncovered lines in py-simple-wrap usually fall into one of three common patterns:

docs.title: 1. Input validation guards
docs.text:
Functions in this library guard against bad input types before running:

if not isinstance(text, str):
    raise EasyTextError("Input text must be a string.")

If you only test valid inputs, the raise line stays red. The fix: Add a test that passes invalid inputs (such as integers, None, or lists) and asserts the exception:

@pytest.mark.parametrize("invalid_input", [123, None, ["a", "b"]])
def test_my_function_rejects_non_string(invalid_input):
    with pytest.raises(EasyTextError):
        my_function(invalid_input)

docs.title: 2. Edge case branches
docs.text:
Functions often contain early returns for empty collections or boundary values:

if not items:
    return []

The fix: Add a test case passing an empty list [] or empty string "" to verify that the early return works as intended.

docs.title: 3. Exception wrappers
docs.text:
When wrapping third-party or standard library operations in custom errors:

try:
    return json.loads(content)
except json.JSONDecodeError as error:
    raise EasyJsonError(f"Could not parse JSON: {error}") from None

The fix: Pass malformed data (like "{bad: json") so that the error handler executes.

docs.title: Visualizing missing lines in your browser
docs.text:
If line numbers in the terminal are hard to navigate, generate a color-coded HTML report:

pytest --cov=py_simple.easy_<module> --cov-report=html tests/test_<module>.py

This creates an htmlcov/ folder. Open htmlcov/index.html in your browser:

WindowsmacOSLinux 
start htmlcov/index.html

open htmlcov/index.html

xdg-open htmlcov/index.html

Click on your module name to inspect the source file: - Green lines were executed by your tests. - Red lines were never executed.

Write a test for each red line until the whole file is green.

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
• Target only your module during development. Running pytest over the entire repository takes longer. Using --cov=py_simple.easy_<module> gives you targeted feedback in seconds.
  • Never commit htmlcov/ or .coverage. These are local generated artifacts. The project's .gitignore already ignores them, but keep git status clean by not force-adding them.
  • Understand Project Coverage vs. Patch Coverage. Codecov measures two distinct metrics on every pull request:
    • Project Coverage: The overall test coverage percentage across the entire repository (which aims for 94%+).
    • Patch Coverage: The coverage percentage of only the newly added or modified lines in your pull request diff. Even if a module already has high overall coverage, Codecov will flag a PR if the specific lines you touched are missing tests. Aim to test 100% of your new lines—including input validation and error branches—so that the patch check passes cleanly.

docs.title: Docstring Template
docs.text: Every public function in py-simple-wrap should have a docstring in this shape. It's Google-style (matching mkdocs.yml's docstring_style: google setting for mkdocstrings), plus a "Py_simple Way vs. Traditional Way" example block that's specific to this project.

docs.title: Module-level docstring
docs.text:
Every module file starts with a short docstring explaining what it wraps and why:

"""
easy_<name> is meant to simplify <what it does>.
Built on top of the <stdlib module> module — no more <the pain point>.
"""

See easy_date_formatter.py:1-4 for a real example.

docs.title: Function-level docstring
docs.text:
Copy this whole block and fill in the placeholders:

def function_name(arg_one: str, arg_two: int = 0) -> str:
    """
    One-line summary of what the function returns, written in the third
    person ("Returns the ...", "Calculates a ...").

    Args:
        arg_one (str): What this argument means.
        arg_two (int): What this argument means. Mention the default
            if it's not obvious from the signature.

    Returns:
        str: What the return value looks like, with a concrete example
            (e.g., 'Monday, July 20, 2026').

    Example:
        === "The Py_simple Way"
            ```python
            from py_simple import function_name

            result = function_name("hello", 7)
            ```

        === "The Traditional Way"
            ```python
            # Show the stdlib-only equivalent here, so readers see
            # exactly what py-simple-wrap is saving them from.
            ```
    """

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
• Args/Returns are required if the function takes arguments or returns something — skip the section entirely if it doesn't apply (see list_available_formats() in easy_date_formatter.py, which has no Args: block).
  • Always include an Example block with both tabs. This is non-negotiable per CONTRIBUTING.md's coding style section ("Always include Docstrings with an example").
  • The "Traditional Way" tab should be honest — show what a developer would actually have to write without this package (e.g., raw strftime codes), not a strawman.
  • Private helper functions (prefixed _, like _format_date) can use a single-line docstring — they don't need the full Args/Returns/Example treatment since they're not part of the public API mkdocstrings renders.
  • Keep examples runnable and consistent with what the function actually returns — copy-paste them into a REPL to check before submitting.

docs.title: Where this gets used
docs.text: Docstrings written this way are what mkdocstrings (configured in mkdocs.yml) renders automatically into the Reference section of the docs site — there's no separate reference doc to hand-write. Writing a good docstring is writing the reference documentation.

docs.title: Custom Exception Template
docs.text:
py-simple-wrap wraps risky operations (network calls, file I/O, JSON parsing, external libraries) so beginners get one clear, readable error instead of a random builtin traceback. This page is the template for adding a new custom exception when a module needs one.

Modeled on the real exceptions already in the codebase — SomethingWentWrongError in easy_web.py, EasyJsonError in easy_json.py, EasyFlowError, EasyAsyncError, EasyGameError, EasyGeneratorError, ImageProcessingError, and InvalidExtension in easy_file_manager.py — all follow the same shape.

docs.title: Why bother with a custom exception at all?
docs.text: If easy_web.get_page_content() just let requests' own exceptions bubble up, a beginner would see something like requests.exceptions.ConnectionError or requests.exceptions.Timeout — different exception types depending on how the network failed, none of which say anything about py-simple-wrap. A custom exception gives one predictable name per module (SomethingWentWrongError) that always means "this py_simple function couldn't do its job," with a plain-English message explaining why. Beginners can write one except clause instead of memorizing every exception type a third-party library might throw.

docs.title: The template
docs.text:
Copy this whole block and fill in the placeholders:

class ModuleNameError(Exception):
    """
    Raised when <the specific situation this covers>.

    <A sentence or two on what this covers and, importantly, what it
    does NOT cover — e.g. "this is only for real failures; a function
    that can succeed with an empty result returns None/[] instead of
    raising.">

    Args:
        message (str): Description of what went wrong, usually
            including the original error message.
    """

    def __init__(self, message):
        self.message = message
        super().__init__(self.message)

And where you raise it, wrap the risky call:

def do_the_risky_thing(...):
    """... normal docstring ..."""
    try:
        return _actually_risky_stdlib_or_third_party_call(...)
    except Exception as e:
        raise ModuleNameError(f"Couldn't do the thing: {e}") from None

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
• Name it <Module>Error. SomethingWentWrongError, EasyJsonError, EasyFlowError all follow this. (InvalidExtension in easy_file_manager.py is the one exception to the pattern in this codebase — new exceptions should still follow <Module>Error rather than add another one-off name.)
  • Always subclass Exception directly, not a more specific builtin like ValueError or IOError. Every custom exception in this codebase does this — it keeps the public API surface to one predictable exception type per module, rather than making users guess which builtin subclass a given failure maps to.
  • Store the message and call super().__init__() exactly like the template — this is what makes str(the_exception) and print(the_exception) show the readable message, and keeps the exception compatible with normal Python exception handling.
  • Use raise ModuleError(...) from None when wrapping another exception. The from None suppresses Python's "During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred" chained traceback — a beginner doesn't need to see requests' internal stack trace, they need to see your message. Compare easy_web.py's get_page_content for a real example.
  • Only raise for real failures. If a function can reasonably return "nothing found" (an empty list, None), do that instead of raising — this is called out explicitly in SomethingWentWrongError's own docstring. Custom exceptions are for "the operation could not complete," not "the operation completed and found nothing."
  • Document what it does and doesn't cover in the exception's own docstring, not just in the function that raises it — someone catching EasyJsonError should be able to read its docstring alone and know what triggers it.

docs.title: A minimal worked example
docs.text:
class EasyColorsError(Exception):
    """
    Raised when a color value can't be parsed or converted.

    Covers malformed hex codes, out-of-range RGB values, and any other
    input that isn't a valid color py_simple can work with.

    Args:
        message (str): Description of what went wrong.
    """

    def __init__(self, message):
        self.message = message
        super().__init__(self.message)


def hex_to_rgb(hex_code: str) -> tuple:
    """... docstring ..."""
    try:
        hex_code = hex_code.lstrip("#")
        return tuple(int(hex_code[i : i + 2], 16) for i in (0, 2, 4))
    except (ValueError, IndexError) as e:
        raise EasyColorsError(f"'{hex_code}' isn't a valid hex color: {e}") from None

And how a user of the package would catch it today:

from py_simple import hex_to_rgb
from py_simple.easy_colors import EasyColorsError

try:
    rgb = hex_to_rgb("not-a-color")
except EasyColorsError as e:
    print(f"Oops: {e}")

docs.title: A known gap worth knowing about
docs.text: None of the eight existing custom exceptions (SomethingWentWrongError, EasyJsonError, EasyFlowError, EasyAsyncError, EasyGameError, EasyGeneratorError, ImageProcessingError, InvalidExtension) are currently exported from py_simple/__init__.py — only functions are. That means today, catching any of them requires importing from the submodule directly (from py_simple.easy_web import SomethingWentWrongError), not the flatter from py_simple import ... style every function in this package uses. This is inconsistent with the project's whole "simple, flat imports" philosophy, but it's the current reality, not a documentation error — worth raising with the maintainer as its own fix rather than quietly working around it here.

docs.title: Adding a Function to an Existing Module
docs.text: Most good first issue tickets in this project ask you to add one named helper to a module that already exists. This page is the copy-paste path for that work. If you are creating a brand-new easy_*.py file instead, use the Adding a New Module Guide.

docs.title: Copy this checklist
docs.text:
Replace easy_<module> and your_helper before you start:

[ ] Add your_helper to py_simple_package/src/py_simple/easy_<module>.py.
[ ] Give it a docstring using the Docstring Template, including both example tabs.
[ ] Raise the module's existing error type, with `from None` on wrapped failures.
[ ] Export your_helper in the existing `.easy_<module>` block in __init__.py.
[ ] Add tests to the existing tests/test_<module>.py file. Do not create a new test file.
[ ] If the module already has a tutorial, add a short section there.

docs.title: The files you usually touch
docs.text:
py_simple_package/src/py_simple/easy_<module>.py
py_simple_package/src/py_simple/__init__.py
tests/test_<module>.py
docs/tutorial/easy_<module>.md   # only if that tutorial already exists

Leave MODULES.md, the README badge table, mkdocs.yml reference pages, and module-book/data/modules.js alone unless the issue is for a new module. Those files already describe the module you are extending.

docs.title: The helper itself
docs.text:
Keep the name specific (miles_to_km(), not process()). Follow the helpers already in that file for arguments, return values, and error messages.

Copy this raise pattern when you wrap a failure:

try:
    return Path(filepath).read_bytes()
except OSError as error:
    raise EasyModuleError(f"\n\nERROR: {error}") from None

from None hides the original traceback so a beginner sees one clear error. Use the exception class the module already defines, such as EasyHashError or EasyCsvError.

Fill in the docstring from the Docstring Template. Public helpers need Args, Returns or Raises when they apply, and an Example block with both The Py_simple Way and The Traditional Way tabs.

docs.title: Tests go in the file that already exists
docs.text:
If tests/test_<module>.py is already there, add your cases at the bottom of that file. Creating tests/test_your_helper.py makes review harder, because the module's tests then live in two places.

Include:

  • a success case
  • the invalid inputs the helper rejects
  • a check that from py_simple import your_helper is the same function as from py_simple.easy_<module> import your_helper

The last check is in the Public API Export Template. The Module Tests Template shows how to write the behavior tests.

docs.title: A real example
docs.text:
hash_file() already hashes one path. A follow-up helper that hashes a list of paths belongs in the same easy_hash.py file, next to hash_file in __init__.py, and in tests/test_hash.py.

After you export your helper, this should print True (swap in your names):

python -c "from py_simple import hash_file; from py_simple.easy_hash import hash_file as module_helper; print(hash_file is module_helper)"

Use uv run python if you set up the project with uv.

docs.title: Before you open the pull request
docs.text:
• Run pytest tests/test_<module>.py from the repository root.
  • Keep the pull request to this one helper. A second function belongs on its own issue.
  • If main moved while you worked, rebase and keep both the merged code and your addition.

The Pull Request Workflow Guide covers branch names, commits, and review replies.

docs.title: Network Test Template
docs.text:
A test for a web helper should not depend on a website being online. Use Python's built-in unittest.mock to replace the request with a response you control. You can check successful responses and failures without an internet connection, API key, or extra mocking library.

This builds on the Module Tests Template, using the same patterns as the project's tests/test_web.py.

docs.title: Copy this working example
docs.text:
After following the environment setup in CONTRIBUTING.md, copy this into tests/test_web_mock_demo.py:

from unittest.mock import MagicMock, patch

import pytest
import requests

from py_simple_package.src.py_simple.easy_web import (
    SomethingWentWrongError,
    get_page_content,
)


def test_get_page_content_with_fake_html():
    response = MagicMock()
    response.ok = True
    response.text = "<html><body><h1>Hello</h1></body></html>"

    with patch("requests.get", return_value=response) as mock_get:
        result = get_page_content("https://example.com")

    assert "<h1>" in result
    assert "Hello" in result
    mock_get.assert_called_once_with("https://example.com", timeout=10)


def test_get_page_content_with_unsuccessful_response():
    response = MagicMock()
    response.ok = False

    with patch("requests.get", return_value=response) as mock_get:
        result = get_page_content("https://example.com")

    assert result is None
    mock_get.assert_called_once_with("https://example.com", timeout=10)


def test_get_page_content_with_timeout():
    with patch(
        "requests.get", side_effect=requests.Timeout("example timeout")
    ) as mock_get:
        with pytest.raises(SomethingWentWrongError, match="example timeout"):
            get_page_content("https://example.com")

    mock_get.assert_called_once_with("https://example.com", timeout=10)

Run the practice file from the repository root:

Using uvUsing pip 
uv run pytest tests/test_web_mock_demo.py

python -m pytest tests/test_web_mock_demo.py

You should see 3 passed. These cases are already covered in the real web tests, so remove the practice file when you're done. For a contribution, add your new cases to the matching module test file instead of submitting the same tests again.

docs.title: Fill in the parts for your helper
docs.text:
Use the example as a starting point, then change these parts:

Part Replace it with easy_web, get_page_content, SomethingWentWrongError Your module, helper, and the error it actually promises to raise. "requests.get" The request name your helper looks up; see the next section. response.ok and response.text The response attributes your helper reads. For example, some web helpers read response.content as bytes. The fake HTML and expected result A small made-up response and the result your helper should return. requests.Timeout(...) An error from the dependency that your helper should handle. assert_called_once_with(...) Your helper's expected request arguments, including its actual timeout.

Keep a normal response, an unsuccessful response if your helper handles one, and a request failure. The expected results come from your helper's behavior: get_page_content returns None when response.ok is false, but another helper may raise an error instead.

docs.title: Why this works
docs.text:
MagicMock gives us a small stand-in for a response. Set the attributes the helper uses explicitly: an unset mock attribute is another mock, which can accidentally act like a successful response.

return_value=response makes the replaced request return our fake response. side_effect=requests.Timeout(...) makes it raise an exception instead. Neither makes a real HTTP request inside the with patch(...) block.

The assert checks the helper's result. assert_called_once_with also checks that it made exactly one request with the expected arguments. Checking only that a mock was called would miss a helper returning the wrong result.

docs.title: Patch the name the helper uses
docs.text:
Read the helper's import and request call before choosing the patch target. The current get_page_content imports requests inside the function, then calls requests.get(...), so patch("requests.get", ...) replaces that call.

If a module instead uses from requests import get, it holds its own get name. Patch that name in the module under test; replacing requests.get afterward would not replace the reference it already imported. Use the same module import path as your test, so you patch the module you're actually calling.

Keep the helper call inside the with block. patch restores the original request when the block ends, even if the test fails, so the replacement does not leak into later tests.

docs.title: Before opening the pull request
docs.text:
• Use made-up HTML, URLs, and error messages. Never include real credentials or a response copied from a private account.
  • Check both the returned result or raised error and the expected request. Do not change the expectation just to make a failing test pass.
  • Keep requests replaced in every test case, including error cases. Running tests should not require a live website or paid service.
  • Run your module tests and the full suite described in CONTRIBUTING.md, plus the repository's hooks.

These tests check how the helper handles the responses you provide. They do not prove that a live website is available or that its response format has stayed the same.

docs.title: Adding a New Module Guide 🚀
docs.text: Want to introduce a brand-new easy_<name>.py module to py-simple-wrap? Amazing! This guide walks you through the exact steps to create a new module from scratch while keeping it consistent with the project's "Simple" philosophy.

docs.title: The "Simple" Checklist for a New Module
docs.text: Before writing any code, make sure your proposed module answers "yes" to these three questions: 1. Does this wrap a complex Python task into plain English? (e.g., turning raw regex or random module boilerplate into a one-liner). 2. Is it beginner-friendly? 3. Does it rely primarily on the standard library where possible? (If it needs external packages like pygame or matplotlib, ensure they are handled gracefully via optional extras).

docs.title: 1. Create your module file
docs.text: Place your new Python file inside the source directory: py_simple_package/src/py_simple/easy_<name>.py

docs.title: 2. Add the Module-Level Docstring
docs.text:
Every module starts with a short docstring explaining what it wraps and why: 

"""
easy_<name> is meant to simplify <what it does>.
Built on top of the <stdlib module> module — no more <the pain point>.
"""

docs.title: 3. Write Your Helper Functions
docs.text:
• Use descriptive, plain-English names (e.g., generate_username instead of gen_u).
  • Follow the Docstring Template for every public function (including Args, Returns, and the === "The Py_simple Way" vs === "The Traditional Way" code tabs).
  • If your module fails on invalid input, follow the Custom Exception Template to raise a clean custom error.

docs.title: 4. Export Your Public Functions
docs.text: Make sure your new functions are accessible from the main package import per the Public API Export Template.

docs.title: 5. Add Automated Tests
docs.text: Create a test file in tests/test_<name>.py using pytest to cover your new helpers thoroughly. Follow the Module Tests Template.

docs.title: 6. Write a Tutorial Page
docs.text: Add a Markdown tutorial page under docs/tutorial/easy_<name>.md demonstrating 2–3 functions used together in a realistic mini-example. Follow the Tutorial Template.

docs.title: Pull Request Workflow Guide
docs.text: Contributing to open source can feel intimidating the first time. This guide breaks down the full lifecycle of a pull request for py-simple-wrap—from creating your feature branch to passing all automated checks and getting your PR merged.

docs.title: Copy this checklist
docs.text:
[ ] Sync your local main branch with upstream/main.
[ ] Create a descriptive branch (e.g. feat/..., fix/..., docs/..., test/...).
[ ] Make your changes following the Contributor Hub templates.
[ ] Run the test suite: pytest tests/test_<module>.py
[ ] Check code formatting: ruff check . && ruff format --check .
[ ] Commit your changes with a clear message (Conventional Commits style).
[ ] Push your branch to your GitHub fork: git push -u origin your-branch-name
[ ] Open your pull request on GitHub and link the matching issue (e.g. Closes #123).
[ ] Watch the CI checks and respond to review comments if requested.

docs.title: Branch naming conventions
docs.text:
Branch names in py-simple-wrap reflect the type of contribution:

Prefix When to use it Example feat/ Adding a new function or helper capability feat/easy-bytes-percent-free fix/ Fixing a bug or unexpected behavior fix/url-duplicate-query-params docs/ Writing tutorials, guides, or documentation docs/study-habit-tracker-tutorial test/ Adding or improving unit tests test/easy-date-formatter-coverage

Create your branch starting from an up-to-date upstream/main:

git fetch upstream
git checkout -b feat/your-feature-name upstream/main

docs.title: Running local checks before committing
docs.text:
Catching issues on your machine is much faster than waiting for GitHub Actions:

# 1. Run unit tests for your module
pytest tests/test_<module>.py

# 2. Check linting and formatting
ruff check .
ruff format --check .

If ruff format reports formatting differences, format your files automatically:

ruff format .

docs.title: Writing commit messages
docs.text:
Use clear, imperative commit messages. If your pull request resolves an issue, mention the issue number:

git add py_simple_package/src/py_simple/easy_<module>.py tests/test_<module>.py
git commit -m "feat(easy_<module>): add helper_name function and tests (#123)"

docs.title: Opening the Pull Request
docs.text:
Push your branch to your fork on GitHub:

git push -u origin your-branch-name

Then visit the repository on GitHub or use the GitHub CLI:

gh pr create --base main --title "feat(easy_<module>): add helper_name function (#123)"

docs.title: Pull Request Description Template
docs.text:
Copy this into your PR description:

### Summary
Brief description of what this PR does and why.

### Changes
- Implemented `helper_name()` in `py_simple_package/src/py_simple/easy_<module>.py`.
- Re-exported `helper_name` in `py_simple_package/src/py_simple/__init__.py`.
- Added unit tests in `tests/test_<module>.py`.
- Updated documentation in `docs/tutorial/easy_<module>.md`.

Closes #<issue_number>

docs.title: What happens after opening?
docs.text:
1. Automated CI Checks: GitHub Actions runs the test suite on Ubuntu across supported Python versions (3.11 through 3.14), along with Pylint and CodeQL static analysis.
  2. Review & Feedback: The maintainer or reviewers will review your code. If any changes are requested, simply make the edits on your local branch, commit, and push. GitHub automatically updates the pull request.
  3. Merge: Once approved and checks pass, your PR will be merged into main and your name will be added to the contributors list!

docs.title: Pre-commit Guide
docs.text: Pre-commit runs small checks before a commit, so you can catch formatting problems before someone reviews your pull request. This project already has a .pre-commit-config.yaml; use it rather than creating another one.

docs.title: Copy this workflow
docs.text:
Start in the repository's main folder, after setting up the development environment in CONTRIBUTING.md. Activate .venv first: use source .venv/bin/activate on macOS/Linux, or .venv\Scripts\activate in Windows Command Prompt. Install the pre-commit tool using the same setup method you chose there:

Using uvUsing pip 
uv pip install pre-commit

python -m pip install pre-commit

Replace path/to/your_file.py below with a file you changed. List more paths after it if your change touches several files, including documentation.

pre-commit install
git add -- path/to/your_file.py
pre-commit run --files path/to/your_file.py
git diff -- path/to/your_file.py

pre-commit install connects this checkout to Git's commit hook. Do it once per checkout; installing the tool alone does not install the Git hook. The first run may download the hook tools. Later runs reuse their cached environments, using the versions pinned in .pre-commit-config.yaml.

git add stages your chosen files, including new ones. The manual run lets you see the checks before committing; once the hook is installed, a normal git commit also checks the staged files.

docs.title: If a check changes your file
docs.text:
Seeing Failed can mean a hook fixed something for you. For example, end-of-file-fixer can add a missing newline, and ruff-format can reformat Python code. Read the output to see which files changed.

Review those edits with git diff, then stage the corrected file and run the checks again:

git diff -- path/to/your_file.py
git add -- path/to/your_file.py
pre-commit run --files path/to/your_file.py
git diff --cached -- path/to/your_file.py

Repeat if another hook makes an edit. A passing run does not stage files for you; git diff --cached shows the version you are about to commit.

If the hook did not fix the problem, follow its message, edit the file, and use the same review, stage and rerun steps. For example, check-yaml reports invalid YAML but cannot decide how your configuration should read. A syntax error needs a correction, not repeated runs of the unchanged file.

docs.title: What this repository checks
docs.text:
These hook IDs come from the repository's .pre-commit-config.yaml:

Hook What to expect trailing-whitespace Removes spaces at the ends of lines. end-of-file-fixer Fixes a missing final newline or extra blank lines at the end. check-yaml Checks YAML syntax; fix reported errors yourself. check-added-large-files Reports added files that exceed its size limit. Check whether the file belongs in the contribution. ruff Checks Python code and applies the fixes it can. This repository's --exit-non-zero-on-fix setting asks you to rerun after a fix. ruff-format Formats Python code. Review and stage any edits it makes.

Skipped (no files to check) is normal when a hook has no matching file type. A documentation-only change, for example, has no Python input for Ruff. This does not mean Python linting was run and passed.

Keep the existing hook versions and settings. If a download or environment setup fails, read that error and check your setup before retrying; changing the project's pins is a separate change, not a fix for your file.

docs.title: Checking more than your changed files
docs.text:
To check all tracked files, you can run:

pre-commit run --all-files

This can report or rewrite files outside your change. Inspect git diff afterward and discuss unrelated cleanup with the maintainer rather than including it automatically in your pull request. It does not include new untracked files, so remember to stage files you intend to contribute.

docs.title: Before opening the pull request
docs.text:
• Inspect your diff, including the staged version, and keep the change focused.
  • Rerun the applicable hooks after your last edit.
  • Run the tests required by CONTRIBUTING.md. The hooks do not run pytest or the CI Pylint check for you.
  • For documentation changes, also run mkdocs build and inspect the pages. A successful hook run alone does not verify examples, behavior or rendering.

For the full command reference, see the pre-commit documentation.

docs.title: Project-Based Tutorial Template
docs.text: A module tutorial explains one easy_* helper set. A project-based tutorial combines at least two modules into a small build someone would actually want to try. This page is the fill-in-the-blanks path for that second kind. For a single-module page, use the Tutorial Template.

docs.title: Copy this page
docs.text:
Save it as docs/tutorial/<short-name>-project.md. Replace the placeholders, then run the code and paste the real output.

# Build a <Project Name> with Easy <A> and Easy <B>

Combine **Easy <A>** and **Easy <B>** to <one-sentence job>.

## A small real-world example

<Two or three sentences. Say who it is for, and whether the sample
writes a temporary file.>

Install the package with `python -m pip install py-simple-wrap`, then run:

```python
from py_simple import helper_a, helper_b

...
```

Example output:

```text
<paste what the script actually printed>
```

## What happened?

<One short paragraph per helper, in the order the script calls them.>

## Try it yourself

<One small tweak: another input, a second file, a stricter check.>

## Why use these helpers?

<What the standard-library version would make you juggle, in one
paragraph. Link the two module tutorials at the end.>

docs.title: Where it goes
docs.text:
Add one line under Tutorial: > Project-Based Tutorials: in mkdocs.yml, after the last existing project, using the same indent as the others:

          - <Project Name>: tutorial/<short-name>-project.md

Do not add a Reference page. Do not add a README badge. Those are for new modules, not for a project write-up.

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
• Two modules minimum. easy_csv plus easy_url is a project. Only easy_csv is a module tutorial.
  • Keep the result fun and small. A club badge, a link shelf, a lunch picker — not a walkthrough of every function in both modules.
  • Run the sample. The output block must match what Python prints on a current checkout.
  • Prefer a TemporaryDirectory when the script writes a file, so readers can re-run it without cluttering their disk.
  • Look at the existing project list first, so you do not repeat Class Link Shelf, Palette Journal, or Message Detective with a new title.

docs.title: A real example
docs.text: Class Link Shelf strips a tracking parameter with Easy URL, then saves the cleaned rows with Easy CSV. That is the shape: one job, two helpers, real output, a "try it yourself" tweak.

docs.title: Public API Export Template
docs.text: Adding a helper to an easy_*.py file makes it available from that module. To let a beginner use from py_simple import your_helper, also add it to py_simple_package/src/py_simple/__init__.py.

docs.title: Copy this checklist
docs.text:
Replace easy_<module> and your_helper with your module and function names:

[ ] Define your_helper in py_simple_package/src/py_simple/easy_<module>.py.
[ ] Write its docstring using the Docstring Template.
[ ] Find the existing import block for .easy_<module> in __init__.py.
[ ] Add your_helper to that block, keeping the existing names.
[ ] Check both import paths in the installed development environment.
[ ] Add behavior tests to the matching tests/test_<module>.py file.

The export entry looks like this (the angle brackets are placeholders, so replace them before using the code):

from .easy_<module> import (
    existing_helper,
    your_helper,
)

Edit the existing block instead of adding another copy. For a new module, add a new block alongside the other module imports.

docs.title: A real example
docs.text:
hash_text lives in easy_hash.py, and the package's __init__.py imports it from .easy_hash. After setting up the development environment using CONTRIBUTING.md, run this from the repository root:

python -c "from py_simple import hash_text; from py_simple.easy_hash import hash_text as module_helper; print(hash_text is module_helper)"

Expected output:

True

Use uv run python instead of python if you set up the project with uv. For your own helper, replace hash_text and easy_hash in the command. This checks that the short import exposes the same function as the module import. It does not replace tests of the function's behavior.

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
Python runs the package's __init__.py when it imports py_simple. The import block gives the package a name pointing to your function, so users can choose either import style.

If the module import works but the short import fails, check the spelling and the export block. If both fail, first check that your development environment has this checkout installed and read the exception for the module that failed to load.

docs.title: Before opening the pull request
docs.text:
• Check that your chosen name is not already exported by another module. An import later in __init__.py can replace a name imported earlier.
  • Export helpers meant for users; leave internal helpers such as _new_hasher inside their module.
  • Follow the Docstring Template and Module Tests Template for the implementation.
  • For a new module, also add its tutorial and reference page to mkdocs.yml.

Keeping the short import working means readers can copy the package's examples without needing to learn its internal file layout first.

docs.title: Testing Random Helpers
docs.text: A random result should not make a test pass only sometimes. Use a controlled random choice when you need an exact answer, and test properties when any valid answer is acceptable.

docs.title: Copy a working example first
docs.text:
Save this as tests/test_random_demo.py while practicing. For a real contribution, add your cases to the existing tests/test_random.py instead.

import pytest

from py_simple_package.src.py_simple import easy_random


@pytest.mark.parametrize("chosen", [1, 6])
def test_roll_dice_includes_both_endpoints(monkeypatch, chosen):
    def fake_randint(start, end):
        assert (start, end) == (1, 6)
        return chosen

    monkeypatch.setattr(easy_random.random, "randint", fake_randint)
    assert easy_random.roll_dice(6) == chosen


@pytest.mark.parametrize("sides", [0, -1])
def test_roll_dice_rejects_invalid_sides_before_drawing(monkeypatch, sides):
    def unexpected_draw(*args):
        pytest.fail("Invalid sides should be rejected before drawing a number")

    monkeypatch.setattr(easy_random.random, "randint", unexpected_draw)
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="at least 1 side"):
        easy_random.roll_dice(sides)


def test_shuffle_preserves_items_and_input():
    original = ["moon", "star", "moon"]
    result = easy_random.shuffle_list(original)

    assert sorted(result) == sorted(original)
    assert original == ["moon", "star", "moon"]
    assert result is not original

From the repository root, run:

python -m pytest tests/test_random_demo.py -q

This example produces 5 passed. The first four cases have controlled outcomes. The shuffle test accepts every valid ordering, including the original ordering.

docs.title: Adapt the example to your helper
docs.text:
1. Replace easy_random.roll_dice with the function you are testing.
  2. Find the random call inside that function. Here it is random.randint(1, sides), so the fake takes start and end.
  3. Replace the expected arguments and chosen results with your own cases. Include boundaries such as the smallest and largest allowed result.
  4. If bad input should fail before a random call, keep the failing fake in the error test. It catches an accidental draw even if the function raises the expected error later.

Patch the name where the helper looks it up. This module uses import random, so easy_random.random.randint is the right target. A module using from random import randint would instead need its own randint attribute patched.

monkeypatch restores the original attribute after each test, including when the test fails. Avoid assigning a fake directly and forgetting to restore it. Here the patched random module is shared, so keep each test focused and avoid calling unrelated random helpers while the fake is active.

docs.title: Check what must stay true
docs.text:
The shuffle example does not choose a fixed ordering. It checks three promises: the same items are present, the original list is unchanged, and the result is a new list. Sorting also preserves duplicate counts; a set comparison would miss a lost duplicate.

Do not assert that a shuffled list always changes order, that two rolls must differ, or that ten flips must contain both coin faces. Those can fail with perfectly valid randomness. Repeating the test until it passes hides the problem.

A fixed seed is useful for reproducing a local experiment, but hard-coded sequences can depend on Python's random helper implementation and earlier calls. For a wrapper's exact behavior, the controlled fake is more direct. These tests check the helper's contract; they do not measure statistical fairness or cryptographic security.

docs.title: Before opening your PR
docs.text: Run your module's tests and the repository's pinned hooks, as shown in the Pre-commit Guide. For more on parametrized inputs and errors, see the Testing Tutorial. For fake HTTP responses, use the separate Network Test Template.

docs.title: Rebase Conflicts on Shared Files
docs.text:
Several pull requests in this project often touch the same tail of a file: __init__.py, mkdocs.yml, MODULES.md, or the README badge table. After main moves, a rebase can stop on those files. This page is the copy-paste path through that stop.

Most people work from a fork. In that setup, origin is your copy and upstream is sara-czasak/py-simple-wrap. The commands below use those names, the same way as the Pull Request Workflow Guide.

docs.title: Copy this checklist
docs.text:
Add the upstream remote once, if you do not have it yet:

git remote add upstream https://github.com/sara-czasak/py-simple-wrap.git

Then:

[ ] git fetch upstream
[ ] git rebase upstream/main
[ ] Open each conflicted file.
[ ] Keep the code that already landed on main.
[ ] Keep your addition too. Do not drop either side.
[ ] Delete every leftover conflict marker: <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>>.
[ ] Check the list for duplicate names, duplicate nav lines, or a
    second copy of the same import block.
[ ] git add the resolved files
[ ] git rebase --continue
[ ] Run pytest on the module you changed.
[ ] git push --force-with-lease origin HEAD

If git remote add says the remote already exists, skip that line and fetch upstream as usual. Do not rebase onto origin/main unless origin is the sara-czasak/py-simple-wrap repo itself.

docs.title: What a conflict looks like
docs.text:
Git wraps both versions in markers:

<<<<<<< HEAD
    hash_file,
=======
    your_helper,
>>>>>>> your-commit

HEAD during a rebase is current main. The other side is your commit. The resolved block should include both names, in the same style as the rest of the list:

from .easy_hash import (
    hash_file,
    your_helper,
)

None of the three marker lines should remain. A leftover <<<<<<< HEAD will break the file, and a name listed twice (two hash_file, lines, or the same tutorial listed twice in mkdocs.yml) is also wrong.

The same rule applies to:

  • a new line in mkdocs.yml under Project-Based Tutorials or Contributor Hub
  • a new row in MODULES.md
  • a new badge cell in the README table

If main grew an extra empty table row, keep that row. Sara has asked for that before when the README table conflicted.

docs.title: After the markers are gone
docs.text:
git add py_simple_package/src/py_simple/__init__.py
git rebase --continue

Repeat for each stop. Then:

pytest tests/test_<module>.py
git push --force-with-lease origin HEAD

--force-with-lease updates the already-pushed fork branch after a rebase. Plain git push will be rejected because the history changed.

docs.title: What not to do
docs.text:
• Do not delete main's new helper to make your rebase "simpler."
  • Do not start a second copy of the from .easy_<module> import ( block. Edit the existing one.
  • Do not leave conflict markers in the file, even in a comment.
  • Do not rebase main itself.

The Pull Request Workflow Guide covers the rest of opening and updating a pull request.

docs.title: Keeping Tests Isolated
docs.text: A test should check your helper without changing the files or settings that the next test depends on. Start with a directory made for that test, and let pytest restore changes to environment variables and the working directory.

docs.title: Copy a working example first
docs.text:
Follow the environment setup in CONTRIBUTING.md, then save this practice file as tests/test_isolation_demo.py:

import os
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

from py_simple_package.src.py_simple.easy_config import (
    EasyConfigError,
    create_env_file,
    read_env_file,
)


def test_env_file_uses_a_test_directory(tmp_path):
    env_file = tmp_path / "settings" / ".env"

    create_env_file({"MODE": "practice"}, file_path=str(env_file))

    assert env_file.read_text(encoding="utf-8") == "MODE=practice\n"
    assert read_env_file(str(env_file)) == {"MODE": "practice"}


def test_default_path_and_environment_are_restored(tmp_path, monkeypatch):
    original_directory = Path.cwd()
    original_mode = os.environ.get("PY_SIMPLE_TEST_MODE")

    with monkeypatch.context() as patch:
        patch.chdir(tmp_path)
        patch.setenv("PY_SIMPLE_TEST_MODE", "practice")

        create_env_file({"MODE": os.environ["PY_SIMPLE_TEST_MODE"]})

        assert Path.cwd() == tmp_path
        assert read_env_file() == {"MODE": "practice"}

    assert Path.cwd() == original_directory
    assert os.environ.get("PY_SIMPLE_TEST_MODE") == original_mode


def test_missing_file_does_not_create_it(tmp_path):
    missing_file = tmp_path / "missing.env"

    with pytest.raises(EasyConfigError):
        read_env_file(str(missing_file))

    assert not missing_file.exists()

From the repository root, run:

Using uvUsing pip 
uv run pytest tests/test_isolation_demo.py -q

python -m pytest tests/test_isolation_demo.py -q

You should see 3 passed. Remove the practice file afterward. For a real contribution, add your cases to the matching module's test file instead of submitting these same examples again.

The helpers here already exist in easy_config. create_env_file writes a file, and read_env_file returns a dictionary; neither loads values into os.environ. The second test supplies a made-up environment value itself.

docs.title: Fill in the parts for your helper
docs.text:
Part Replace it with easy_config and its imports The module and helper you are testing. Read its signature and implementation first. tmp_path / "settings" / ".env" A path inside tmp_path for every input and output file your helper uses. "MODE": "practice" Small, made-up input and the exact result your helper promises. patch.chdir(tmp_path) Keep this when testing relative paths or a default filename. Prefer an explicit test path when possible. patch.setenv(...) The specific environment variables your test or helper reads or changes. EasyConfigError The error your helper actually raises for this input.

Keep a successful case and an error case. Check the result or file contents, not just that the call finished. A helper with several input/output paths needs all of them pointed at the test directory.

docs.title: Why the next test stays independent
Files belong inside tmp_path
docs.text:
tmp_path gives each test invocation its own pathlib.Path directory. It keeps a practice .env away from your real configuration and gives each parametrized case its own starting point. Create the test's inputs there, too; do not copy your real .env or read files from your home directory.

Files are not deleted when the test function returns. Pytest normally retains temporary directories from recent runs for debugging. Treat their contents as potentially retained, and use synthetic data only. Pytest's --basetemp option clears the directory you give it before a run, so never point it at your project or another directory you need to keep.

docs.title: Restore environment variables and the working directory
docs.text:
monkeypatch is a pytest fixture, just like tmp_path. Its setenv, delenv and chdir methods record the previous state and restore it during teardown, including when an assertion fails. To simulate a missing variable, use monkeypatch.delenv("PY_SIMPLE_TEST_MODE", raising=False).

The example uses monkeypatch.context() so restoration happens at the end of the with block. That lets the assertions afterward check it in the same test, without depending on which test runs next. Calling monkeypatch.chdir(...) or monkeypatch.setenv(...) directly instead keeps the change until that fixture's teardown.

The original working directory and the presence or value of the example variable are preserved. Do not print the original value: it might come from the person running the test.

docs.title: Register changes made by the code under test
docs.text:
Monkeypatch only undoes changes it manages. It does not automatically watch every assignment to os.environ or every call to os.chdir.

If a helper directly assigns an environment variable, first register that exact key with patch.setenv(key, "test value") inside the context, then call the helper there. Teardown restores the value or absence recorded before setenv, even if the helper overwrites or deletes the key. Register every key the helper can change, not only the ones you assert on. Likewise, call patch.chdir(tmp_path) before a helper that changes the working directory, and keep any destination it uses inside the test area.

Do not clear the whole environment to isolate one key. If the helper's contract requires a different cleanup step, such as closing a file or database connection, use its context manager or try/finally. Restoring process state does not close resources or delete files for you.

docs.title: Before opening your PR
docs.text:
• Keep all example data synthetic, including environment values and files.
  • Run the affected tests alone and with the rest of the suite, as described in CONTRIBUTING.md. Tests should not need a particular order or a leftover file from an earlier run.
  • Run the repository's pinned hooks.

For basic assertions and parametrized errors, see the Testing Tutorial. For fake HTTP responses, use the Network Test Template; a temporary directory does not prevent a real network request.

docs.title: Testing Tutorial
docs.text:
Every function in py-simple-wrap has tests, and every pull request runs them automatically. This page walks you through writing your first one. You don't need to know anything about testing already — if you can write a Python function, you can write a test.

Modeled on the real tests already in the repo (like tests/test_strings.py and tests/test_json.py), so what you learn here is exactly what you'll see in the codebase.

docs.title: What is a test, really?
docs.text:
A test is a small function that answers one question: "when I give my function this input, do I get the output I expected?"

You already do this by hand. You write a function, run it with a few values, look at what prints, and think "yep, that looks right." A test is the same thing, except you write your expectation down once and let the computer check it — every time, in a second, forever. If someone changes the code later and accidentally breaks something, the test notices before anyone else has to.

docs.title: Why bother?
docs.text:
• You find out when something breaks. Not a week later when someone opens an issue.
  • You can change code without fear. Run the tests after your change. Green means you didn't break anything.
  • Reviewers trust your pull request more. A PR with a test says "I checked this works," and it makes the review quicker.

docs.title: Setting up
docs.text:
You only need pytest. If you followed CONTRIBUTING.md to set up the project, you already have it. To check:

pytest --version

If that prints a version number, you're ready. (If it says "command not found", install the project with pip install -e .[all,test,docs] or uv sync --all-extras --dev, as described in CONTRIBUTING.)

docs.title: Your first test
docs.text:
Say you're adding a test for count_words, which counts the words in a piece of text. Create a practice file in the tests/ folder (test_strings.py already exists for real, so we'll call ours test_count_words_demo.py). The name must start with test_ — that's how pytest knows it's a test file.

# tests/test_count_words_demo.py

from py_simple_package.src.py_simple.easy_strings import count_words


def test_count_words_counts_a_sentence():
    result = count_words("Hello world! How are you?")
    assert result == 5

That's the whole test. Let's read it top to bottom:

  1. The import brings in the function you want to test. Every test file in this repo imports from py_simple_package.src.py_simple.<module>.
  2. def test_... — the function name must start with test_, or pytest will ignore it. Make the rest of the name say what you're checking.
  3. result = count_words(...) — call your function with an example input.
  4. assert result == 5 — this is the actual check. assert means "I expect this to be true." If it is, the test passes. If it isn't, the test fails.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
From the project's main folder, run:

pytest -v

-v means "verbose", which shows each test by name. (The project already turns this on for you in pyproject.toml, but it doesn't hurt to know what it does.)

Example output:

tests/test_count_words_demo.py::test_count_words_counts_a_sentence PASSED [100%]

============================== 1 passed in 0.02s ===============================

PASSED and 1 passed are what you want to see. Congratulations, that's a working test.

docs.title: What a failing test looks like
docs.text:
Failing tests are not bad news. They're the whole point — they're the test doing its job. Let's break ours on purpose by changing 5 to 6:

assert result == 6

Run pytest again:

=================================== FAILURES ===================================
______________________ test_count_words_counts_a_sentence __________________

    def test_count_words_counts_a_sentence():
        result = count_words("Hello world! How are you?")
>       assert result == 6
E       assert 5 == 6

tests/test_count_words_demo.py:6: AssertionError
=========================== short test summary info ============================
FAILED tests/test_count_words_demo.py::test_count_words_counts_a_sentence - a...
============================== 1 failed in 0.03s ===============================

How to read this:

  • The > arrow points at the exact line that failed.
  • The E lines say why: assert 5 == 6 means "the function gave back 5, but you said it should be 6."
  • The last line tells you which test failed, so you know where to look.

When a test fails, there are two possibilities: either the function has a bug, or your expectation was wrong. Figuring out which one is part of the job — and here, the function was right (it is five words) and the test was wrong. Change it back to 5 and it goes green again.

docs.title: Testing lots of inputs at once
docs.text:
A function should work for more than one input, including weird ones (empty text, only spaces). Writing a separate test for each gets repetitive, so pytest has parametrize: one test, many examples.

import pytest

from py_simple_package.src.py_simple.easy_strings import remove_extra_spaces


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "text, expected",
    [
        ("  hello   world  ", "hello world"),
        ("hello world", "hello world"),
        ("", ""),
        ("   ", ""),
    ],
)
def test_remove_extra_spaces(text, expected):
    assert remove_extra_spaces(text) == expected

Read the list as a little table: each row is one example, with the input first and the answer you expect second. pytest runs the test once per row and reports each one separately, so if row three fails you'll know exactly which input caused it.

To add a new case later, you just add one more row. This is the pattern used all over tests/test_strings.py.

docs.title: Testing that a function raises an error
docs.text:
Sometimes the correct behaviour is an error. In this project, functions raise a clear custom error (see the Custom Exception Template) instead of letting a confusing one leak through. You test that with pytest.raises:

import pytest

from py_simple_package.src.py_simple.easy_json import EasyJsonError, open_json


def test_open_json_missing_file_raises(tmp_path):
    missing_file = tmp_path / "nope.json"

    with pytest.raises(EasyJsonError):
        open_json(str(missing_file))

Two new things here:

  • with pytest.raises(EasyJsonError): means "the code inside this block must raise EasyJsonError." If it does, the test passes. If it raises nothing, or a different error, the test fails.
  • tmp_path is a built-in pytest helper that gives your test its own temporary folder. Anything you create there is deleted afterwards, so your tests never leave junk files behind or touch real ones. Just add tmp_path as a parameter and pytest fills it in for you. Use it any time your test needs a file.

docs.title: The template
docs.text:
Copy this block into a tests/test_<module>.py file and fill in the placeholders:

````python
import pytest

from py_simple_package.src.py_simple.easy_<module> import <function_name>


def test_<function_name>_<what_you_are_checking>():
    result = <function_name>(<example input>)
    assert result == <expected output>


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "<input_name>, expected",
    [
        (<normal example>, <expected>),
        (<edge case, e.g. empty>, <expected>),
    ],
)
def test_<function_name>_many_inputs(<input_name>, expected):
    assert <function_name>(<input_name>) == expected


def test_<function_name>_raises_on_bad_input():
    with pytest.raises(<ModuleError>):
        <function_name>(<bad input>)
````

Delete the parts you don't need. A function that never raises doesn't need the third test.

docs.title: What should I test?
docs.text:
You don't have to test everything. For each function, aim for:

  • One normal example — the thing the function is meant to do.
  • One or two edge cases — empty text, an empty list, zero, a single item. Edge cases are where bugs hide.
  • One error case — only if the function is supposed to raise something.

That's usually three to five tests per function, and it's plenty.

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
• Test names describe the behaviour. test_count_words_counts_a_sentence tells the reader what broke without opening the file. test_1 doesn't.
  • One idea per test. If a test fails, you want to know immediately which thing went wrong.
  • Run the test before you trust it. Make sure it can actually fail. If you've never seen it fail, you don't know it's checking anything.
  • Use tmp_path for files. Never read or write real files from a test.
  • Don't hit the internet or paid APIs in tests. Tests must run anywhere, quickly, and for free. Look at tests/test_web.py and tests/test_ai.py to see how the project fakes those calls.
  • Put the file in the right place. Tests go in tests/, named test_<module>.py, one file per module.

docs.title: Running just your tests
docs.text:
Once the project has lots of tests, you don't want to wait for all of them while you work. Run one file:

pytest tests/test_strings.py

Or only the tests whose name contains a word:

pytest tests/test_strings.py -k count_words

Example output:

tests/test_strings.py::test_count_words[hello 123 world-3] PASSED        [100%]

======================= 8 passed, 53 deselected in 0.04s =======================

Before you open your pull request, run plain pytest once with no extras, so you know the whole suite is still green. GitHub will run it again on Python 3.11 through 3.14 when you push.

docs.title: Still stuck?
docs.text: That's okay. Open a draft pull request with your test file as it is — even a failing one — and say what you're stuck on. Someone will help you get it green. See CONTRIBUTING.md for how to reach out.

docs.title: Tutorial Template
docs.text:
Each module gets at least one tutorial page under docs/tutorial/, added to the Tutorial section of mkdocs.yml's nav. This is the narrative, "here's why you'd use this" companion to the auto-generated Reference page — it's hand-written, not pulled from docstrings.

Modeled on docs/tutorial/easy_date_formatter.md, which is a good reference example to open side-by-side while writing a new one.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
Copy this whole block and fill in the placeholders:

# <Module Display Name>

One or two sentences: what everyday problem does this module solve, and
what stdlib module is it built on? (Mirror the module docstring here,
but written for a reader, not a code comment.)

## A small real-world example

A short paragraph setting up a realistic scenario — not "here's every
function," but "here's a task you'd actually have."

````python
from py_simple import function_one, function_two

result = function_one(...)
````

Example output:

````text
<what actually prints, for real — run it and paste the real output>
````

## What happened?

One short paragraph per function used above, explaining what it does
in plain language. Cross-reference other functions in the module even
if they weren't in the main example, so the page covers the whole
module, not just the one demo.

## Why use these helpers?

Closing paragraph: what would the reader have had to do without this
module (stdlib-only), and why is the wrapped version better for a
beginner? Keep it short — this echoes the "Traditional Way" contrast
from the docstrings, at the module level instead of function level.

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
• Example output must be real. Run the code and paste the actual output — don't hand-write a plausible-looking result. easy_date_formatter.md uses real dates for this reason.
  • Lead with a scenario, not a function list. "Imagine you're creating a report and want to display today's date..." is more useful than "This module has 12 functions, here they are."
  • Don't duplicate the Reference page. The tutorial explains why and walks through one coherent example; it doesn't need to demonstrate every single function exhaustively — that's what the auto-generated Reference page (from docstrings) is for.
  • Keep tone consistent with the rest of the docs: plain language, beginner-friendly, no jargon introduced without explanation.

docs.title: Wiring it into the nav
docs.text: After writing docs/tutorial/easy_<name>.md, add it to mkdocs.yml under the Tutorial → Module Tutorials list, alphabetically among the existing entries.

docs.title: Contributing to py-simple-wrap 🚀
docs.text:
First of all, thank you for being here! I created py-simple-wrap to help others on their learning journey, and I'm excited to have you join me.

I struggle with anxiety myself, so I totally understand if you're feeling nervous about contributing. Please don't be! The absolute worst thing that could happen is that I might ask for a few changes before merging your code. This is a safe space to learn, make mistakes, and grow together.

📚 New here? The Contributor Hub has copy-paste templates for docstrings and tutorial pages, so you're not guessing at formatting on your first PR.

docs.title: ⭐ Enjoying the project?
docs.text: If py-simple-wrap has been useful, or you just like what it's doing, a star means a lot — it helps other beginners discover the project and keeps me motivated to keep building it. It takes two seconds and costs nothing. 🙏

docs.title: The "Simple" Philosophy
docs.text: Before submitting a new feature, ask yourself: "Does this make a complex task easier for a beginner?" My goal is to keep things intuitive and easy to read.

docs.title: 📂 Understanding the Project Structure
docs.text:
Before making your first contribution, here's a quick overview of where everything lives.

py-simple-wrap/
├── py_simple_package/
│   └── src/
│       └── py_simple/       # Python package source code
├── tests/                   # Automated tests
├── docs/                    # Documentation and tutorials
├── module-book/             # Module reference website
├── landing/                 # Website landing page
├── .github/                 # GitHub workflows and templates
├── scripts/                 # Project maintenance scripts
├── pyproject.toml           # Package configuration and dependencies
├── CONTRIBUTING.md          # Contribution guidelines
└── README.md                # Project overview

docs.title: Where should I make changes?
docs.text:
Adding or updating a helper?

Look inside py_simple_package/src/py_simple/. This is where the Python source code lives.

Adding tests?

Look inside tests/. Tests verify that helpers work correctly and help prevent bugs.

Improving documentation?

Start with docs/ or the relevant Markdown files in the repository. The module-book/ directory contains the module reference website.

docs.title: Why is the Python package inside src/?
docs.text:
The project uses a source-based layout to separate the Python code from the rest of the repository.

The package is located at:

py_simple_package/src/py_simple/

But when you install py-simple-wrap, you import it using:

from py_simple import make_blank_file

You don't need to include the repository's directory structure in your imports.

docs.title: What's an editable installation?
docs.text:
When contributing, you want to test changes to your local code without reinstalling the package every time.

An editable installation, such as:

pip install -e .

connects your Python environment to the source code in your cloned repository. Changes you make to Python files can then be tested directly.

A normal installation, such as:

pip install py-simple-wrap

installs the published package instead.

Tip: If you're contributing, follow the environment setup instructions below rather than installing the published package.

docs.title: 🛠️ Step-by-Step Guide for Beginners
docs.text:
If you've never contributed to an open-source project before, here is exactly how to do it:

  1. Fork the Project: Click the "Fork" button at the top right of this GitHub page. This creates your own copy of the project.
  2. Get the Clone Link:
  3. On your fork's GitHub page, click the green <> Code button.
  4. Make sure the HTTPS tab is selected.
  5. Click the little "copy" icon (two overlapping squares) next to the URL to copy it to your clipboard.
  6. Clone Your Fork: Open your terminal, type git clone, and then paste the link you just copied:
git clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/py-simple-wrap.git
  1. Create a Branch: It's best to do your work on a new branch:
git checkout -b my-new-feature
  1. Set up the Environment: We recommend using uv for lightning-fast dependency management, but standard pip works too!
  2. Using uv (Recommended):
    • Install uv if you haven't already: Installation Guide
    • Sync the project dependencies: 
      uv sync --all-extras --dev
    • Run the tests to make sure everything works: 
      uv run pytest

  3. Using pip:

    • Create a virtual environment and install the package with every extra — the test suite covers every module, including the ones that need extra packages (pygame, matplotlib, Pillow, and so on), so [all] is needed to run it in full: 
      python -m venv .venv
# Activate the virtual environment
# Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
# macOS/Linux: source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e .[all,test,docs]
    • Run the tests: 
      pytest

  4. Preview the Docs Locally: If you are modifying documentation or adding new tutorials, you can preview the site locally using MkDocs.

  5. Using uv: 
    uv run mkdocs serve

  6. Using pip: 

    mkdocs serve
    Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 in your browser to view the site.

  7. Write Your Code: Add your awesome new function or fix that bug! If you're not sure how to format a docstring or write a tutorial page, check the Contributor Hub on the docs site — it has copy-paste templates for both, built from this project's actual conventions.

  8. Commit Your Changes: Save your progress with a helpful message:

git add .
git commit -m "Added a new helper for list cleaning"
  1. Push to GitHub: Send your changes back to your fork:
git push origin my-new-feature
  1. Open a Pull Request: Go to the original py-simple-wrap repository on GitHub, and you'll see a button that says "Compare & pull request." Click it and tell me a bit about what you did!

docs.title: 💡 What should I contribute?
docs.text:
• Report Bugs: If something isn't working, open an "Issue" and let me know.
  • New Ideas: Want to add a "Simple" module for math, strings, or colors? Open an Issue and we can brainstorm it together!
  • Documentation: Spot a typo in this README? I'd love for you to fix it!

docs.title: Coding Style
docs.text:
I try to keep the code "Clean" and "Explicit."

  • Use descriptive function names (like is_file_there instead of check).
  • Always include Docstrings with an example — see the Docstring Template in the Contributor Hub for the exact shape we use.
  • Use existing helper functions (like is_valid_extension) to keep things consistent.

Thank you for being brave enough to try! I can't wait to see what you build. 🌈✨

docs.title: py_simple.easy_ai
docs.text: easy_ai wraps common LangChain functionality to make it easier to use.

docs.title: EasyAIError
docs.text:
Bases: Exception

Raised when a call to an AI model or provider cannot be completed.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default message str

Description of what went wrong.

required

docs.title: ai_chat(ai_model)
docs.text:
Runs an interactive chat loop in the terminal against a LangChain chat model, without you having to write the input/print loop, exit handling, or conversation memory yourself.

Prompts for input with "You: ", prints each reply prefixed with "AI: ", and keeps going until the user types "exit", "quit", "stop", or "bye" (at which point it prints a goodbye message and returns). Each turn is appended to an internal history list of HumanMessage/ AIMessage objects, and the full history is sent to the model on every call, so the model has memory of the whole conversation for as long as the loop runs. The history is local to this call and is not preserved once the loop exits. Errors from ask_ai() are caught and printed instead of raising, so a single bad call doesn't end the session.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default ai_model BaseChatModel

A LangChain chat model instance, such as one returned by get_model().

required

Returns:

Type Description None

None. Runs until the user exits the loop.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
from py_simple import get_model, ai_chat

model = get_model("anthropic", "claude-sonnet-4-6")
ai_chat(model)

from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage, AIMessage

model = ChatAnthropic(model_name="claude-sonnet-4-6")

history = []
while True:
    user_input = input("You: ")
    if user_input.lower() in ("exit", "quit", "stop", "bye"):
        print("AI: Talk to you later!")
        break
    history.append(HumanMessage(content=user_input))
    response = model.invoke(history).content
    history.append(AIMessage(content=response))
    print(f"AI: {response}")

docs.title: chunk_text(text, max_chars=500)
docs.text:
Split text into pieces that fit inside a character limit.

Useful before sending a long note to an AI model that only accepts a short prompt. Words stay whole when they fit. A single word longer than the limit is split so nothing is dropped.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default text str

The text to split.

required max_chars int

Maximum characters in each piece. Defaults to 500.

500

Type Description list[str]

If text is not a string or max_chars is less than 1.

from py_simple import chunk_text

pieces = chunk_text("Pack a lunch and a notebook", max_chars=16)

current = ""
for word in words:
    candidate = word if not current else f"{current} {word}"
    if len(candidate) <= 16:
        current = candidate
    else:
        pieces.append(current)
        current = word
if current:
    pieces.append(current)
