docs.title: zip_folder(folder_path, zip_name=None)
docs.text:
Zips an entire folder (including empty subfolders) into a single .zip file.

Entries are relative to the source folder. An empty source folder produces an empty archive.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default folder_path str

Path to the folder to zip.

required zip_name str

Name/path for the resulting zip file. Defaults to the folder's own name with '.zip' appended.

None

Name Type Description str str

Path to the created zip file.

from py_simple import zip_folder

import os
import zipfile

folder_path = "my_project"
zip_name = "my_project.zip"
with zipfile.ZipFile(zip_name, "w", zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as zf:
    for root, dirs, files in os.walk(folder_path):
        relative_root = os.path.relpath(root, folder_path)
        if not dirs and not files and relative_root != ".":
            zf.write(root, relative_root)
        for file in files:
            full_path = os.path.join(root, file)
            arcname = os.path.relpath(full_path, folder_path)
            zf.write(full_path, arcname)

Waits asynchronously before running a function.

Raises EasyAsyncError if the function raises an exception after the delay finishes.

Parameters:

The function to execute.

import asyncio

def greet(name):

docs.title: run_at_the_same_time_no_params(functions) async
docs.text:
Runs multiple zero-argument functions at the same time and returns their results.

Raises EasyAsyncError if any function raises an exception while running.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default functions list

Functions to run, each taking no arguments.

required

Returns:

Name Type Description list list

A list of (name, result) tuples, one per function. Exception objects returned by callbacks are preserved as values.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
import asyncio
from py_simple import run_at_the_same_time_no_params

def add():
    return 1 + 1

def sub():
    return 4 - 2

async def main():
    return await run_at_the_same_time_no_params([add, sub])

asyncio.run(main())  # -> [("add", 2), ("sub", 2)]

import asyncio

def add():
    return 1 + 1

def sub():
    return 4 - 2

async def main():
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    functions = [add, sub]
    tasks = [loop.run_in_executor(None, f) for f in functions]
    results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
    return list(zip((f.__name__ for f in functions), results))

asyncio.run(main())

Runs multiple functions at the same time, each with its own arguments, and returns their results.

Raises EasyAsyncError if any function raises an exception while running.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default functions_and_args list[tuple]

Functions to run, each given as a tuple where the first item is the function and the remaining items are the positional arguments to call it with, e.g. (func, arg1, arg2).

required

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
import asyncio
from py_simple import run_at_the_same_time_with_params

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

def sub(a, b):
    return a - b

async def main():
    return await run_at_the_same_time_with_params([
        (add, 1, 1),
        (sub, 4, 2),
    ])

asyncio.run(main())  # -> [("add", 2), ("sub", 2)]

import asyncio

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

def sub(a, b):
    return a - b

async def main():
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    functions_and_args = [(add, 1, 1), (sub, 4, 2)]
    tasks = [
        loop.run_in_executor(None, item[0], *item[1:])
        for item in functions_and_args
    ]
    results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
    names = [item[0].__name__ for item in functions_and_args]
    return list(zip(names, results))

asyncio.run(main())

import asyncio

docs.title: run_concurrent_map_limited(func, items, max_concurrency) async
docs.text:
Applies a synchronous function with a limit on concurrent executor jobs.

Uses at most max_concurrency workers, each submitting one item at a time to the event loop's executor. Results keep the input order. An ordinary callback error does not stop the remaining items: all workers are awaited before the first error in input order is raised.

Cancelling the await propagates asyncio.CancelledError and cancels the internal workers so they submit no more items. Already running Python threads cannot be forcibly stopped and may finish afterward.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default func callable

Ordinary synchronous function called with each item. Async callbacks are not supported.

required items list

Items passed one by one to func.

required max_concurrency int

Positive maximum number of submitted jobs at once. Booleans are not accepted. The executor may run fewer.

required

Returns:

Name Type Description list list

Callback results in the same order as items, or an empty list for empty input.

Raises:

Type Description EasyAsyncError

If the limit is not a positive integer or a callback/executor call raises an ordinary exception.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
import asyncio
from py_simple import run_concurrent_map_limited

def square(number):
    return number * number

async def main():
    return await run_concurrent_map_limited(square, [1, 2, 3, 4], 2)

print(asyncio.run(main()))  # [1, 4, 9, 16]

import asyncio

def square(number):
    return number * number

async def main():
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    items = [1, 2, 3, 4]
    results = [None] * len(items)
    work = iter(enumerate(items))

    async def worker():
        for index, item in work:
            results[index] = await loop.run_in_executor(None, square, item)

    await asyncio.gather(worker(), worker())
    return results

print(asyncio.run(main()))  # [1, 4, 9, 16]

docs.title: run_first_completed(functions) async
docs.text:
Runs multiple zero-argument functions concurrently and returns the result of whichever finishes first.

Pending tasks are cancelled once the first function completes. Note that cancelling an asyncio task does not forcibly terminate an already running thread in the thread pool. Raises EasyAsyncError if functions is empty, contains non-callable items, or if the first completed function raises an exception.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default functions list

Functions to run concurrently, each taking no arguments. Must be a non-empty list.

required

Returns:

Name Type Description tuple tuple

A tuple containing (func_name, result) of the first function to finish.

Raises:

Type Description EasyAsyncError

If functions is not a list, is empty, contains non-callable elements, or if the first completed function raises an exception.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
import asyncio
from py_simple import run_first_completed

def fetch_fast():
    return "quick response"

def fetch_slow():
    return "slow response"

async def main():
    return await run_first_completed([fetch_fast, fetch_slow])

asyncio.run(main())  # -> ("fetch_fast", "quick response")

import asyncio

def fetch_fast():
    return "quick response"

def fetch_slow():
    return "slow response"

async def main():
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    tasks = [
        asyncio.ensure_future(loop.run_in_executor(None, f))
        for f in [fetch_fast, fetch_slow]
    ]
    task_to_fn = {
        t: f for t, f in zip(tasks, [fetch_fast, fetch_slow])
    }
    try:
        done, pending = await asyncio.wait(
            tasks, return_when=asyncio.FIRST_COMPLETED
        )
    finally:
        for t in tasks:
            if not t.done():
                t.cancel()
    first = next(iter(done))
    return (task_to_fn[first].__name__, first.result())

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: run_periodically(func, interval, times, *args) async
docs.text:
Runs the same function repeatedly on a fixed schedule and returns the results in order.

Waits interval seconds before each run (including the first), runs func in a thread pool so it never blocks the event loop, and collects one result per run. Raises EasyAsyncError if any run raises an exception while running.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default func callable

The function to run, each time with the same positional arguments.

required interval float

Seconds to wait before each run, including the first one. Must be greater than 0.

required times int

How many times to run the function. Must be at least 1.

required *args

Positional arguments to pass to func on every run.

()

Returns:

Name Type Description list list

One result per run, in the order the runs finished, e.g. [4, 4, 4] for a function that returns 2 + 2.

Raises:

Type Description EasyAsyncError

If a run raises an exception, or if interval or times are out of range.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
import asyncio
from py_simple import run_periodically

def add():
    return 2 + 2

async def main():
    return await run_periodically(add, 1.0, 3)

asyncio.run(main())  # -> [4, 4, 4]

import asyncio

def add():
    return 2 + 2

async def main():
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    results = []
    for _ in range(3):
        await asyncio.sleep(1.0)
        results.append(await loop.run_in_executor(None, add))
    return results

asyncio.run(main())  # -> [4, 4, 4]

docs.title: run_with_default(func, fallback, *args) async
docs.text:
Runs a function asynchronously, returning a fallback value if it fails.

When the function succeeds you get its result; when it raises, you get the fallback instead of an exception. Useful for optional work where a default is fine, such as reading an optional config file or fetching a best-effort value. This is the async counterpart of the synchronous run_with_fallback in easy_flow: it runs the function in an executor and returns a (name, result) tuple like the other helpers in this module.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default func callable

The function to execute.

required fallback

The value to return if the function raises.

required *args

Positional arguments to pass to the function.

()

Returns:

Name Type Description tuple tuple

A tuple containing (name, result) on success or (name, fallback) on failure, where name is func.__name__ when present and repr(func) otherwise (same approach as run_first_completed).

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
import asyncio
from py_simple import run_with_default

def read_config():
    raise FileNotFoundError("no config file")

async def main():
    return await run_with_default(read_config, {"theme": "light"})

asyncio.run(main())  # -> ("read_config", {"theme": "light"})

import asyncio

def read_config():
    raise FileNotFoundError("no config file")

async def main():
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    try:
        result = await loop.run_in_executor(None, read_config)
        return (read_config.__name__, result)
    except Exception:
        return (read_config.__name__, {"theme": "light"})

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: run_with_retry(func, attempts, delay, *args) async
docs.text:
Runs a function repeatedly until it succeeds or all attempts are
exhausted, waiting between attempts.

Raises EasyAsyncError if every attempt fails.

Args:
    func (callable): The function to execute.
    attempts (int): Number of attempts to make before giving up.
    delay (float): Time to wait between failed attempts, in seconds.
    *args: Positional arguments to pass to the function.

Returns:
    tuple: A tuple containing `(func.__name__, result)`.

Example:
    === "The Py_simple Way"
        ```python
        import asyncio
        from py_simple import run_with_retry

        def add(a, b):
            return a + b

        async def main():
            return await run_with_retry(add, 4, 2.0, 2, 3)

        asyncio.run(main())  # -> ("add", 5)
        ```

    === "The Traditional Way"
        ```python
        import asyncio

        def add(a, b):
            return a + b

        async def main():
            loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
            attempts = 4
            for attempt in range(attempts):
                try:
                    result = await loop.run_in_executor(None, add, 2, 3)
                    return (add.__name__, result)
                except Exception as e:
                    if attempt == attempts - 1:
                        raise EasyAsyncError(f"

ERROR: {e}") from None await asyncio.sleep(2.0)

        asyncio.run(main())
        ```

docs.title: run_with_timeout(func, timeout, *args) async
docs.text:
Runs a function asynchronously with a timeout limit.

Raises EasyAsyncError if the function times out or raises an exception.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default func callable

The function to execute.

required timeout float

Maximum time to wait in seconds.

required *args

Positional arguments to pass to the function.

()

Returns:

Name Type Description tuple tuple

A tuple containing (func.__name__, result).

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
import asyncio
from py_simple import run_with_timeout

def slow_add(a, b):
    return a + b

async def main():
    return await run_with_timeout(slow_add, 2.0, 3, 5)

asyncio.run(main())  # -> ("slow_add", 8)

import asyncio

def slow_add(a, b):
    return a + b

async def main():
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    result = await asyncio.wait_for(
        loop.run_in_executor(None, slow_add, 3, 5),
        timeout=2.0,
    )
    return (slow_add.__name__, result)

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: hsl_to_rgb(h, s, lightness)
docs.text:
Converts an (H, S, L) color to an (R, G, B) integer tuple.

Hue is measured in degrees (0-360), while Saturation and Lightness are measured as percentages (0-100).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default h float

Hue in degrees (0 to 360).

required s float

Saturation as a percentage (0 to 100).

required lightness float

Lightness as a percentage (0 to 100).

required

Returns:

Type Description tuple[int, int, int]

tuple[int, int, int]: RGB values as (r, g, b) integers in range 0-255.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If hue is outside the 0-360 range or saturation/lightness are outside the 0-100 range.

TypeError

If any value is not an int or float.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
from py_simple import hsl_to_rgb

hsl_to_rgb(120, 100, 50)  # -> (0, 255, 0)
hsl_to_rgb(0, 0, 100)  # -> (255, 255, 255)

h, s, lightness = 120, 100, 50
s, lightness = s / 100, lightness / 100
chroma = (1 - abs(2 * lightness - 1)) * s
secondary = chroma * (1 - abs((h / 60) % 2 - 1))
match = lightness - chroma / 2
if h < 60:
    red, green, blue = chroma, secondary, 0
elif h < 120:
    red, green, blue = secondary, chroma, 0
elif h < 180:
    red, green, blue = 0, chroma, secondary
elif h < 240:
    red, green, blue = 0, secondary, chroma
elif h < 300:
    red, green, blue = secondary, 0, chroma
else:
    red, green, blue = chroma, 0, secondary
r = round((red + match) * 255)
g = round((green + match) * 255)

docs.title: is_light_color(hex_code, threshold=LUMINANCE_LIGHT_THRESHOLD)
docs.text:
Takes a hex color and returns whether it's "light" based on perceived luminance. Uses the sRGB relative luminance formula (ITU-R BT.709 weights). Threshold ~0.179 is commonly used for WCAG contrast calculations.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default hex_code str

Hex color string to convert (e.g., "#FFFFFF" or "fff").

required threshold float

Luminance threshold for "light" classification (default 0.179).

LUMINANCE_LIGHT_THRESHOLD

Returns:

Name Type Description bool bool

True if it's "light" based on perceived luminance.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If hex_code is not a valid hex color.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
from py_simple import is_light_color

is_light_color("#FFFFFF")  # -> True
is_light_color("#000000")  # -> False

hex_code = "#FFFFFF".lstrip("#")
if len(hex_code) == 3:
    hex_code = "".join(c * 2 for c in hex_code)
r, g, b = (int(hex_code[i:i + 2], 16) / 255 for i in (0, 2, 4))

def linearize(c):
    return c / 12.92 if c <= 0.03928 else ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4

luminance = sum(w * linearize(v)
                for w, v in zip((0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722), (r, g, b)))
is_light = luminance > 0.179  # -> True

docs.title: rgb_to_hsl(r, g, b)
docs.text:
Converts (R, G, B) color values to an (H, S, L) tuple.

Hue is measured in degrees (0-360), while Saturation and Lightness are measured as percentages (0-100).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default r int

Red channel value (0 to 255).

required g int

Green channel value (0 to 255).

required b int

Blue channel value (0 to 255).

required

Returns:

Type Description float

tuple[float, float, float]: HSL values as (h, s, l), where h is in

float

the 0-360 range and s/l are percentages in the 0-100 range.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If any channel is outside the 0-255 range.

TypeError

If any channel is not an integer.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
from py_simple import rgb_to_hsl

rgb_to_hsl(255, 0, 0)  # -> (0.0, 100.0, 50.0)
rgb_to_hsl(18, 52, 86)  # -> (210.0, 65.38, 20.39)

r, g, b = 18, 52, 86
r, g, b = r / 255, g / 255, b / 255
color_max, color_min = max(r, g, b), min(r, g, b)
delta = color_max - color_min
lightness = (color_max + color_min) / 2
if delta == 0:
    hue = saturation = 0
else:
    saturation = delta / (1 - abs(2 * lightness - 1))
    if color_max == r:
        hue = (60 * ((g - b) / delta)) % 360
    elif color_max == g:
        hue = 60 * ((b - r) / delta) + 120
    else:
        hue = 60 * ((r - g) / delta) + 240

docs.text:
Creates a .env.example file from an existing .env file.

Copies every key and drops the values, so the example documents which variables a project needs without leaking secrets. Comment lines and blank lines are kept as-is. If the example file already exists and overwrite is False, it is left alone.

Name Type Description Default file_path str

Path to the source .env file. Defaults to ".env".

'.env' example_path str

Destination path for the example file. Defaults to ".env.example".

'.env.example' overwrite bool

Whether to overwrite an existing example file. Defaults to False.

False

Returns:

Type Description None

None

Raises:

Type Description EasyConfigError

If the source file cannot be read or the example file cannot be written.

EasyConfigError

If the source and destination paths point to the same file, including symbolic links and hard links.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
from py_simple import create_env_example_file

create_env_example_file(".env")

with open(".env", encoding="utf-8") as source:
    lines = source.readlines()
with open(".env.example", "w", encoding="utf-8") as target:
    for line in lines:
        stripped = line.strip()
        if not stripped or stripped.startswith("#"):

        elif "=" in stripped:

docs.title: dockerfile_config(at_root=True)
docs.text:
Creates a starter Dockerfile for a Python project from a template.

The generated Dockerfile is a starting point, not a finished build. The template assumes the project has a requirements.txt and a main.py (COPY requirements.txt ., CMD ["python", "main.py"]), so expect to adjust it for your own entry point, dependency manager, base image and ignore rules before shipping.

The Dockerfile is written to 'Dockerfile'. If the file already exists, it is left alone. Any missing parent directories are created automatically.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default at_root bool

When True, the path is relative to the current working directory. When False, the git repository root is looked up and the Dockerfile is placed there. Defaults to True.

True

Returns:

Type Description None

None

Raises:

Type Description EasyConfigError

If the template cannot be read, the git repository cannot be found, or the file cannot be written.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
from py_simple import dockerfile_config

dockerfile_config()

template = """FROM python:3.12-slim

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

CMD ["python", "main.py"]
"""
with open("Dockerfile", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write(template)

docs.text:
Loads variables from a .env file directly into os.environ.

Reads key-value pairs from the specified file and sets them in the current process environment (os.environ). Ignores blank lines and comments. If override is False, variables that already exist in os.environ are not overwritten.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default file_path str

'.env' override bool

False

Type Description EasyConfigError

If the file cannot be read.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
import os
from py_simple import load_env_file

load_env_file(".env")
port = os.getenv("PORT")

import os

with open(".env", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        stripped = line.strip()

            stripped
            and not stripped.startswith("#")
            and "=" in stripped

            key, val = stripped.split("=", 1)
            key = key.strip()
            if key not in os.environ:

docs.title: merge_csv_files(filepaths, output_filepath, delimiter=',')
docs.text:
Combines CSV files with matching headers into one file in input order.

Reads UTF-8 files one record at a time and writes the header only once. Header names and their order must match exactly. Header-only files are accepted; empty files or files with a blank first record are rejected. Data records are copied without changing their field count or values.

Writes to a temporary file beside the output, then replaces the output only after all inputs succeed. Inputs and any existing output are left unchanged on failure. The output must not refer to an input, including through a symbolic or hard link. An unrelated output symlink is replaced itself, leaving its target unchanged. File metadata is not copied.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default filepaths list[str]

Non-empty list of input paths, in merge order.

required output_filepath str

Destination path; its parent must exist.

required delimiter str

Field delimiter for all files (default is comma).

','

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If there are no inputs, an input has no header, headers differ, or the output refers to an input.

OSError

If a file cannot be read, written or replaced.

UnicodeError

If an input cannot be decoded as UTF-8.

Error

If CSV parsing fails.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
from py_simple import merge_csv_files

merge_csv_files(["january.csv", "february.csv"], "combined.csv")

import csv
import os
import tempfile

inputs = ["january.csv", "february.csv"]
output = "combined.csv"
if not inputs:
    raise ValueError("At least one input is required")
for path in inputs:
    if os.path.realpath(path) == os.path.realpath(output) or (
        os.path.exists(output) and os.path.samefile(path, output)
    ):
        raise ValueError("Output must not be an input")

temporary_path = None
try:
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(
        "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8", delete=False,
        dir=os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(output))
    ) as temporary:
        temporary_path = temporary.name
        writer = csv.writer(temporary)
        header = None
        for path in inputs:
            with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as source:
                reader = csv.reader(source, strict=True)
                current = next(reader, None)
                if not current:
                    raise ValueError(f"File has no header: {path}")
                if header is None:
                    header = current
                    writer.writerow(header)
                elif current != header:
                    raise ValueError(f"Headers do not match: {path}")
                writer.writerows(reader)
    os.replace(temporary_path, output)
finally:
    if temporary_path is not None and os.path.exists(temporary_path):
        os.remove(temporary_path)

docs.title: retry(func, attempts=3, delay=1)
docs.text:
Calls a function, automatically retrying it if it raises an exception up to a specified number of attempts, with a pause between tries.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default func callable

The function to execute.

required attempts int

Maximum number of times to try running the function. Defaults to 3.

3 delay int or float

Time to wait in seconds between failed attempts. Defaults to 1.

1

Returns:

Name Type Description Any

The return value of func if it succeeds.

Raises:

Type Description Exception

The last exception raised by func if all attempts fail.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
from py_simple import retry

def flaky_api():
    # Might fail sometimes
    pass

result = retry(flaky_api, attempts=5, delay=2)

import time

def flaky_api():
    pass

attempts = 5
delay = 2
for i in range(attempts):
    try:
        result = flaky_api()
        break
    except Exception as e:
        if i == attempts - 1:
            raise e
        time.sleep(delay)

docs.title: generate_passphrase(words=4, separator='-')
docs.text:
Generates a random, easy-to-remember passphrase in one call, like
"Brave-river-Calm-lamp-47". It is the readable counterpart to
`generate_password`: words alternate between adjectives and nouns,
each one is randomly capitalized, and a 2-digit number is added at
the end, all picked with the `secrets` module.

For high-security needs, prefer `generate_password`, or ask for more
words: each extra word makes the passphrase stronger.

Args:
    words (int, optional): Number of words in the passphrase, not
        counting the number at the end. Defaults to `4`.
    separator (str, optional): The character placed between words.
        Defaults to `-`.

Returns:
    str: The generated passphrase (e.g., "Brave-river-Calm-lamp-47").

Raises:
    EasyGeneratorError: If `words` is less than 1.

Example:
    === "The Py_simple Way"

python from py_simple import generate_passphrase passphrase = generate_passphrase(separator="_")

    === "The Traditional Way"

python import secrets adjectives = ["brave", "calm", "bright", "quick"] nouns = ["river", "lamp", "cloud", "stone"] words = [] for i in range(4): word = secrets.choice(adjectives if i % 2 == 0 else nouns) if secrets.randbelow(2): word = word.capitalize() words.append(word) words.append(str(secrets.randbelow(90) + 10)) passphrase = "_".join(words)

docs.title: generate_password(pass_length=12, uppercase_chars=2, digit_chars=2, special_chars=2)
docs.text:
Generates a randomized password of a given length in one call, handling the character-pool selection, shuffling, and repeated-character checks every password generator needs, instead of writing that logic by hand each time.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default pass_length int

Total number of characters in the generated password. Defaults to 12.

12 uppercase_chars int

Number of uppercase letters to include. Defaults to 2.

2 digit_chars int

Number of digits to include. Defaults to 2.

2 special_chars int

Number of punctuation characters to include. Defaults to 2.

2

Returns:

Name Type Description str str

The generated password, made up of lowercase letters, uppercase letters, digits, and special characters shuffled together, with no two identical characters placed next to each other. The number of lowercase letters is calculated as pass_length - (uppercase_chars + digit_chars + special_chars).

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
from py_simple import generate_password

password = generate_password(16, uppercase_chars=3, digit_chars=3, special_chars=3)

import string
import random

length = 16
uppercase_chars = 3
digit_chars = 3
special_chars = 3
lowercase_chars = length - (uppercase_chars + digit_chars + special_chars)

chars = (
    [random.choice(string.ascii_lowercase) for _ in range(lowercase_chars)]
    + [random.choice(string.ascii_uppercase) for _ in range(uppercase_chars)]
    + [random.choice(string.digits) for _ in range(digit_chars)]
    + [random.choice(string.punctuation) for _ in range(special_chars)]
)
random.shuffle(chars)
password = ''.join(chars)

import hashlib

def get_checksum(filepath):
    hasher = hashlib.sha256()
    with open(filepath, "rb") as f:

            hasher.update(chunk)
    return hasher.hexdigest()

docs.title: hash_directory(dirpath, algorithm='sha256')
docs.text:
Create a single checksum for a whole directory tree.

Files are hashed in sorted order by their path relative to the directory, so the same tree always produces the same checksum no matter what order the files were created in. Each file contributes its relative path, a null separator, and the hex digest of its contents (fixed length for the chosen algorithm), so record boundaries are unambiguous and renaming a file or changing its contents changes the checksum.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default dirpath str | Path

Path to the directory.

required algorithm str

One of "sha256", "sha1", or "md5". Defaults to "sha256".

'sha256'

Returns:

Name Type Description str str

The checksum as lowercase hex.

Raises:

Type Description EasyHashError

If dirpath is not a directory, a directory cannot be scanned, a file cannot be read, or the algorithm is not supported.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
from py_simple import hash_directory

digest = hash_directory("project")
print(digest)

import hashlib
from pathlib import Path

hasher = hashlib.sha256()
root = Path("project")
for path in sorted((p for p in root.rglob("*") if p.is_file()), key=lambda p: p.relative_to(root).as_posix()):
    hasher.update(path.relative_to(root).as_posix().encode("utf-8"))
    hasher.update(b"\0")
    hasher.update(hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest().encode("ascii"))
digest = hasher.hexdigest()

docs.title: verify_file_hash(filepath, expected, algorithm='sha256')
docs.text:
Checks whether a file matches an expected checksum using chunked reads.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default filepath str | Path

Path to the file to check.

required expected str

Expected hex checksum, ignoring letter case. Whitespace is not stripped.

required algorithm str

One of "sha256", "sha1", or "md5". Defaults to "sha256".

'sha256'

Returns:

Name Type Description bool bool

True when the file's checksum equals expected. A mismatch, malformed checksum, or non-string expected returns False. Non-string checksums are rejected before reading the file or checking the algorithm, as with hashes_match().

Raises:

Type Description EasyHashError

If the file cannot be read or the algorithm is not supported.

TypeError

If filepath is not a string or path-like object.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
from pathlib import Path
from py_simple import verify_file_hash

Path("notes.txt").write_bytes(b"hello")
expected = "2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824"
matches = verify_file_hash("notes.txt", expected)
print(matches)  # True

import hashlib
from pathlib import Path

Path("notes.txt").write_bytes(b"hello")
expected = "2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824"
hasher = hashlib.sha256()
with open("notes.txt", "rb") as file:
    while chunk := file.read(64 * 1024):
        hasher.update(chunk)
matches = hasher.hexdigest() == expected.lower()
print(matches)  # True

docs.title: convert_to_greyscale(input_path, output_path)
docs.text:
Convert an image to grayscale and save it.

Each pixel becomes a brightness value from 0 (black) to 255 (white), giving 256 possible shades of gray. Pillow calls this 8-bit grayscale. Mode L stores the gray value; mode LA also stores opacity. Outputs ending in .jpg, .jpeg or .bmp use L because Pillow's JPEG/BMP encoders cannot save LA and would raise OSError. Other extensions use LA. The original dimensions are kept.

PNG, TIFF and WebP output retain transparency. JPEG, BMP and GIF output discard it without blending a background. Only the first frame of animated or multi-frame images is converted.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default input_path str | PathLike[str]

Path of the source image.

required output_path str | PathLike[str]

Path to save the grayscale image to. The file extension determines the output format.

required

Raises:

Type Description ImageProcessingError

OSError

ValueError

If the output file extension is not recognized.

    img.convert("LA").save("photo_gray.png")

docs.title: compare_json(data1=None, data2=None, filepath1=None, filepath2=None, path='')
docs.text:
Compares two JSON objects or files and returns a dictionary describing the differences: added keys, removed keys, and changed values. Supports comparison of both dictionaries and lists. Nested structures are traversed recursively.

Provide exactly one of data arguments or filepath arguments — not both for each side.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data1 dict | list

First JSON object to compare.

None data2 dict | list

Second JSON object to compare.

None filepath1 str

Path to the first JSON file.

None filepath2 str

Path to the second JSON file.

None path str

Internal use only — the current dot-notation path during recursion.

''

Returns:

Name Type Description dict dict

A dictionary with three keys: - added: dict of keys present in data2 but not in data1. - removed: dict of keys present in data1 but not in data2. - changed: dict of keys whose values differ between the two objects. All nested differences use dot-notation keys (e.g. user.address.city).

Raises:

Type Description EasyJsonError

If neither or both of data/filepath are provided for either side, or if the JSON data is not a dict or list.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
from py_simple import compare_json

diff = compare_json(
    data1={"name": "Sara", "age": 25},
    data2={"name": "Sara", "age": 26, "city": "NYC"}
)
print(diff)
# {"added": {"city": "NYC"}, "removed": {}, "changed": {"age": (25, 26)}}

def compare_dicts(d1, d2, path=""):
    result = {"added": {}, "removed": {}, "changed": {}}
    all_keys = set(d1.keys()) | set(d2.keys())
    for key in all_keys:
        current_path = f"{path}.{key}" if path else key
        if key not in d2:
            result["removed"][current_path] = d1[key]
        elif key not in d1:
            result["added"][current_path] = d2[key]
        elif d1[key] != d2[key]:
            result["changed"][current_path] = (d1[key], d2[key])
    return result

docs.title: log_function(message_template)
docs.text:
Creates a decorator that logs each call to a synchronous function and method.

Formats the message using the function's argument names and values, including default values for omitted arguments. Excludes self and cls from the formatting context. Uses log_step to log the start, successful completion, or exception with a traceback through the root logger. Preserves the function's metadata and return value.

Argument binding and message formatting happen before logging starts; errors in those steps propagate without being logged by this helper. For async functions or generators, this decorator only logs creation of the coroutine or generator, not its later execution.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default message_template str

Message with named str.format_map fields matching function parameters, such as "Add {a} and {b}". Format specifications such as "{price:.2f}" are supported.

required

Returns:

Type Description Callable[[Callable[P, R]], Callable[P, R]]

Callable[[Callable[P, R]], Callable[P, R]]: Decorator that wraps a function with logging while preserving its parameters and return type.

Raises:

Type Description KeyError

A message field is missing from the formatting context.

ValueError

The message template or a format specification is invalid.

TypeError

The supplied arguments cannot be bound to the wrapped function's signature.

Exception

Re-raises any Exception from the wrapped function after logging it.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
import logging
from py_simple.easy_logging import log_function

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

@log_function("Add {a} and {b}")
def add(a: int, b: int = 10) -> int:
    return a + b

print(add(5))  # -> 15; logs "Add 5 and 10"

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

def add(a: int, b: int = 10) -> int:
    message = f"Add {a} and {b}"
    try:
        logging.info(f"Starting: {message}")
        result = a + b
    except Exception:
        logging.exception(f"Error during: {message}")
        raise
    else:
        logging.info(f"Finished: {message}")
        return result

print(add(5))  # -> 15; logs "Add 5 and 10"

docs.title: log_step(message)
docs.text:
Logs the start, successful completion, or failure of a code block.

Writes "Starting:" and "Finished:" messages at INFO level. If the block raises an Exception, logs "Error during:" at ERROR level with the traceback and re-raises the original exception instead of logging a successful completion. Uses the root logger and its configuration.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default message str

Description of the operation, such as "Calculate total".

required

Yields:

Name Type Description None None

Runs the enclosed code block without providing an object for an optional as target.

Raises:

Type Description Exception

Re-raises any Exception raised by the enclosed block after logging it.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
import logging
from py_simple.easy_logging import log_step

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

with log_step("Calculate total"):
    total = sum([10, 20, 30])

print(total)  # -> 60

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

try:
    logging.info("Starting: Calculate total")
    total = sum([10, 20, 30])
except Exception:
    logging.exception("Error during: Calculate total")
    raise
else:
    logging.info("Finished: Calculate total")

print(total)  # -> 60

docs.title: setup_file_logger(log_file, level=logging.INFO, format_string='%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s', name=None)
docs.text:
Sets up and returns a logger configured to write to a file.

Creates parent directories for the log file if they do not exist. Adds a logging.FileHandler formatted with format_string at the specified logging level. If a handler for the same file path is already attached to the logger, duplicate handlers are not added.

Calling this again for the same logger and file updates both the handler level and format without adding another handler.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default log_file str

Path to the log file to write to.

required level int or str

Logging level such as logging.INFO, logging.DEBUG, or string equivalents like "INFO". Defaults to logging.INFO.

INFO format_string str

Message format for the log handler. Defaults to "%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s".

'%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s' name str

Name of the logger to configure. Defaults to None, which uses log_file as the logger name.

None

Returns:

Type Description Logger

logging.Logger: The configured logger instance.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
from py_simple import setup_file_logger

logger = setup_file_logger("app.log")
logger.info("Application started")

import logging

logger = logging.getLogger("app.log")
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)
handler = logging.FileHandler("app.log", encoding="utf-8")
handler.setLevel(logging.INFO)
formatter = logging.Formatter(
    "%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s"
)
handler.setFormatter(formatter)
logger.addHandler(handler)
logger.info("Application started")

docs.title: temporary_log_level(logger, level)
docs.text:
Changes a logger's level for a block and restores its previous level.

Restores the exact explicit level, including NOTSET, even if the block raises. Nested blocks restore the level that was active on entry. Handler levels/filters, logger filters, propagation and global logging settings still apply and are not changed. A shared logger's temporary level is visible to other users of that logger; this is not thread-local.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default logger Logger

Logger to adjust, normally obtained with logging.getLogger(). Its explicit level will change.

required level int | str

Integer logging level or a registered level name, such as logging.DEBUG or "debug". String names are uppercased, matching setup_file_logger. Integers follow Logger.setLevel.

required

Yields:

Name Type Description None None

Runs the block without providing an as target value.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

If logger is not a logging.Logger or level is neither an integer nor a string accepted by logging.

ValueError

If a string does not name a registered logging level.

BaseException

Propagates any exception from the enclosed block after restoring the previous level.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
import logging
from py_simple.easy_logging import temporary_log_level

logger = logging.getLogger("example")
logger.setLevel(logging.WARNING)
with temporary_log_level(logger, "debug"):
    print(logger.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG))  # True
print(logger.level == logging.WARNING)  # True

import logging

logger = logging.getLogger("example")
logger.setLevel(logging.WARNING)
previous_level = logger.level
logger.setLevel("DEBUG")
try:
    print(logger.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG))  # True
finally:
    logger.setLevel(previous_level)
print(logger.level == logging.WARNING)  # True

docs.title: collatz_sequence(n)
docs.text:
Returns the Collatz conjecture sequence for a given positive integer.

The sequence starts with n. If n is even, the next number is n / 2. If n is odd, the next number is 3 * n + 1. This repeats until n reaches 1.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n int

Positive integer to start the sequence.

required

Returns:

Type Description list[int]

list[int]: The Collatz sequence ending in 1.

Type Description ValueError

n = 6

    n = n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else 3 * n + 1
    sequence.append(n)

docs.title: split_bill_exact(total, people)
docs.text:
Splits a bill into cent-precise shares that preserve the rounded total.

Rounds the full bill once using ROUND_HALF_UP, then gives leftover cents to the first shares. Shares differ by at most one cent. Refunds use the same allocation with negative shares; zero shares are 0.00. Existing split_bill still returns one independently rounded share.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default total int | float | str | Decimal

Finite amount. Floats are converted through their string representation.

required people int

Number of shares. Must be at least 1; booleans and non-integers are not accepted.

required

Returns:

Type Description list[Decimal]

list[Decimal]: Exactly people shares with two decimal places. For example, 10 split three ways gives 3.34, 3.33 and 3.33.

Raises:

Type Description EasyMoneyError

If the amount/count is invalid or rounding cannot be completed in the current Decimal context.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
from py_simple import split_bill_exact

shares = split_bill_exact("10.00", 3)
print(shares)  # [Decimal('3.34'), Decimal('3.33'), Decimal('3.33')]
print(sum(shares))  # 10.00

from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

total, people = Decimal("10.00"), 3
rounded = total.quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)
numerator, denominator = rounded.as_integer_ratio()
cents = abs(numerator) * 100 // denominator
base, remainder = divmod(cents, people)
sign = -1 if rounded < 0 else 1
shares = []
for i in range(people):
    cent_share = Decimal(sign * (base + (i < remainder)))
    parts = cent_share.as_tuple()
    shares.append(Decimal((parts.sign, parts.digits, -2)))
print(shares)  # [Decimal('3.34'), Decimal('3.33'), Decimal('3.33')]
print(sum(shares))  # 10.00

Returns true if the number is prime and false if it is not.

Uses an integer square root to avoid floating-point overflow or rounding when finding the trial-division limit. Trial division can still be slow for large primes or numbers with large prime factors.

docs.text:
Returns a list of US/Canadian-style phone numbers found in the text.

Supports standard North American Numbering Plan (NANP) formats including optional country code (+1 or 1), parentheses around the area code, and separators such as hyphens, dots, or spaces. This function is tailored for US and Canadian phone numbers rather than general international formats.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default text str

Type Description list[str]

    r"(?<!\w)(?<!\d[-.\s])"
    r"(?:(?:\+?1[\s.-]?)?\(\d{3}\)[\s.-]?\d{3}[\s.-]?\d{4}"
    r"|(?<!\()(?:\+?1[\s.-]?)?(?<!\()\d{3}[\s.-]?\d{3}[\s.-]?\d{4})"
    r"(?!\w)(?![-.\s]?\d)"
)

from py_simple import extract_urls

result = extract_urls("Visit https://www.example.com or www.test.org today")
# -> ['https://www.example.com', 'www.test.org']

import re

pattern = (
    r'(?:https?://(?:www\.)?|www\.)[a-zA-Z0-9-]+\.'
    r'(?:(?:[a-zA-Z0-9-]+\.)*)?(?:(?:[a-zA-Z0-9-]+\\)*)?'
    r'[a-zA-Z]{2,}(?:\.[a-zA-Z]{2,})?(?:/\S*)?'
)
result = re.findall(pattern, "Visit https://www.example.com or www.test.org today")
# -> ['https://www.example.com', 'www.test.org']

Checks whether a table exists in the SQLite database.

The table_name is validated before being used in the query because SQLite does not support parameterized table names. The validation ensures that only letters, numbers, and underscores are allowed, preventing invalid input from being interpolated into the query.

required

docs.title: correlation_coefficient(x, y)
docs.text:
Returns Pearson's correlation coefficient for two lists of paired numbers.

Uses Python's statistics module, with input checks and readable errors.

Values at the same position must describe the same observation. For example, x[0] and y[0] could be one student's study hours and test score. Do not sort the lists independently, as this would change the pairs.

A positive result means the values tend to increase together; a negative result means one tends to decrease as the other increases. A result near zero means little linear association, not necessarily no relationship. Correlation does not show that one variable causes changes in the other.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default x list[float]

First list of finite numbers (integers or floats).

required y list[float]

Second list of finite numbers, in matching order. Both lists must have the same length and at least two values. Neither list can contain only one repeated value.

required

Returns:

Name Type Description float float

Pearson's r, from -1.0 to 1.0, without rounding. Values of -1.0 and 1.0 indicate perfect negative and positive linear relationships, respectively.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

If either list contains a value that is not a number.

ValueError

If the lengths differ, there are fewer than two pairs, a value is NaN or infinite, or either list is constant.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
from py_simple import correlation_coefficient

study_hours = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
test_scores = [60, 65, 75, 70, 80]
result = correlation_coefficient(study_hours, test_scores)
print(round(result, 2))  # -> 0.9

from statistics import correlation

study_hours = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
test_scores = [60, 65, 75, 70, 80]
result = correlation(study_hours, test_scores)
print(round(result, 2))  # -> 0.9

docs.title: interquartile_range(nums)
docs.text:
Returns the spread of the middle 50% of a list of numbers.

This is the difference between the 75th percentile (Q3) and the
25th percentile (Q1). Unlike variance or standard deviation, it
isn't affected by extreme outliers.

Args:
    nums (list[float]): List of numbers.

Returns:
    float: The difference between the 75th and 25th percentiles.

Raises:
    ValueError: If the list is empty.

Example:
    === "The Py_simple Way"

python from py_simple import interquartile_range result = interquartile_range([1, 2, 3, 4]) # -> 2

    === "The Traditional Way"

python import math nums = [1, 2, 3, 4] ordered = sorted(nums) def _percentile(ordered, percent): position = math.ceil(len(ordered) * percent / 100) return ordered[max(0, position - 1)] result = _percentile(ordered, 75) - _percentile(ordered, 25)

Returns how spread out the numbers are, as sample variance.

docs.title: z_score(nums, value)
docs.text:
Returns how many standard deviations a value is from the average.

A positive result means the value is above average, negative means
below average.

Args:
    nums (list[float]): List of numbers used to calculate the average
        and spread.
    value (float): The number to measure against the list.

Returns:

Raises:
    ValueError: If the list has fewer than two numbers.

Example:
    === "The Py_simple Way"

python from py_simple import z_score result = z_score([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 5) # -> 1.26

    === "The Traditional Way"

python from statistics import mean, stdev nums, value = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 5 result = round((value - mean(nums)) / stdev(nums), 2)

docs.title: EasyTerminal
docs.text:
Builds styled terminal text by chaining style methods, then prints it.

Nothing is printed until show() is called, so you can chain as many styles as you like first. Every set_* method returns the object itself, which is what makes the chaining work.

Parameters:

The text to print.

required Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
from py_simple import EasyTerminal

EasyTerminal("Hello World").set_color("red").set_bold().show()

from rich.console import Console

console = Console()
console.print("Hello World", style="bold red")

docs.title: add_query_param(url, key, value)
docs.text:
Add or replace one query parameter on a link.

Replaces all occurrences of the selected key with one value at its first position, or appends it if absent. Other parameters retain their order, repeated values, and blank values.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default url str

A full link.

required key str

Parameter name, such as "page".

required value str

Parameter value, such as "2".

required

Returns:

Name Type Description str str

The link with that parameter set.

Raises:

Type Description EasyUrlError

If url is not a full link, or if key or value is not a string.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
from py_simple import add_query_param

print(add_query_param("https://school.example/clubs", "page", "2"))

from urllib.parse import parse_qsl, urlencode, urlparse, urlunparse

parsed = urlparse("https://school.example/clubs")
pairs = parse_qsl(parsed.query, keep_blank_values=True)
query = []
replaced = False
for key, value in pairs:
    if key == "page":
        if not replaced:
            query.append(("page", "2"))
            replaced = True
    else:
        query.append((key, value))
if not replaced:
    query.append(("page", "2"))
print(urlunparse(parsed._replace(query=urlencode(query))))

docs.title: is_password_secure(password)
docs.text:
Returns true if password is valid.

Validation checks
  • minimum length of 8 characters
  • at least one special character
  • at least one upper case letter
  • at least two lowercase letters
  • at least two digits
  • no repeating characters

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default password str

password to validate.

required

Returns:

Name Type Description bool bool

True if the password meets all checks, False otherwise.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
from py_simple import is_password_secure

result = is_password_secure("1andkrf!AG5")  # -> True

from string import punctuation

password = "1andkrf!AG5"
min_length = 8
upper_letters = 0
lower_letters = 0
digits = 0
special_characters = 0
last_char = ''
result = False

if len(password) > min_length:
    for char in password:
        if char.isdigit():
            digits += 1
            if char == last_char:
                result = False
                break
            last_char = char
        elif char.isalpha():
            if char.upper() == char:
                upper_letters += 1
                if char == last_char:
                    result = False
                    break
                last_char = char
            elif char.lower() == char:
                lower_letters += 1
                if char == last_char:
                    result = False
                    break
                last_char = char
        elif char in punctuation:
            special_characters += 1
            if char == last_char:
                result = False
                break
            last_char = char
    else:
        result = (
            upper_letters >= 1 and lower_letters >= 2 and
            digits >= 2 and special_characters >= 1
        )

docs.title: is_valid_creditcard(card_num)
docs.text:
Returns true if the credit card number is valid according to the Luhn algorithm. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luhn_algorithm)

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default card_num str

The credit card number. Valid strings are 13 to 19 digits long, with optional dashes or spaces.

required

Returns:

Name Type Description bool

True if the credit card number is valid, False otherwise.

Example The Py_simple WayThe Traditional Way 
from py_simple import is_valid_creditcard

result = is_valid_creditcard("4242-4242-4242-4242")  # -> True

import re

card_num = card_num.replace("-", "").replace(" ", "")
pattern = r"[0-9]{13,19}"

if not re.fullmatch(pattern, card_num):
    return False

digits = [int(digit) for digit in card_num]
reversed_digits = reversed(digits)

sum = 0
for index, digit in enumerate(reversed_digits):
    if index % 2 == 0:
        # every other digit, starting with the last
        sum += digit
    else:
        doubled = 2 * digit
        sum += doubled if doubled < 10 else doubled - 9

return sum % 10 == 0

from py_simple import count_links

print(count_links("https://github.com")) #-> 144

import requests
try:
    response = requests.get(url, timeout=10)
    soup = BeautifulSoup(response.content, 'html.parser')
    link_count = 0
    if response is not None:

docs.title: Build an Arcade Leaderboard with Easy SQL and Easy Text
docs.text: Combine Easy SQL and Easy Text to store player scores in an in-memory database, format gamer tags and shoutouts, and filter tournament qualifiers.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Arcade games and competitive leagues need clean leaderboards to showcase player achievements. This example runs entirely in memory using SQLite's :memory: mode, so you can test database queries and text formatting without creating temporary files or leaving databases on disk.

Install the package:

python -m pip install py-simple-wrap

Save this as arcade_leaderboard.py:

from py_simple import (
    capitalize_title,
    conditional_run_select,
    open_db,
    pluralize,
    run_insert,
    run_select,
    truncate,
)

# 1. Connect to a temporary in-memory database and set up the table
connection, cursor = open_db(":memory:")
cursor.execute("CREATE TABLE leaderboard (player TEXT, score INTEGER, shoutout TEXT)")

# 2. Raw player submissions with unformatted names and long victory messages
submissions = [
    ("pixel knight", 9800, "GG everyone! Catch me on the next stream."),
    ("shadow ninja", 18200, "Unstoppable combo! New personal record achieved today."),
    ("star voyager", 14500, "GG!"),
    ("speed runner", 7200, "Almost had the gold split!"),
]

# 3. Clean player details and save each score to the database
for raw_name, score, shout in submissions:
    player_name = capitalize_title(raw_name)
    shoutout = truncate(shout, 24)
    run_insert(
        connection,
        cursor,
        [player_name, score, shoutout],
        "leaderboard",
        ["player", "score", "shoutout"],
    )

# 4. Retrieve all scores and display the full arcade rankings
print("--- Arcade Leaderboard ---")
all_records = run_select(connection, cursor, "leaderboard", "player, score, shoutout")
for player, score, shout in sorted(all_records, key=lambda row: row[1], reverse=True):
    print(f'{player} - {score:,} pts | "{shout}"')

# 5. Query players who scored at least 10,000 points to qualify for the tournament
qualifiers = conditional_run_select(
    connection, cursor, "leaderboard", "player, score, shoutout", "score >= ?", (10000,)
)
count = len(qualifiers)
print(f"\nTournament qualifiers: {count} {pluralize('player', count)}")
for player, score, _ in sorted(qualifiers, key=lambda row: row[1], reverse=True):
    print(f"  Qualified: {player} ({score:,} pts)")

Run the script from your terminal:

python arcade_leaderboard.py

Example output:

--- Arcade Leaderboard ---
Shadow Ninja - 18,200 pts | "Unstoppable combo! New p…"
Star Voyager - 14,500 pts | "GG!"
Pixel Knight - 9,800 pts | "GG everyone! Catch me on…"
Speed Runner - 7,200 pts | "Almost had the gold spli…"

Tournament qualifiers: 2 players
  Qualified: Shadow Ninja (18,200 pts)
  Qualified: Star Voyager (14,500 pts)

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
open_db() establishes a connection to a lightweight SQLite database and returns both the connection and execution cursor. Passing ":memory:" builds the database inside RAM, leaving zero residual files when the script ends.

capitalize_title() converts lowercase player handles (such as "pixel knight") into proper title case ("Pixel Knight").

truncate() caps long victory messages to 24 characters and appends an ellipsis (…) so descriptions display cleanly within leaderboard columns.

run_insert() safely commits each cleaned record into the leaderboard table using parameterized inputs that defend against SQL injection.

run_select() queries all rows from the specified table and columns, returning the stored leaderboard records as a list of tuples.

conditional_run_select() filters the table with a parameterized SQL WHERE clause (score >= ?), cleanly returning only the players who achieved 10,000 points or more.

pluralize() checks the count of qualified players and selects the grammatically correct word ("player" for 1, "players" for any other count).

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
• Change the score threshold: Adjust the condition parameter in conditional_run_select() from 10000 to 15000 to see only top grandmasters qualify (1 player).
  • Update a player score: Use run_update(connection, cursor, "leaderboard", {"score": 20000}, "player = ?", ("Pixel Knight",)) to simulate a player beating their previous high score.
  • Wipe the board: Call delete_all_from_table(connection, cursor, "leaderboard") to reset the arcade cabinet between seasons.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Without py-simple-wrap, managing databases and text formatting in standard Python requires writing substantial boilerplate: - Writing manual sqlite3 setup code, creating cursors, and remembering to call connection.commit() after every query. - Manually writing parameterized SQL queries with string concatenation while carefully checking for injection vulnerabilities. - Writing custom text truncation loops with slices and conditional checks (len(s) > limit) and conditional pluralization logic ("player" if count == 1 else "players").

Combining easy_sql and easy_text replaces database plumbing and string handling with intuitive, readable single-line helpers.

For more examples and detailed function references, see Easy SQL and Easy Text.

docs.title: Build a Backup Checker with Easy Archive and Easy Hash
docs.text: Combine Easy Archive and Easy Hash to zip a note, restore it, and check whether the restored contents match the original. This is a small practice version of checking that a backup can actually be read back.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine saving your game ideas before editing them. This example creates its own temporary folder, so you can run it repeatedly without replacing your real notes. The folder and its files are removed when the example ends.

Install the package with python -m pip install py-simple-wrap, then run:

from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

from py_simple import extract_file_from_zip, hash_file, verify_file_hash, zip_files

with TemporaryDirectory() as workspace:
    folder = Path(workspace)
    note = folder / "ideas.txt"
    note.write_text("Build a moon garden game.\n", encoding="utf-8")
    original_checksum = hash_file(str(note))

    archive = zip_files([str(note)], str(folder / "ideas.zip"))
    restored = extract_file_from_zip(archive, "ideas.txt", str(folder / "restored"))

    print("Restored note matches:", verify_file_hash(restored, original_checksum))

    Path(restored).write_text("Build an underwater garden game.\n", encoding="utf-8")
    print("Edited note matches:", verify_file_hash(restored, original_checksum))

Example output:

Restored note matches: True
Edited note matches: False

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
hash_file() records a SHA-256 checksum of the original file's bytes. Keep this value from before editing: calculating a new checksum after changing the file would give you a different baseline.

zip_files() puts the note into a ZIP archive. With this single input, the archive member is named ideas.txt, without its temporary parent path. extract_file_from_zip() restores that member into a separate directory and returns the restored file's path. We extract only the archive we just created in this example.

verify_file_hash() compares the restored file with the saved checksum. The first check succeeds. After we change the restored note, the second check fails. A missing or unreadable file raises EasyHashError rather than returning False; False means the checksum did not match.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text: Add another note to the list passed to zip_files(). Record its checksum, restore it by its own filename, and check that one too. Keep filenames distinct so each archive member is easy to identify.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text: The standard-library version needs ZIP member handling and checksum calculation code. These helpers let you focus on the useful sequence: save a baseline, archive, restore, and compare. For more examples, see Easy Archive and Easy Hash.

docs.title: BookQuest: Build a Monthly Reading Tracker
docs.text:
In this tutorial, you'll build BookQuest, a simple Python application that helps you maintain a reading list, set a monthly reading goal, and review your reading progress over time.

You'll combine several py_simple modules:

  • Easy JSON to save your books and monthly goal.
  • Easy Date Formatter to display today's date.
  • Easy Stats to analyze your monthly reading activity.
  • Easy Data Visualization to visualize books completed per month.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
BookQuest lets you add books, record their start and finish dates, set a monthly target, and view a summary of your reading habits.

A book counts as completed in the month its finish date is recorded. A book still in progress is not counted as completed.

docs.title: Step 1: Import the helpers
docs.text:
Create a Python file named bookquest.py and import the required helpers:

from datetime import date

from py_simple import (
    save_json_data,
    open_json,
    update_json,
    is_json_file,
    get_pretty_date,
    plot_bar_chart,
    plot_line_chart,
    median,
    standard_deviation,
    data_range,
)

Python's built-in date class records the start and finish dates. The py_simple helpers handle JSON storage, readable dates, statistics, and chart creation.

docs.title: Step 2: Store your reading data
docs.text:
We need to remember the reading list and monthly goal between program runs.

DATA_FILE = "books.json"


def load_data():
    """Load the reading tracker or create a new one."""
    if is_json_file(DATA_FILE):
        data = open_json(DATA_FILE)
        data.setdefault("monthly_goal", 4)
        data.setdefault("books", [])
        return data

    data = {
        "monthly_goal": 4,
        "books": [],
    }
    save_json_data(DATA_FILE, data)
    return data


def save_data(data):
    """Save the latest reading tracker data."""
    if is_json_file(DATA_FILE):
        update_json(DATA_FILE, data)
    else:
        save_json_data(DATA_FILE, data)

load_data() opens the existing JSON file or creates a new reading tracker. save_data() persists changes to the file.

docs.title: Step 3: Add a book
docs.text:
Each book has a title, an optional author, a start date, a finish date, and a status.

def add_book(data):
    """Add a book to the reading shelf."""
    title = input("Enter book title: ").strip()

    if not title:
        print("Book title cannot be empty.")
        return

    author = input("Enter author (optional): ").strip()

    book = {
        "title": title,
        "author": author,
        "start_date": date.today().isoformat(),
        "finish_date": None,
        "status": "reading",
    }

    data["books"].append(book)
    save_data(data)
    print(f"'{title}' added to your reading shelf!")

The start date is recorded when the book is added. Its finish date remains None until you complete it.

docs.title: Step 4: Complete a book
docs.text:
When you finish reading, record the finish date and update the status. In the full application, select a book from the list of books currently in progress first.

book["finish_date"] = date.today().isoformat()
book["status"] = "completed"
save_data(data)

The finish date is stored in ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD), which makes it easy to group completed books by month.

docs.title: Step 5: Set a monthly goal
docs.text:
BookQuest starts with a goal of four books per month. You can change the goal and save it:

try:
    goal = int(input("Enter your monthly book target: "))

    if goal >= 1:
        data["monthly_goal"] = goal
        save_data(data)
    else:
        print("Your goal must be at least one book.")

except ValueError:
    print("Please enter a whole number.")

The goal must be a positive whole number. Invalid input is handled without crashing the application.

docs.title: Step 6: Count books completed each month
docs.text:
We can use the first seven characters of a finish date, such as 2026-10, as a month key.

def get_monthly_totals(data):
    """Count books in the month they were finished."""
    totals = {}

    for book in data["books"]:
        finish_date = book.get("finish_date")

        if finish_date:
            month = finish_date[:7]
            totals[month] = totals.get(month, 0) + 1

    return totals

This function returns a dictionary containing the number of completed books per month. Books without a finish date are excluded.

For example, if two books were completed in October 2026 and one in September 2026, the result would be:

{
    "2026-10": 2,
    "2026-09": 1,
}

docs.title: Step 7: Generate consecutive month labels
docs.text:
If no books were completed in a particular month, that month should still appear in the reading history with a count of zero.

def get_month_labels(start_month, end_month):
    """Create consecutive month labels, including months with zero books."""
    labels = []
    year, month = map(int, start_month.split("-"))
    end_year, end_month_number = map(int, end_month.split("-"))

    while (year, month) <= (end_year, end_month_number):
        labels.append(f"{year}-{month:02d}")

        month += 1
        if month > 12:
            month = 1
            year += 1

    return labels

For example:

months = get_month_labels("2026-08", "2026-11")
print(months)

Output:

['2026-08', '2026-09', '2026-10', '2026-11']

This helper also handles year boundaries, such as December to January.

docs.title: Step 8: Display reading statistics
docs.text:
Easy Stats provides helpers for summarizing the monthly totals.

First, calculate the monthly totals, generate the month labels, and create a corresponding count for each month:

totals = get_monthly_totals(data)

if totals:
    first_month = min(totals)
    current_month = date.today().strftime("%Y-%m")

    months = get_month_labels(first_month, current_month)
    counts = [totals.get(month, 0) for month in months]

    print("Median monthly total:", median(counts))
    print("Highest monthly total:", max(counts))
    print("Lowest monthly total:", min(counts))
    print("Monthly total range:", data_range(counts))

    if len(counts) >= 2:
        print("Standard deviation:", standard_deviation(counts))
    else:
        print("Standard deviation requires at least two months.")
else:
    print("Finish your first book to start your monthly history.")

Here:

  • months contains consecutive month labels.
  • counts contains the number of books completed in each month, including months with zero completions.
  • median() returns the middle value of the monthly totals.
  • data_range() returns the difference between the highest and lowest totals.
  • standard_deviation() measures how spread out the totals are.

The if totals: condition ensures that the statistics are calculated only when at least one book has been completed.

docs.title: Step 9: Display a friendly date
docs.text:
Use Easy Date Formatter to show today's date in a readable format:

print("Reading summary for", get_pretty_date())

The start and finish dates remain in ISO format so they can be grouped by month.

docs.title: Step 10: Visualize monthly reading activity
docs.text:
Once the monthly totals have been calculated, use plot_bar_chart() and plot_line_chart() from py_simple to visualize the results.

The variables months and counts were defined in Step 8. The following examples assume that at least one book has been completed and that those variables are available.

First, convert the month labels into a more readable format:

display_months = [
    date(int(month[:4]), int(month[5:7]), 1).strftime("%b %Y")
    for month in months
]

For example, "2026-10" becomes "Oct 2026".

docs.title: Create a bar chart
docs.text:
Use plot_bar_chart() to compare the number of books completed each month:

plot_bar_chart(
    display_months,
    counts,
    title="Books Completed per Month",
    x_label="Month",
    y_label="Books Completed",
)

The bars make it easy to compare reading activity across months.

docs.title: Create a line chart
docs.text:
Use plot_line_chart() to visualize changes in your reading activity over time:

plot_line_chart(
    display_months,
    counts,
    title="Monthly Reading Trend",
    x_label="Month",
    y_label="Books Completed",
)

The line chart helps you observe increases, decreases, and months with no completed books.

Both functions use the same month labels and counts, but display the information in different ways.

docs.title: Test your project
docs.text:
1. Add two books.
  2. View your reading shelf.
  3. Mark one book as completed.
  4. Change your monthly goal.
  5. Open the reading summary.
  6. Check the monthly totals and charts.
  7. Exit and run the application again.
  8. Confirm that the books and goal are still saved.

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text: You combined JSON storage, date formatting, statistics, and visualization to create a small reading tracker. Each helper handles a common task, leaving the application code to focus on managing books and displaying progress.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text: Without py_simple, you would need to write more of the file handling, date formatting, statistical calculations, and plotting setup yourself. These helpers make the project easier to read and provide a practical example of multiple modules working together.

docs.title: Build a Class Link Shelf with Easy URL and Easy CSV
docs.text: Combine Easy URL and Easy CSV to keep a clean list of class links. Tracking parameters are removed before the links are saved, so the file stays readable.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
A classmate drops two resource links in chat. Each one has a utm_source tag from the messaging app. This example writes a temporary CSV shelf, so you can run it repeatedly without touching a real file. The folder is removed when the example ends.

Install the package with python -m pip install py-simple-wrap, then run:

from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

from py_simple import get_domain, read_csv_to_list, remove_query_param, write_csv_from_list

raw_links = [
    "https://school.example/science?utm_source=chat&week=3",
    "https://library.example/math?utm_source=chat&week=3",
]

with TemporaryDirectory() as workspace:
    cleaned = []
    for link in raw_links:
        without_tracker = remove_query_param(link, "utm_source")
        cleaned.append(
            {
                "site": get_domain(without_tracker),
                "link": without_tracker,
            }
        )

    shelf = str(Path(workspace) / "class_links.csv")
    write_csv_from_list(shelf, cleaned)

    for row in read_csv_to_list(shelf):
        print(row["site"], row["link"])

Example output:

school.example https://school.example/science?week=3
library.example https://library.example/math?week=3

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
remove_query_param() drops the utm_source tag and leaves week=3. A missing tag would leave the link unchanged.

get_domain() pulls the host name, such as school.example, so the shelf can show the site without repeating the whole URL in your head.

write_csv_from_list() saves the rows, using the dictionary keys as headers. read_csv_to_list() reads them back as dictionaries with site and link.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text: Add a third link, or remove week as well. Keep the keys the same so the CSV columns stay aligned.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text: The standard-library version needs urlparse, query-pair filtering, and a CSV writer. These helpers let you focus on the useful sequence: clean the link, name the site, save the shelf. For more examples, see Easy URL and Easy CSV.

docs.title: Build a Club Badge with Easy Colors and Easy JSON
docs.text: Combine Easy Colors and Easy JSON to pick ink and paper colors for a club badge, check that they contrast, and save the choice.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
A club needs a dark ink on a light card. This example writes a temporary JSON file, so you can run it repeatedly without replacing a real badge file. The folder is removed when the example ends.

Install the package with python -m pip install py-simple-wrap, then run:

from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

from py_simple import contrast_ratio, is_light_color, open_json, save_json_data

ink = "#1B4D3E"
paper = "#F4EFE6"
badge = {
    "ink": ink,
    "paper": paper,
    "ink_is_light": is_light_color(ink),
    "paper_is_light": is_light_color(paper),
    "contrast": round(contrast_ratio(ink, paper), 2),
}

with TemporaryDirectory() as workspace:
    path = str(Path(workspace) / "club_badge.json")
    save_json_data(path, badge)
    saved = open_json(path)
    print(saved["ink"], saved["paper"], saved["contrast"])

Example output:

#1B4D3E #F4EFE6 8.42

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
is_light_color() says the ink is dark and the paper is light, using perceived brightness rather than a guess from the hex code.

contrast_ratio() returns 8.42. A ratio of 4.5 or more is the usual bar for readable body text; 8.42 clears that.

save_json_data() writes the badge once and refuses to overwrite an existing file. open_json() reads it back as a dictionary.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text: Swap the ink for "#88AA99" and print the new contrast. If it drops below 4.5, pick a darker ink.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text: The standard-library version needs luminance math and a JSON dump with an exists-check. These helpers let you focus on the useful sequence: choose colors, check contrast, save the badge. For more examples, see Easy Colors and Easy JSON.

docs.title: Building a Dice Roll Arena with Easy Random and Easy Game
docs.text: Combine Easy Random and Easy Game to build a visual, interactive dice rolling game window with Pygame in just a few lines of Python.

docs.title: What we are building
docs.text:
Imagine you want to build a quick tabletop dice roller or mini-game where a player can click the window or press the spacebar to roll dice, rendering live game status on the screen without dealing with Pygame setup boilerplate.

from py_simple import (
    basic_game_setup,
    check_if_quit,
    fill_background,
    draw_text,
    update_screen,
    is_key_pressed,
    is_left_mouse_button_clicked,
    roll_dice,
)

# 1. Initialize a 600x400 window with title and clock
screen, clock = basic_game_setup(600, 400, "Dice Roll Arena")

current_roll = roll_dice(6)
rolling = True
running = True

while running:
    # 2. Check if the user clicked the window's close button
    if check_if_quit():
        running = False

    # 3. Roll a new value when pressing SPACE or clicking the left mouse button
    if is_key_pressed("SPACE") or is_left_mouse_button_clicked():
        if not rolling:
            current_roll = roll_dice(6)
            rolling = True
    else:
        rolling = False

    # 4. Render the background and current dice result
    fill_background(screen, (30, 30, 40))
    draw_text(screen, "Dice Roll Arena", (200, 50), font_size=42, color=(255, 215, 0))
    draw_text(screen, f"You rolled: {current_roll}", (220, 160), font_size=48, color=(255, 255, 255))
    draw_text(screen, "Press SPACE or Click to Roll", (160, 280), font_size=28, color=(180, 180, 180))

    # 5. Flip display buffer and lock framerate
    update_screen()
    clock.tick(30)

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
1. basic_game_setup(600, 400, "Dice Roll Arena") initializes the Pygame engine, generates the window surface, sets the caption, and returns the screen and clock instances in a single line.
  2. check_if_quit() inspects the Pygame event queue so you don't have to write manual event loops.
  3. roll_dice(6) uses easy_random to simulate rolling a standard 6-sided die.
  4. is_key_pressed("SPACE") and is_left_mouse_button_clicked() monitor keyboard and mouse inputs without raw Pygame key constant lookups.
  5. fill_background() and draw_text() paint the background color and text surfaces directly onto the active screen.
  6. update_screen() handles the display refresh cycle.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Building even a simple graphic window with raw Pygame usually requires: - Initializing pygame.init() and instantiating pygame.display.set_mode(). - Managing a for event in pygame.event.get(): loop just to prevent the window from freezing. - Setting up custom fonts, rendering surfaces, and calling .blit() with custom coordinates.

By combining easy_game and easy_random, all the low-level rendering, event handling, and random number logic are reduced to declarative, readable function calls.

docs.title: Easy AI
docs.text: Working with artificial intelligence models often requires managing multiple vendor-specific libraries, API keys, and initialization parameters. Whether you're connecting to cloud providers like OpenAI or running models locally with Ollama, easy_ai provides a beginner-friendly helper function that unifies model creation across different AI providers.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're building an application that needs to interact with AI models. Depending on your environment, you might want to use a cloud provider like OpenAI for production or a local model with Ollama for offline testing, without rewriting your model initialization logic.

from py_simple import get_model

# Initialize a cloud model using OpenAI
openai_model = get_model(provider="openai", model_name="gpt-4o", api_key="your-api-key")

# Initialize a local model using Ollama
ollama_model = get_model(provider="ollama", model_name="llama3")

# Generate a response using the initialized model
response = ollama_model.invoke("Hello, world!")
print(response.content)

Example output:

Hello! How can I assist you today?

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
