get_model() provides a single, unified function to instantiate chat models from popular AI providers including OpenAI, Ollama, Anthropic, Google, and Mistral.

When provider="openai" is passed, get_model() imports and returns a ChatOpenAI instance configured with the specified model name and API key.

When provider="ollama" is passed, get_model() connects to your local Ollama server (defaulting to http://localhost:11434) and returns a ChatOllama instance ready to execute prompts locally.

You can also pass provider="anthropic", provider="google", or provider="mistral" to initialize ChatAnthropic, ChatGoogleGenerativeAI, or ChatMistralAI models with optional parameters like api_key, base_url, and timeout.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of installing and importing separate provider libraries (langchain_openai, langchain_ollama, langchain_anthropic, etc.) and writing different initialization code for each platform, you can simply write:

model = get_model(provider="openai", model_name="gpt-4o", api_key="your-api-key")

This keeps AI model setup simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while allowing you to easily switch between cloud and local AI providers with a single function call.

docs.title: Easy Archive
docs.text: Backing up a small folder should not require learning the details of Python's zipfile module. easy_archive provides straightforward helpers for creating, inspecting, and extracting .zip files.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you want to send a week's notes to a teammate. Before sharing the archive, you can check that it contains both files and then restore a copy to confirm it opens correctly.

from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

from py_simple import list_zip_contents, unzip_file, zip_folder

with TemporaryDirectory() as workspace:
    source = Path(workspace) / "weekly_notes"
    source.mkdir()
    (source / "monday.txt").write_text("Plan the week.")
    (source / "friday.txt").write_text("Review the week.")

    archive = zip_folder(str(source), str(Path(workspace) / "weekly_notes.zip"))
    print(Path(archive).name)
    print(sorted(list_zip_contents(archive)))

    restored = unzip_file(archive, str(Path(workspace) / "restored"))
    print(sorted(path.name for path in Path(restored).iterdir()))

Example output:

weekly_notes.zip
['friday.txt', 'monday.txt']
['friday.txt', 'monday.txt']

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
zip_folder() collected every file in weekly_notes and created one archive. It also keeps files in any subfolders, so it is useful for saving a small project instead of only a single file.

list_zip_contents() let us check the archive before sharing it. If you only need selected files rather than a whole folder, use zip_files() instead.

unzip_file() created the restored folder when needed and extracted the archive into it. is_zip_file() is useful when you want to check a path before trying to extract it, and add_to_zip() adds one more file to an archive that already exists. If a path is missing or an archive is invalid, the helpers raise EasyArchiveError with a clear explanation.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text: With the standard library, you need to create a ZipFile, choose the correct mode, walk folders yourself, and create the extraction directory. These helpers keep those steps behind descriptive function names, so a beginner can focus on the files they want to save.

docs.title: Easy Async
docs.text: Running multiple tasks at the same time can make programs faster and more efficient. Whether you're processing data, running independent operations, or automating tasks, easy_async provides simple helpers that make asynchronous execution easier to understand and use.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you are building a tool that needs to perform several independent calculations. Instead of waiting for each function to finish one by one, you want to run them at the same time.

from py_simple import run_at_the_same_time_no_params


def download_file():
    return "File downloaded"


def update_database():
    return "Database updated"


results = run_at_the_same_time_no_params(
    [
        download_file,
        update_database,
    ]
)

print(results)

Example output:

[
    ('download_file', 'File downloaded'),
    ('update_database', 'Database updated')
]

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
run_at_the_same_time_no_params() runs multiple functions at the same time when they do not need any arguments.

It uses a thread pool internally to execute each function independently and collects all the results in a simple list.

If your functions need arguments, you can use:

from py_simple import run_at_the_same_time_with_params


def add(a, b):
    return a + b


def multiply(a, b):
    return a * b


results = run_at_the_same_time_with_params(
    [
        (add, 2, 3),
        (multiply, 4, 5),
    ]
)

print(results)

Example output:

[
    ('add', 5),
    ('multiply', 20)
]

run_at_the_same_time_with_params() allows every function to receive its own arguments while still running all tasks together.

docs.title: Limit concurrent map jobs
docs.text:
Use run_concurrent_map_limited() when you want to process a list without submitting every item at once. It runs ordinary synchronous callbacks in the event loop's executor and returns results in input order.

import asyncio
from py_simple import run_concurrent_map_limited


def square(number):
    return number * number


async def main():
    return await run_concurrent_map_limited(square, [1, 2, 3, 4], 2)


print(asyncio.run(main()))  # [1, 4, 9, 16]

The final argument is the maximum number of submitted jobs at once. It must be a positive integer, excluding booleans. A limit of one processes items one at a time; a larger limit still uses only as many workers as there are items. The executor may run fewer jobs than the chosen limit. Empty input returns []. Async callbacks are not supported.

An invalid limit or an ordinary callback failure raises EasyAsyncError. If a callback fails, the other items are still attempted and all workers are awaited; the first error in input order is then reported. Side effects from successful calls are not rolled back.

Cancelling the await propagates asyncio.CancelledError and stops the internal workers from submitting more items. It cannot forcibly terminate an already running Python thread; those callbacks may finish later. When using asyncio.run(), its executor shutdown can wait for those threads.

docs.title: Return the first completed result
docs.text:
Use run_first_completed() to run multiple zero-argument functions concurrently and get the result of whichever finishes first:

import asyncio
import time
from py_simple import run_first_completed


def query_primary():
    return "primary data"


def query_mirror():
    time.sleep(0.05)
    return "mirror data"


async def main():
    return await run_first_completed([query_primary, query_mirror])


print(asyncio.run(main()))  # ("query_primary", "primary data")

In this example, query_primary returns immediately while query_mirror has a short delay, so query_primary finishes first.

Once the first function completes, all other pending tasks are cancelled. Note that cancelling an asyncio task cannot forcibly terminate an already running thread in Python's thread pool; those callbacks may complete in the background. If the first completed function raises an exception, an EasyAsyncError is raised.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of manually creating thread pools and handling results every time, you can simply write:

run_at_the_same_time_no_params(
    [
        task_one,
        task_two,
    ]
)

or:

run_at_the_same_time_with_params(
    [
        (task_one, value),
        (task_two, value),
    ]
)

These helpers keep asynchronous code simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while providing consistent error handling when tasks fail.

docs.title: Easy Base64
docs.text: Sometimes a program needs to tuck a short message into a form field, a filename, or a chat that only allows plain text. Base64 does that, but the standard library asks you to juggle bytes and encodings. easy_base64 keeps the job to one readable call.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine a classroom quiz that hides the answer key inside a shareable code. You encode the answer before you send it, then decode it when you are ready to check.

from py_simple import decode_text, encode_text, is_base64

answer = "The capital of France is Paris"
code = encode_text(answer)

print(code)
print(is_base64(code))
print(decode_text(code))

Example output:

VGhlIGNhcGl0YWwgb2YgRnJhbmNlIGlzIFBhcmlz
True
The capital of France is Paris

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
encode_text() turns the answer into a Base64 string you can paste anywhere plain text is allowed.

is_base64() checks that a string really is Base64 before you try to read it.

decode_text() turns a valid code back into the original sentence.

docs.title: Working with files
docs.text:
To encode an entire file (such as an image or an icon) into Base64 without opening and reading bytes yourself, use encode_file():

from py_simple import encode_file

image_data = encode_file("icon.png")

To decode a Base64 string and save it directly to a file (such as restoring an image or document from an API response), use decode_to_file():

from py_simple import decode_to_file

decode_to_file(image_data, "restored_icon.png")

docs.title: URL-safe Base64
docs.text:
When embedding Base64 strings into URLs, tokens, or filenames, standard characters like + and / can cause issues. Use encode_urlsafe_text() and decode_urlsafe_text() to use - and _ instead:

from py_simple import decode_urlsafe_text, encode_urlsafe_text

safe_code = encode_urlsafe_text("hello?world")
print(safe_code)

original = decode_urlsafe_text(safe_code)
print(original)

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
The usual version needs encode, decode, and a validate=True flag that is easy to forget:

import base64

code = base64.b64encode(answer.encode("utf-8")).decode("ascii")
original = base64.b64decode(code, validate=True).decode("utf-8")

easy_base64 keeps that detail inside named functions, so the quiz code reads like the task you are actually doing.

docs.title: Easy Bytes
docs.text: File sizes arrive as large numbers of bytes. 1536 is harder to read than 1.5 KB, and the other direction matters when a form asks you to type a size. easy_bytes converts both ways, adds sizes together, and can tell you what percent of a drive is full or how many bytes remain.

docs.title: Which units mean what
docs.text:
By default, KB, MB, GB and TB count in factors of 1024. This is how easy_bytes has always worked, so existing code keeps returning the same numbers. The KiB, MiB, GiB and TiB units are also accepted, and they mean exactly the same thing as the default KB-style units.

If you need KB to mean 1000 bytes (the way drive makers and many websites count), pass decimal=True.

Unit Default With decimal=True B 1 1 KB 1,024 1,000 MB 1,048,576 1,000,000 GB 1,073,741,824 1,000,000,000 TB 1,099,511,627,776 1,000,000,000,000 KiB 1,024 1,024 MiB 1,048,576 1,048,576 GiB 1,073,741,824 1,073,741,824 TiB 1,099,511,627,776 1,099,511,627,776

Units are case-sensitive: "1 kb" and "1 kib" are rejected.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine a homework folder that can hold 10 MB, and the files inside already use 2.5 MB.

from py_simple import (
    bytes_to_human,
    human_to_bytes,
    percent_free,
    percent_used,
    remaining_bytes,
)

used = human_to_bytes("2.5 MB")
total = human_to_bytes("10 MB")

print(bytes_to_human(used))
print(percent_used(used, total))
print(percent_free(used, total))
print(bytes_to_human(remaining_bytes(used, total)))

Example output:

2.5 MB
25.0
75.0
7.5 MB

docs.title: Adding sizes together
docs.text:
add_bytes() takes a list that mixes plain byte counts and size labels, and returns the total in bytes.

from py_simple import add_bytes, bytes_to_human

total = add_bytes([512, "1 KB", "1 KiB"])

print(total)
print(bytes_to_human(total))

Example output:

2560
2.5 KB

Here 512 is already a byte count, and "1 KB" and "1 KiB" are both 1024 bytes, in order to preserve beckwards compatibility. To count "1 KB" as 1000 bytes, pass decimal=True. The decimal=True parameter only works with values such as KB, MB, GB and TB. KiB, MiB, GiB and TiB are binary by default, so the decimal=True parameter doesn't affect them. Here's an example:

from py_simple import add_bytes

print(add_bytes([512, "1 KB", "1 KiB"], decimal=True))

2536

docs.title: Averaging sizes together
docs.text:
average_bytes() takes the same kind of list as add_bytes() and returns the average size in bytes. A fractional average is truncated to a whole byte count.

from py_simple import average_bytes, bytes_to_human

average = average_bytes([512, "1 KB", "1 KiB"])

print(average)
print(bytes_to_human(average))

Example output:

853
853 B

docs.title: Comparing two sizes
docs.text:
is_smaller() and is_larger() answer a yes-or-no question: is one size strictly smaller (or larger) than the other? Each side can be a plain byte count or a size label, and both sides can be different kinds.

from py_simple import is_smaller, is_larger

print(is_smaller("500 B", "1 KB"))
print(is_smaller("1.5 GB", "1000 MB"))
print(is_larger("1.5 GB", "1000 MB"))
print(is_larger("500 B", "1 KB"))

Example output:

True
False
True
False

Both functions take the same optional decimal=True switch as the rest of the module, and it works the same way: it changes what KB-style units mean, and leaves KiB-style units alone. This is a good way to see the difference:

from py_simple import is_smaller

print(is_smaller("1 KB", "1 KiB"))
print(is_smaller("1 KB", "1 KiB", decimal=True))

False
True

By default "1 KB" and "1 KiB" are both 1024 bytes, so neither is smaller. With decimal=True, "1 KB" drops to 1000 bytes while "1 KiB" stays at 1024, so the first one is now smaller.

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
human_to_bytes() reads a label like "2.5 MB" and returns the byte count. The scaling is exact, so "1.001 KB" is 1001 bytes with decimal=True. A real fractional byte is cut off, so "0.1 KiB" becomes 102.

bytes_to_human() turns a count back into a short label. Whole numbers drop the decimal, so 2048 bytes becomes "2 KB". It has two optional switches:

from py_simple import bytes_to_human

print(bytes_to_human(1536))
print(bytes_to_human(1536, binary=True))
print(bytes_to_human(1500, decimal=True))

1.5 KB
1.5 KiB
1.5 KB

binary=True writes the same numbers with KiB, MiB, GiB and TiB. decimal=True counts in thousands instead. The two cannot be combined.

add_bytes() converts each string with human_to_bytes() first, then adds everything up. Each item must be a non-negative whole number or a valid size label, and the input must be a list or a tuple. An empty list adds up to 0.

average_bytes() works on the same kind of list, but divides the total by how many items there are. An empty list raises EasyBytesError, since an average of nothing is undefined.

percent_used() compares the two counts and returns the filled share rounded to one decimal place.

percent_free() returns the percentage of capacity still free.

remaining_bytes() subtracts used bytes from the total. It accepts whole, non-negative byte counts, including a total of zero when usage is also zero. Booleans and usage greater than the total raise EasyBytesError instead of returning a misleading count. A full storage total returns zero.

is_smaller() and is_larger() convert both sides to bytes and compare them. They are strict: two equal sizes are neither smaller nor larger, so both return False. A size that cannot be converted raises EasyBytesError, the same as everywhere else in the module.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text: Mixing up 1000 and 1024 is easy once the unit climbs from KB to MB to GB. These functions keep the unit list in one place, let you choose which one you mean, and reject a negative size, a unit they do not know, or an item that is not a number or a size label.

docs.title: Easy Colors
docs.text: Working with colors is common when building websites, user interfaces, data visualizations, or graphics. Whether you're converting between color formats, validating user input, or checking color accessibility, easy_colors provides beginner-friendly helpers that make color manipulation simple and easy to read. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're creating a website where users can choose a theme color. Before saving it, you want to verify that the color is valid, convert it to RGB, and determine whether it's considered a light color.

from py_simple import is_valid_hex, hex_to_rgb, is_light_color

color = "#4CAF50"

if is_valid_hex(color):
    print(hex_to_rgb(color))
    print(is_light_color(color))
else:
    print("Invalid color.")

Example output:

(76, 175, 80)
True

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
is_valid_hex() checks whether the input is a valid hexadecimal color code.

hex_to_rgb() converts the hexadecimal color into an (R, G, B) tuple.

is_light_color() calculates the perceived luminance of the color and determines whether it should be considered light, making it useful for choosing readable text colors. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of writing regular expressions, manually converting color formats, or implementing luminance calculations yourself, you can simply write:

if is_valid_hex(color):
    rgb = hex_to_rgb(color)
    light = is_light_color(color)

These helpers keep color manipulation simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while providing useful tools for validation, conversion, accessibility, and working with RGB, HSL, RGBA, and hexadecimal colors.

docs.title: Easy Config
docs.text: GitHub Actions workflow files are easy to start and just as easy to leave unfinished. easy_config creates a commented starter workflow file, so you can focus on choosing when it runs and what jobs your project needs.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you have started a Python project and want a place to add automated checks later. From your project root, create a workflow called checks:

from pathlib import Path

from py_simple import gh_workflow_config

workflow = Path(".github/workflows/checks.yml")

gh_workflow_config("checks")

print(workflow.exists())
print("name: checks" in workflow.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

Example output:

True
True

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
gh_workflow_config() created the .github/workflows folder when it was missing, copied the built-in starter template into checks.yml, and replaced the template's workflow name with checks.

Path() points to the file that will be created. exists() confirms that the file is there, and read_text() lets the example check that the workflow has the expected name. If checks.yml already exists, gh_workflow_config() leaves it unchanged.

docs.title: Working from a subfolder
docs.text:
If you run a setup script from a subfolder instead of the project root, pass at_root=False. The helper finds the Git repository root and creates the workflow there:

from py_simple import gh_workflow_config

gh_workflow_config("checks", at_root=False)

docs.title: Loading Environment Files
docs.text:
When developing web services or CLI tools, configuration values are often stored in .env files. load_env_file() reads key-value pairs from a .env file and loads them directly into os.environ so standard calls like os.getenv() work without third-party dependencies:

import os
from py_simple import create_env_file, load_env_file

# Create a sample .env file
create_env_file({"PORT": "8080", "APP_ENV": "development"})

# Load variables into os.environ
load_env_file(".env")

print(os.getenv("PORT"))
print(os.getenv("APP_ENV"))

Example output:

8080
development

Existing environment variables can be preserved by keeping override=False (the default) or updated by passing override=True.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text: Without this helper, you would need to create the .github/workflows folders, copy a workflow skeleton, and remember the basic YAML structure yourself. gh_workflow_config() gives you a commented starting point while still leaving the trigger, permissions, and commands under your control.

docs.title: Easy Converter
docs.text: Converting between different units is something you'll encounter in many Python projects. Whether you're working with time, distance, temperature, weight, or speed, easy_converter provides beginner-friendly helpers that make common conversions simple and easy to read. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're building a fitness application. Before displaying the user's information, you want to convert their weight from kilograms to pounds, their running distance from kilometers to miles, and today's temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit.

from py_simple import kg_to_lb, km_to_mile, celsius_to_fahrenheit

weight = kg_to_lb(75)
distance = km_to_mile(10)
temperature = celsius_to_fahrenheit(22)

print(weight)
print(distance)
print(temperature)

Example output:

165.35
6.21
71.6

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
kg_to_lb() converts kilograms into pounds.

km_to_mile() converts kilometers into miles.

celsius_to_fahrenheit() converts temperatures from Celsius to Fahrenheit.

The module also includes many other conversion helpers for time, temperature, length, weight, area, volume, and speed, so you don't need to remember conversion formulas. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of writing conversion formulas every time, you can simply write:

weight = kg_to_lb(75)
distance = km_to_mile(10)
temperature = celsius_to_fahrenheit(22)

These helpers keep unit conversions simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while providing a wide range of commonly used conversions.

docs.title: Easy CSV
docs.text: Working with CSV files is common when storing or exchanging structured data. Whether you're reading information, creating CSV files, checking columns, or filtering rows, easy_csv provides simple helpers that make working with CSV data easy to read and understand.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're managing a list of people stored in a CSV file. You want to read the data, check which columns are available, and find a specific person without writing the CSV parsing logic yourself.

from py_simple import read_csv_to_list, get_csv_columns, filter_csv_rows

columns = get_csv_columns("people.csv")
print(columns)

people = read_csv_to_list("people.csv")
print(people)

alice = filter_csv_rows(
    filepath="people.csv",
    column="Name",
    value="Alice",
)
print(alice)

Example output:

['Name', 'Age']
[{'Name': 'Alice', 'Age': '24'}, {'Name': 'Bob', 'Age': '31'}]
[{'Name': 'Alice', 'Age': '24'}]

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
get_csv_columns() retrieves the column names from the first row of the CSV file.

read_csv_to_list() reads the CSV file and returns its contents as a list of dictionaries by default. You can also set return_dict=False to receive the rows as lists.

filter_csv_rows() finds rows where a specific column matches the value you provide.

You can also use write_csv_from_list() to create a CSV file from a list of dictionaries or lists.

from py_simple import write_csv_from_list

people = [
    {"Name": "Alice", "Age": "24"},
    {"Name": "Bob", "Age": "31"},
]

write_csv_from_list("people.csv", people)

docs.title: Combine files with matching headers
docs.text:
Use merge_csv_files() to join CSV files without loading them all into memory:

from py_simple import merge_csv_files, write_csv_from_list, read_csv_to_list

write_csv_from_list("january.csv", [{"Name": "Alice", "Age": "24"}])
write_csv_from_list("february.csv", [{"Name": "Bob", "Age": "31"}])
merge_csv_files(["january.csv", "february.csv"], "combined.csv")
print(read_csv_to_list("combined.csv"))
# [{'Name': 'Alice', 'Age': '24'}, {'Name': 'Bob', 'Age': '31'}]

Files are read as UTF-8, in the order supplied. The header appears once and must match exactly, including column order. Quoted commas, embedded newlines, Unicode, empty fields and data record field counts are preserved. Use delimiter=";" if all the files use semicolons.

Header-only files are accepted. An empty input list, a zero-byte file or a blank first record raises ValueError, as do mismatched headers. Invalid CSV quoting raises csv.Error; file and decoding errors propagate.

Choose an output path different from every input, including symbolic and hard links. Its parent directory must already exist. The helper uses a temporary file there and replaces the destination only after every input succeeds. Inputs and an existing destination remain unchanged if merging fails. An unrelated output symlink is replaced, leaving its target unchanged; file permissions and other metadata are not copied to the new output.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of repeatedly opening files, creating CSV readers and writers, handling headers, and filtering rows manually, you can simply write:

people = read_csv_to_list("people.csv")

alice = filter_csv_rows(
    "people.csv",
    column="Name",
    value="Alice",
)

These helpers keep working with CSV files simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while making common tasks such as reading, writing, inspecting, and filtering CSV data easier.

docs.title: Easy Data Visualization
docs.text: Working with data visualization often means choosing the right chart and writing several lines of plotting code. The easy_data_visualization module simplifies this process by automatically identifying whether your data is quantitative or categorical and suggesting an appropriate chart.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're analyzing a set of values and want to quickly visualize the data without deciding which chart type to use or writing the usual Matplotlib setup yourself.

from py_simple import plot_data

data = [1, 2, 2, 3, 5, 5, 5, 8]

plot_data(data)

Example output:

Plotting data...

The function automatically creates suitable visualizations, such as a histogram and a line chart, for the quantitative data.

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
plot_data() examines the data and determines whether it is quantitative or categorical before selecting appropriate chart types.

For example, numerical data can be visualized with a histogram and line chart:

plot_data([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

Categorical data can be visualized with a bar chart and pie chart:

plot_data(["Python", "Python", "Java", "C++"])

You can also provide two data series. When both are quantitative, plot_data() creates a scatter plot:

x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
y = [2, 4, 5, 8, 10]

plot_data(x, y)

The module uses _infer_type() internally to classify each series as either quantitative or categorical, allowing plot_data() to choose the appropriate visualization automatically.

docs.title: Dedicated Chart Functions
docs.text:
When you already know the exact visualization you want and want to label axes and titles, easy_data_visualization provides dedicated helpers:

from py_simple import (
    plot_bar_chart,
    plot_line_chart,
    plot_pie_chart,
    plot_scatter_chart,
)

# Scatter plot: Explore relationships between two numeric sets
plot_scatter_chart(
    x_values=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
    y_values=[10, 20, 25, 30, 50],
    title="Study Hours vs Test Score",
    x_label="Hours Studied",
    y_label="Score (%)",
)

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of manually checking your data, choosing a chart, creating Matplotlib figures, and configuring each axis, you can simply write:

plot_data(data)

or:

plot_data(x, y)

This keeps data visualization simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while letting easy_data_visualization handle the chart selection and Matplotlib boilerplate for you.

docs.title: Easy Date Formatter
docs.text: Working with dates often means remembering strftime formatting codes and writing the same date calculations repeatedly. The easy_date_formatter module provides simple helpers for getting current, past, and future dates in common formats without needing to memorize those formatting codes.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're creating a report and want to display today's date, the date from one week ago, and the date one week from now in a readable format.

from py_simple import (
    get_pretty_date,
    get_past_pretty_date,
    get_future_pretty_date,
)

today = get_pretty_date()
last_week = get_past_pretty_date(7)
next_week = get_future_pretty_date(7)

print(today)
print(last_week)
print(next_week)

Example output:

Monday, August 10, 2026
Monday, August 03, 2026
Monday, August 17, 2026

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
get_pretty_date() returns the current date in a human-friendly format such as Monday, August 10, 2026.

get_past_pretty_date() calculates a date a specific number of days in the past and returns it in the same readable format.

get_future_pretty_date() does the same thing for a date in the future.

The module also provides common formats such as DD-MM-YYYY, MM-DD-YYYY, DD/MM/YYYY, and MM/DD/YYYY.

For example:

from py_simple import dd_mm_yyyy, slash_dd_mm_yyyy

print(dd_mm_yyyy())
print(slash_dd_mm_yyyy())

Example output:

10-08-2026
10/08/2026

You can also use list_available_formats() to see which formats are supported:

from py_simple import list_available_formats

print(list_available_formats())

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of remembering strftime codes and repeatedly writing date calculations, you can simply use:

today = get_pretty_date()
last_week = get_past_pretty_date(7)
next_week = get_future_pretty_date(7)

These helpers keep working with dates simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while providing several common date formats and easy ways to calculate past and future dates.

docs.title: Easy Dict
docs.text: Working with dictionaries is something you'll do in almost every Python project. Whether you're combining data, searching for values, sorting keys, or accessing nested information, easy_dict provides beginner-friendly helpers that make common dictionary operations simple and easy to read.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're working with user information stored in several dictionaries. You want to combine the data, rename a key, and access information stored inside a nested dictionary.

from py_simple import merge_dicts, rename_key, get_nested_value

user = {"name": "Ana", "age": 25}
extra_data = {"country": "Spain"}

user = merge_dicts(user, extra_data)
user = rename_key(user, "name", "username")

print(user)

Example output:

{'age': 25, 'country': 'Spain', 'username': 'Ana'}

You can also retrieve values from nested dictionaries without manually checking every level:

from py_simple import get_nested_value

data = {"user": {"profile": {"name": "Ana"}}}

name = get_nested_value(data, "user.profile.name")

print(name)

Example output:

Ana

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
merge_dicts() combines two dictionaries into one. If both dictionaries contain the same key, the value from the second dictionary is kept.

rename_key() creates a copy of a dictionary with one key renamed without modifying the original dictionary.

get_nested_value() retrieves a value from a nested dictionary using a simple dot-separated path such as "user.profile.name".

The module also provides helpers for other common dictionary operations, such as converting two lists into a dictionary, inverting keys and values, sorting by keys or values, finding keys with a specific value, counting values, and finding the most common value.

For example:

from py_simple import sort_dict_by_value, find_keys, most_common_value

data = {"a": 2, "b": 1, "c": 2}

print(sort_dict_by_value(data))
print(find_keys(2, data))
print(most_common_value(data))

Example output:

{'b': 1, 'a': 2, 'c': 2}
['a', 'c']
2

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of repeatedly writing dictionary comprehensions, loops, .update(), .pop(), and nested dictionary checks, you can simply write:

user = merge_dicts(user, extra_data)
user = rename_key(user, "name", "username")

name = get_nested_value(data, "user.profile.name")

These helpers keep dictionary operations simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while providing useful tools for manipulating, searching, sorting, and analyzing dictionaries.

docs.title: Easy File Manager
docs.text: Working with files is something you'll do in many Python projects. Whether you're checking if a file exists, creating files, reading their contents, renaming them, or making backups, easy_file_manager provides simple helpers that make common file operations easy to read and understand.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're working on a project where you need to create a text file, add some information to it, read its contents, and then create a backup.

from py_simple import (
    make_blank_file,
    add_a_line,
    read_file_to_list,
    copy_file,
)

make_blank_file("notes", "txt")
add_a_line("notes.txt", "My first project")
add_a_line("notes.txt", "Learning Python")

lines = read_file_to_list("notes.txt")
print(lines)

copy_file("notes.txt", "notes_backup.txt")

Example output:

['My first project', 'Learning Python']

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
make_blank_file() creates a new empty file using one of the supported extensions: txt, md, log, or csv.

add_a_line() adds a new line to an existing file. If the file doesn't exist, it creates it automatically.

read_file_to_list() reads the file and returns its lines as a list.

copy_file() creates a copy of a file at another location or under another name without overwriting an existing file.

You can also check, rename, remove, or list files:

from py_simple import (
    is_file_there,
    rename_file,
    list_files,
    remove_file,
)

if is_file_there("notes.txt"):
    print("The file exists.")

print(list_files("txt"))

rename_file("notes.txt", "project_notes.txt")

remove_file("project_notes.txt")

Example output:

The file exists.
['notes.txt']

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of repeatedly writing os.path.isfile(), open(), os.rename(), os.remove(), and shutil.copy2(), you can simply write:

if is_file_there("notes.txt"):
    add_a_line("notes.txt", "New information")

copy_file("notes.txt", "notes_backup.txt")

These helpers keep file management simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while providing useful tools for creating, reading, modifying, copying, renaming, removing, and listing common file types.

docs.title: Easy Flow
docs.text: Running Python files from other scripts can be useful when building tools, automation scripts, or simple workflows. The easy_flow module provides a simple helper that lets you execute Python files while handling errors in a clean and readable way.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you have a small automation project with different Python scripts. Instead of opening each file manually, you want to run them from a main program.

from py_simple import run_py_file

run_py_file("backup.py")

Example output:

RUNNING: backup.py
Backup completed successfully!

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
run_py_file() runs a Python file as if it was executed directly from the command line, making it easy to launch scripts from another program.

If something goes wrong while running the file, easy_flow catches the error and raises an EasyFlowError with a clear message instead of exposing different types of Python exceptions.

For example:

from py_simple import run_py_file

run_py_file("broken_script.py")

Output:

RUNNING: broken_script.py


ERROR: Something went wrong inside the script

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of writing the same execution logic and error handling every time, you can simply use:

run_py_file("script.py")

This keeps your workflow automation simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while providing consistent error handling when running Python files.

docs.title: Easy Game
docs.text: Working with games in Python often means setting up Pygame, creating a game window, handling events, and checking mouse input. The easy_game module provides simple helpers that remove some of this boilerplate and make getting started with Pygame easier.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're creating a simple game where you need to open a window, keep track of the game clock, detect when the player closes the window, and check whether the player is pressing the mouse buttons.

from py_simple import (
    basic_game_setup,
    check_if_quit,
    get_mouse_position,
    is_left_mouse_button_clicked,
)

screen, clock = basic_game_setup(800, 600, "My Game")

running = True

while running:
    if check_if_quit():
        running = False

    x, y = get_mouse_position()

    if is_left_mouse_button_clicked():
        print(f"Mouse clicked at: {x}, {y}")

    clock.tick(60)

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
basic_game_setup() initializes Pygame, creates the game window, sets its title, and creates a clock for controlling the game loop.

check_if_quit() checks the Pygame event queue and returns True when the player closes the game window.

get_mouse_position() returns the current (x, y) position of the mouse cursor.

is_left_mouse_button_clicked() checks whether the left mouse button is currently being held down.

The module also provides helpers for checking the middle and right mouse buttons:

from py_simple import (
    is_middle_mouse_button_clicked,
    is_right_mouse_button_clicked,
)

if is_middle_mouse_button_clicked():
    print("Middle mouse button!")

if is_right_mouse_button_clicked():
    print("Right mouse button!")

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of repeatedly writing Pygame initialization, event handling, and mouse input code, you can simply use:

screen, clock = basic_game_setup(800, 600, "My Game")

while True:
    if check_if_quit():
        break

    x, y = get_mouse_position()

    if is_left_mouse_button_clicked():
        print(x, y)

    clock.tick(60)

These helpers keep common Pygame tasks simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while letting you focus on building the actual game.

docs.title: Easy Generator
docs.text: Generating random values, passwords, QR codes, UUIDs, API keys, and OTP codes is something you'll often need in different Python projects. The easy_generator module provides simple helpers that make these common generation tasks easy to use without writing the underlying logic yourself.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're creating a small application that needs a secure password for a new account, a unique identifier for a user, and an API key for accessing a service.

from py_simple import generate_password, generate_uuid, generate_api_key

password = generate_password(16, uppercase_chars=3, digit_chars=3, special_chars=3)
user_id = generate_uuid()
api_key = generate_api_key()

print(password)
print(user_id)
print(api_key)

Example output:

gT7@qL2#xP9!mK4z
3f2504e0-4f89-11d3-9a0c-0305e82c3301
J4Yx8Qv3...

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
generate_password() creates a randomized password containing lowercase letters, uppercase letters, digits, and special characters according to the options you provide.

generate_slug() converts a valid string to a URL-friendly string.

generate_uuid() generates a random UUID version 4, which is useful when you need a unique identifier.

generate_api_key() generates a secure, URL-safe random string using Python's secrets module, making it suitable for API keys and access tokens.

You can also generate QR codes and OTP codes:

from py_simple import generate_qr_code, generate_otp

generate_qr_code("https://example.com")

otp = generate_otp(6)
print(otp)

generate_qr_code() creates a PNG QR code in the current directory without overwriting an existing QR code file.

generate_otp() generates a random OTP code with a minimum length of 4 characters. You can also include letters:

from py_simple import generate_otp

code = generate_otp(6, with_letters=True)
print(code)

Example output:

a7K2p9

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of repeatedly writing password generation, UUID, token, QR code, or OTP logic yourself, you can simply use:

password = generate_password()
user_id = generate_uuid()
api_key = generate_api_key()
otp = generate_otp(6)

These helpers keep common generation tasks simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while handling the underlying character selection, randomness, formatting, and file creation for you.

docs.title: Easy Hash
docs.text: A checksum is a short fingerprint of some text or a file. People use one to notice when a download changed or when a note was edited. Building that fingerprint with hashlib means remembering encoder names and hex output. easy_hash names the job directly.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you saved a class note and want a fingerprint you can compare later. If the fingerprint changes, the file changed.

from py_simple import hash_file, hash_text, hashes_match

note = "Bring a pencil and a notebook"
fingerprint = hash_text(note)

print(fingerprint)
print(hashes_match(note, fingerprint))
print(hash_file("notes.txt"))

hash_file("notes.txt") reads whatever is in that file. The other two lines work on the sentence itself.

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
hash_text() turns the sentence into a SHA-256 checksum.

hashes_match() compares a sentence with a checksum you already have, and accepts uppercase or lowercase hex.

hash_file() does the same job for a file on disk. You can pass "md5" or "sha1" when a tool asks for that kind of checksum instead.

docs.title: Check a file against a checksum
docs.text:
verify_file_hash() compares a file with an expected checksum. It reads in 64 KiB chunks, so a large file does not need to fit in memory.

from pathlib import Path
from py_simple import verify_file_hash

Path("notes.txt").write_bytes(b"hello")
expected = "2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824"

print(verify_file_hash("notes.txt", expected))  # True
print(verify_file_hash("notes.txt", "0" * 64))  # False

Pass a string path or a pathlib.Path, and use algorithm="sha1" or algorithm="md5" if that is how the expected checksum was made. Hex letters can be uppercase or lowercase. Non-string or malformed checksums return False; surrounding whitespace is not stripped. A non-string checksum returns False before the file or algorithm is checked. With a string checksum, missing/unreadable files and unsupported algorithms raise EasyHashError, just as hash_file() does.

Checksums help detect changed contents. Compare against a checksum from a trusted source; a matching checksum alone does not prove who made the file.

docs.title: Compare two files by checksum
docs.text:
Use compare_file_hashes() to check whether two files on disk have identical checksums without loading either file completely into memory. It reads both files in 64 KiB chunks:

from py_simple import compare_file_hashes

identical = compare_file_hashes("notes.txt", "backup.txt")
print(identical)  # True or False

Like verify_file_hash(), you can pass string paths or pathlib.Path objects and specify "sha256", "sha1", or "md5" (defaults to "sha256"). If either file cannot be read or the algorithm is unsupported, an EasyHashError is raised.

docs.title: Fingerprint several files at once
docs.text:
hash_files() returns one checksum per path. Use it when you want to check a handful of notes separately, instead of one checksum for a whole folder.

from py_simple import hash_files

checksums = hash_files(["notes.txt", "backup.txt"])
print(checksums["notes.txt"])

Pass a list or a tuple. An empty list returns an empty dictionary. A string path by itself is rejected, because Python would otherwise walk its characters. Missing files and unsupported algorithms raise EasyHashError.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
The usual version is a few steps every time:

import hashlib

fingerprint = hashlib.sha256(note.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
same = fingerprint == expected.lower()

easy_hash keeps the algorithm choice in one argument and raises a clear error when the file is missing or the algorithm name is not one of the three it supports.

docs.title: Easy Images
docs.text:
Working with images is something you'll often need in Python projects. Resizing, converting, rotating, and inspecting images are common operations that usually require several lines of Pillow code.

The easy_images module provides simple helpers that make these common image-processing tasks easy to use without writing the underlying logic yourself.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're creating an application that needs to resize a profile picture, convert an image to another format, and inspect its dimensions.

from py_simple import resize_image, convert_image, get_image_info

resize_image("profile.png", "profile_small.png", 320, 320)
convert_image("profile.png", "profile.jpg")

info = get_image_info("profile.png")

print(info)

Example output:

{'width': 1920, 'height': 1080, 'format': 'PNG', 'mode': 'RGBA'}

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
resize_image() resizes an image to the width and height you provide and saves the result to the output path.

convert_image() converts an image to another format based on the output file extension, such as converting PNG to JPG.

rotate_image() rotates an image by the angle you provide and saves the rotated image.

get_image_info() returns basic information about an image, including its width, height, format, and mode.

For example:

from py_simple import rotate_image

rotate_image("photo.jpg", "photo_rotated.jpg", 90)

You can also inspect an image without modifying it:

from py_simple import get_image_info

info = get_image_info("photo.jpg")
print(info)

docs.title: Save a grayscale copy
docs.text:
from py_simple import convert_to_greyscale

convert_to_greyscale("photo.jpg", "photo_gray.png")

convert_to_greyscale() removes the colour while keeping the original dimensions. Each pixel becomes one of 256 shades of gray, from black (0) to white (255). Mode L stores the gray value; mode LA also stores opacity. Outputs ending in .jpg, .jpeg or .bmp use L because Pillow's JPEG/BMP encoders cannot save LA and would raise OSError. Other extensions use LA.

The output extension selects the file format, so you can also save to "photo_gray.jpg". Using a different output path keeps the source file unchanged. Both paths can be strings or pathlib.Path objects.

For transparent inputs:

Output Transparency PNG, TIFF, WebP Preserved JPEG, BMP, GIF Discarded without blending a background

Only the first frame of an animated or multi-frame image is converted.

docs.title: The Py_simple Way
docs.text:
from py_simple import resize_image, convert_image, rotate_image, convert_to_greyscale

resize_image("photo.jpg", "small.jpg", 320, 240)
convert_image("photo.png", "photo.jpg")
rotate_image("photo.jpg", "rotated.jpg", 90)
convert_to_greyscale("photo.jpg", "photo_gray.png")

docs.title: The Traditional Way
docs.text:
Without py_simple, you would normally have to work directly with Pillow:

from PIL import Image

with Image.open("photo.jpg") as img:
    img.resize((320, 240)).save("small.jpg")

with Image.open("photo.png") as img:
    img.convert("RGB").save("photo.jpg")

with Image.open("photo.jpg") as img:
    img.rotate(90, expand=True).save("rotated.jpg")

with Image.open("photo.jpg") as img:
    img.convert("LA").save("photo_gray.png")

docs.title: Crop an image
docs.text:
To extract a specific region of an image, use crop_image() with left, top, right, and bottom pixel coordinates:

from py_simple import crop_image

crop_image("photo.jpg", "cropped.jpg", 10, 10, 200, 200)

docs.title: Getting image information
docs.text:
get_image_info() returns a dictionary containing:

  • width — Image width in pixels.
  • height — Image height in pixels.
  • format — Image format, such as PNG or JPEG.
  • mode — Image color mode, such as RGB or RGBA.
from py_simple import get_image_info

info = get_image_info("photo.jpg")
print(info)

Example output:

{'width': 1920, 'height': 1080, 'format': 'JPEG', 'mode': 'RGB'}

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
The easy_images module provides ImageProcessingError to give image-related failures a consistent and easy-to-understand exception.

For example:

from py_simple import get_image_info, ImageProcessingError

try:
    info = get_image_info("missing.jpg")
except ImageProcessingError as error:
    print(error)

This prevents errors from Pillow or the operating system from leaking directly into your application.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of repeatedly writing Pillow code for common image operations, you can simply use:

resize_image("photo.jpg", "small.jpg", 320, 240)
convert_image("photo.png", "photo.jpg")
rotate_image("photo.jpg", "rotated.jpg", 90)
convert_to_greyscale("photo.jpg", "photo_gray.png")
info = get_image_info("photo.jpg")

These helpers keep common image-processing tasks simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while handling the underlying Pillow logic for you.

docs.title: Easy JSON
docs.text: Working with JSON files is common when storing application settings, configuration data, or other structured information. 'easy_json' provides beginner-friendly helpers that make reading, updating, and formatting JSON files simple and easy to understand.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're working with a configuration file for an application. You want to read the current settings, update the theme, and print the updated configuration in an easy-to-read format.

Suppose config.json contains:

{
  "name": "My App",
  "theme": "light"
}
You can update and display the configuration like this: 
from py-simple import open_json, update_json, pretty_json

config=open_json("config.json")
print("Current theme: ", config["theme"])

update_json("config.json", {"theme": "dark"})

updated_config=open_json("config.json")
print(pretty_json(data=updated_config))

Example output:

Current theme: light
{
  "name": "My App",
  "theme": "dark"
}

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
open_json() reads the contents of config.json and returns them as a dictionary.

update_json() updates the existing "theme" value from "light" to "dark" while keeping the other settings unchanged.

pretty_json() formats the updated configuration as an indented JSON string, making it easier to read.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of manually opening JSON files, updating dictionaries, saving changes, and formatting the output yourself, you can use a few simple helper functions:

config = open_json("config.json")
update_json("config.json", {"theme": "dark"})
config = open_json("config.json")
print(pretty_json(data=config))

These helpers keep common JSON file operations simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while reducing repetitive code.

docs.title: Easy JSON
docs.text:
Working with JSON files is something you'll often need in Python projects. Reading, writing, updating, formatting, and inspecting JSON data can require repetitive file-handling and parsing code.

The easy_json module provides simple helpers that make these common JSON operations easier to use without writing the underlying logic yourself.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're creating an application that stores its configuration in a JSON file. You need to create the configuration, update it later, and read its values.

from py_simple import save_json_data, open_json, update_json

save_json_data("config.json", {"name": "Sara", "theme": "dark"})

update_json("config.json", {"theme": "light"})

config = open_json("config.json")

print(config["name"])
print(config["theme"])

Example output:

Sara
light

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
save_json_data() creates a new JSON file from a dictionary. It refuses to overwrite an existing file, helping prevent accidental data loss.

open_json() opens a JSON file and returns its contents as a dictionary.

update_json() merges new data into an existing JSON file. Existing keys with the same name are replaced while other data remains untouched.

You can also format JSON, check whether a file is a JSON file, and inspect nested data:

from py_simple import pretty_json, is_json_file, is_nested_json

print(pretty_json(data={"name": "Sara", "settings": {"theme": "dark"}}))

print(is_json_file("config.json"))

print(is_nested_json(data={"name": "Sara", "settings": {"theme": "dark"}}))

docs.title: The Py_simple Way
docs.text:
from py_simple import save_json_data, open_json, update_json, pretty_json

save_json_data("config.json", {"name": "Sara"})

update_json("config.json", {"age": 25})

data = open_json("config.json")

print(pretty_json(data=data))

docs.title: The Traditional Way
docs.text:
Without py_simple, you would normally have to handle JSON files directly with Python's json module:

import json
import os

filepath = "config.json"

if not os.path.exists(filepath):
    with open(filepath, "w", encoding="utf-8") as json_file:
        json.dump({"name": "Sara"}, json_file, indent=4)

with open(filepath, encoding="utf-8") as json_file:
    data = json.load(json_file)

data.update({"age": 25})

with open(filepath, "w", encoding="utf-8") as json_file:
    json.dump(data, json_file, indent=4)

print(json.dumps(data, indent=2))

docs.title: Formatting JSON
docs.text:
pretty_json() returns an indented JSON string from either a dictionary or a JSON file.

from py_simple import pretty_json

print(pretty_json(data={"name": "Sara", "settings": {"theme": "dark"}}))

Example output:

{
  "name": "Sara",
  "settings": {
    "theme": "dark"
  }
}

You can also provide a file instead:

from py_simple import pretty_json

print(pretty_json(filepath="config.json"))

Provide exactly one of data or filepath.

docs.title: Working with nested JSON
docs.text:
is_nested_json() checks whether a dictionary or JSON file contains nested dictionaries or lists at the top level.

from py_simple import is_nested_json

print(is_nested_json(data={"name": "Sara", "age": 25}))
# False

print(is_nested_json(data={"name": "Sara", "settings": {"theme": "dark"}}))
# True

flatten_json() can then convert nested JSON into a single-level dictionary:

from py_simple import flatten_json

data = {"user": {"name": "Sara", "age": 25}}

print(flatten_json(data=data))

Example output:

{
    'user-name': 'Sara',
    'user-age': 25
}

You can choose a different separator:

flatten_json(".", data=data)

This produces keys such as:

user.name
user.age

docs.title: Checking JSON files
docs.text:
is_json_file() checks whether a path points to an existing file with a .json extension.

from py_simple import is_json_file

if is_json_file("config.json"):
    print("Looks good!")

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
The easy_json module provides EasyJsonError so JSON-related failures can be handled with one consistent exception.

For example, attempting to open a file that doesn't exist can be handled like this:

from py_simple import open_json, EasyJsonError

try:
    data = open_json("missing.json")
except EasyJsonError as error:
    print(error)

The same exception is used for problems such as invalid JSON syntax, file permissions, attempting to overwrite an existing file, or invalid arguments.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of repeatedly writing JSON file-handling and parsing logic, you can simply use:

data = open_json("config.json")

save_json_data("new.json", {"name": "Sara"})

update_json("config.json", {"age": 25})

pretty = pretty_json(data=data)

nested = is_nested_json(data=data)

flat = flatten_json(data=data)

These helpers keep common JSON operations simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while handling the underlying file operations, parsing, formatting, and nested-data processing for you.

docs.title: Working with Lists Made Easy
docs.text: When processing data—like cleaning up user submissions or formatting query results—you often find yourself repeating the same boilerplate list operations. The easy_lists module wraps common list-wrangling tasks into simple, readable functions.

docs.title: Real-World Example: Cleaning Survey Feedback
docs.text:
Imagine you are managing feedback submissions from a community survey. Respondents frequently submit duplicate answers, and some entries include unwanted repetition.

Here is how you can use easy_lists functions together to clean, de-duplicate, and organize the feedback for review:

from py_simple_wrap import easy_lists

# Raw survey responses containing duplicates
raw_responses = [
    "Great service!",
    "Needs improvement",
    "Great service!",
    "Fast delivery",
    "Needs improvement",
    "Loved the UI",
]

# Step 1: Find duplicate responses to track repeating trends
duplicates = easy_lists.find_duplicates(raw_responses)
print("Duplicate feedback found:", duplicates)

# Step 2: Get unique items for a clean final review list
unique_feedback = easy_lists.unique_items(raw_responses)
print("Unique feedback:", unique_feedback)

# Step 3: Chunk the unique feedback into pages of 2 items each
paginated_feedback = easy_lists.chunk_list(unique_feedback, 2)
print("Paginated feedback reports:", paginated_feedback)

docs.title: 1. find_duplicates()
docs.text:
find_duplicates(raw_responses) identified every item that appeared more than once, such as "Great service!" and "Needs improvement".

It keeps the order in which the duplicate items first occurred without repeating them in the output.

docs.title: 2. unique_items()
docs.text:
unique_items(raw_responses) removed duplicate submissions while preserving the original insertion order.

This avoids the unordered behavior of converting the list directly to a standard set().

docs.title: 3. chunk_list()
docs.text:
chunk_list(unique_feedback, 2) divided the cleaned list into smaller sub-lists containing two items each.

This makes the feedback ready for pagination, display batches, or split reporting.

docs.title: Preserves Insertion Order
docs.text: unique_items() keeps items in their original sequence without requiring extra boilerplate such as dict.fromkeys() or custom loops.

docs.title: Readable and Intent-Driven
docs.text: Functions like find_duplicates() and chunk_list() make your code self-documenting compared to complex list comprehensions or nested slicing.

docs.title: Zero Boilerplate
docs.text: These helpers replace repetitive tracking sets, index calculations, and boundary checks with clean, beginner-friendly one-liners.

docs.title: Easy Logging
docs.text: Recording when an operation starts, finishes, or fails often means repeating the same logging calls. The easy_logging module wraps Python's standard logging module with helpers for code blocks, functions, and methods.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're preparing an order summary and want to see which customer's total is being calculated.

import logging
from py_simple import log_function, log_step

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s: %(message)s")


@log_function("Calculate total for {customer}")
def calculate_total(customer: str, prices: list[float], discount: float = 0) -> float:
    return sum(prices) - discount


with log_step("Prepare order summary"):
    total = calculate_total("Ada", [20, 30], discount=5)

Example output:

INFO: Starting: Prepare order summary
INFO: Starting: Calculate total for Ada
INFO: Finished: Calculate total for Ada
INFO: Finished: Prepare order summary

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
logging.basicConfig() enables INFO messages and sets their format. Configure logging once when your application starts; these helpers use the root logger and its existing configuration.

log_step() logs entry into the with block and its successful completion.

log_function() logs the function call and replaces {customer} with "Ada". Templates can use positional arguments, keyword arguments, and default values for omitted arguments. The function still returns its normal result, so total is 45. The decorator also works on synchronous methods; self and cls are excluded from template fields.

If a block or decorated function raises an exception, the helper logs an ERROR message with the traceback and re-raises the original exception. It does not log a successful completion for that operation.

docs.title: Temporarily enable more detailed logging
docs.text:
Use temporary_log_level() to change one logger's level just for a block:

import logging
from py_simple.easy_logging import temporary_log_level

logger = logging.getLogger("example")
logger.setLevel(logging.WARNING)
with temporary_log_level(logger, "debug"):
    print(logger.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG))  # True
print(logger.level == logging.WARNING)  # True

The helper accepts integer levels and registered string names, including lowercase names like "debug", as setup_file_logger() does. It restores the exact previous explicit level even when the block raises. An original NOTSET level returns to NOTSET, so the logger inherits its parent's current level again. Nested blocks restore the level active at each entry. Exceptions from the block propagate unchanged.

This changes only the logger's level. Handler thresholds and filters, logger filters, disabled settings and global logging settings still apply. In particular, a handler set to INFO will still discard DEBUG records; configuring that handler remains the application's responsibility. Other users of the same logger see the temporary level too, so this does not provide thread isolation.

docs.title: Inspect initial and recent log entries
docs.text:
When reviewing log files, you often need to check how an application booted or inspect its latest messages. read_first_log_lines() lets you stream the initial lines of a log file without reading unneeded lines into memory, while read_recent_log_lines() fetches the tail of the log:

from py_simple import read_first_log_lines, read_recent_log_lines

# Read the first 3 lines (e.g. startup banners or initialization messages)
startup_lines = read_first_log_lines("app.log", line_count=3)

# Read the latest 5 lines (e.g. recent errors or heartbeats)
recent_lines = read_recent_log_lines("app.log", line_count=5)

Both functions return a list of lines with trailing newline characters stripped, and return an empty list if the target file does not exist or if line_count < 1.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
These helpers handle the repeated start, success, and failure logging around an operation, keeping the code focused on its task. Use log_step() for a selected block and log_function() when every call to a synchronous function or method should be logged.

See the Easy Logging reference for argument details and examples alongside their standard-library equivalents.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: For the reasoning behind these helpers and a walkthrough of using context managers and decorators for logging, read How to Add Logging Without Cluttering Your Code by SpaceShaman.

docs.title: Easy Math
docs.text: Working with numbers is an essential part of programming, from simple calculations to data analysis and cryptography. easy_math provides beginner-friendly helpers that make some common math tasks simple and easy to read.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're building a simple lottery ticket generator for a charity raffle. Each ticket gets a number from the Fibonacci sequence. The organisers will later use two properties of the ticket number to decide the prize: the sum of its digits and its prime factors.

from py_simple import fibonacci, sum_of_digits, prime_factorization

ticket_numbers = fibonacci(10)
winning_ticket = ticket_numbers[-1]
digit_sum = sum_of_digits(winning_ticket)
factors = prime_factorization(winning_ticket)

print(f"Winning ticket number: {winning_ticket}")
print(f"Sum of digits: {digit_sum}")
print(f"Prime factors: {factors}")

Example output:

Winning ticket number: 34
Sum of digits: 7
Prime factors: [2, 17]

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
fibonacci() returns the first N Fibonacci numbers as a list.

sum_of_digits() returns the sum of all digits in a number.

prime_factorization() returns the prime factors of a number, including repeats.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of writing loops to generate sequences, manually summing digits, or implementing factorisation code by yourself, you can use a few simple functions:

ticket_numbers = fibonacci(10)
winning_ticket = ticket_numbers[-1]
digit_sum = sum_of_digits(winning_ticket)
factors = prime_factorization(winning_ticket)

This makes your code simpler, more readable, and approachable for beginners.

docs.title: Easy Math
docs.text:
Performing common mathematical operations is something you'll often need in Python projects. Calculating factorials, Fibonacci sequences, prime factors, divisors, and least common multiples can require repetitive mathematical logic.

The easy_math module provides simple helpers for these common operations without requiring you to write the underlying algorithms yourself.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're creating a program that needs to analyze a number. You want to find its divisors, prime factors, and the sum of its digits.

```python id="p7k2mz" from py_simple import divisors, prime_factorization, sum_of_digits

number = 12

print(divisors(number)) print(prime_factorization(number)) print(sum_of_digits(number)) 

Example output:

```text id="q8s4nd"
[1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12]
[2, 2, 3]
3

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
divisors() returns every positive integer that divides a number evenly.

prime_factorization() breaks a positive integer into its prime factors, including repeated factors.

sum_of_digits() adds all the digits of an integer together.

The module also provides helpers for factorials, Fibonacci sequences, and least common multiples:

```python id="v5j9kx" from py_simple import factorial, fibonacci, get_least_common_multiple

print(factorial(5))
print(fibonacci(6))
print(get_least_common_multiple(4, 6))

## The Py_simple Way

```python id="n3x7qa"
from py_simple import (
    get_least_common_multiple,
    factorial,
    fibonacci,
    prime_factorization,
    sum_of_digits,
    divisors,
)

print(get_least_common_multiple(4, 6))
print(factorial(5))
print(fibonacci(5))
print(prime_factorization(12))
print(sum_of_digits(1234))
print(divisors(12))

docs.title: The Traditional Way
docs.text:
Without py_simple, you would normally have to implement these operations yourself or combine Python's built-in functionality with your own algorithms.

For example, calculating a factorial manually:

```python id="c4m8pw" n = 5 result = 1

for number in range(2, n + 1): result *= number

print(result) 

Generating Fibonacci numbers:

```python id="x2q6vs"
count = 5
sequence = [0, 1]

while len(sequence) < count:
    sequence.append(sequence[-1] + sequence[-2])

print(sequence[:count])

Finding prime factors:

```python id="j9r3kf" n = 12 factors = [] divisor = 2

while divisor * divisor <= n: while n % divisor == 0: factors.append(divisor) n //= divisor divisor += 1

if n > 1: factors.append(n)

print(factors) 

The `easy_math` helpers package these common mathematical patterns into reusable functions.

## Working with numbers

`factorial()` calculates the factorial of a non-negative integer:

```python id="r5v2hb"
from py_simple import factorial

print(factorial(5))

Output:

```text id="z1m7pd" 120 

`fibonacci()` returns the number of Fibonacci values you request:

```python id="m8q4sx"
from py_simple import fibonacci

print(fibonacci(7))

Output:

```text id="e3k9wf" [0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8] 

`get_least_common_multiple()` finds the smallest positive number that is divisible by both inputs:

```python id="u6p3nx"
from py_simple import get_least_common_multiple

print(get_least_common_multiple(4, 6))

Output:

```text id="a7v2kc" 12 

If either number is `0`, the result is `0`.

## Prime factors and divisors

`prime_factorization()` returns the prime factors of a positive integer:

```python id="h4q8zm"
from py_simple import prime_factorization

print(prime_factorization(60))

Output:

```text id="w2n5jr" [2, 2, 3, 5] 

`divisors()` returns every positive divisor:

```python id="k7s3fd"
from py_simple import divisors

print(divisors(12))

Output:

```text id="m9x1vc" [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12] 

## Working with digits

`sum_of_digits()` adds all digits in an integer together.

```python id="q5b8ln"
from py_simple import sum_of_digits

print(sum_of_digits(1234))

Output:

```text id="t3r6kp" 10 

Negative numbers are supported as well. The minus sign is ignored:

```python id="y8c2vf"
print(sum_of_digits(-1234))

Output:

```text id="d4m7qs" 10 

## Error handling

The math helpers validate their inputs and raise `ValueError` when an operation receives an invalid value.

For example, factorials cannot be calculated for negative numbers:

```python id="p2x9zk"
from py_simple import factorial

try:
    print(factorial(-5))
except ValueError as error:
    print(error)

Similar validation is performed for operations that require positive integers or specific input types.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of repeatedly implementing mathematical algorithms yourself, you can simply use:

python id="r7n4bc" get_least_common_multiple(4, 6) factorial(5) fibonacci(10) prime_factorization(60) sum_of_digits(1234) divisors(12)

These helpers keep common mathematical operations simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while handling the underlying algorithms and calculations for you.

docs.title: Easy Money
docs.text: Prices show up in club sales, bake sales, and split lunches. Formatting them by hand is where extra pennies and missing zeros sneak in. easy_money rounds to cents and prints a currency symbol for you.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine three friends sharing a $48 pizza, and the shop adds 8.5% tax first.

from py_simple import add_tax, format_money, split_bill

with_tax = add_tax(48, 8.5)
each = split_bill(with_tax, 3)

print(format_money(with_tax))
print(format_money(each))

Example output:

$52.08
$17.36

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
add_tax() takes the price and a percent, then returns the total rounded to cents.

remove_tax() finds the original pre-tax price from a tax-inclusive total.

calculate_tip() calculates the tip amount to add based on a percentage.

split_bill() divides that total by the number of people and rounds each share to cents.

format_money() prints the result with a dollar sign and two decimal places. Pass another symbol, such as "€", when you need one.

docs.title: Calculating tips and discounts
docs.text:
Use calculate_tip() to find the tip on a bill:

from py_simple import calculate_tip, format_money

tip = calculate_tip(50, 18)
print(format_money(tip))  # $9.00

Use calculate_discount() to find the price after subtracting a discount:

from py_simple import calculate_discount, format_money

sale_price = calculate_discount(100, 15)
print(format_money(sale_price))  # $85.00

Use remove_tax() to reverse a tax rate and find the original pre-tax price:

from py_simple import format_money, remove_tax

pre_tax = remove_tax(10.85, 8.5)
print(format_money(pre_tax))  # $10.00

docs.title: Keep every cent when splitting a bill
docs.text:
Use split_bill_exact() when you need all the shares to add up to the full bill, even when it cannot be divided evenly:

from py_simple import split_bill_exact

shares = split_bill_exact("10.00", 3)
print(shares)  # [Decimal('3.34'), Decimal('3.33'), Decimal('3.33')]
print(sum(shares))  # 10.00

It returns one Decimal per person, each with two decimal places. The total is rounded once to cents using ROUND_HALF_UP, then leftover cents go to the first shares. For example, "0.015" shared by two people becomes [Decimal('0.01'), Decimal('0.01')]. Refunds follow the same allocation: split_bill_exact(-10, 3) gives -3.34, -3.33, -3.33. Zero shares are Decimal('0.00'), including when a negative amount rounds to zero.

The amount may be an integer, float, numeric string or Decimal. Floats are converted through their string representation; strings or Decimal values are useful when entering exact amounts. Non-finite amounts and invalid inputs raise EasyMoneyError. The number of people must be a positive integer, excluding booleans. Amounts must be representable to cents in the current Decimal context; precision or rounding-trap failures also raise EasyMoneyError.

split_bill() keeps its existing behavior: it returns one rounded share, so split_bill(10, 3) is still Decimal('3.33').

docs.title: Growing savings with compound interest
docs.text:
Use calculate_compound_interest() to find what savings grow to when interest is added to the balance each period:

from py_simple import calculate_compound_interest, format_money

balance = calculate_compound_interest(1000, 5, 2)
print(format_money(balance))  # $1102.50

Pass 12 as the fourth argument for monthly compounding instead of the default yearly compounding. The rate is a percent per year, and the result is rounded to cents.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text: Float math can print 17.359999999 when you only wanted $17.36. These helpers use decimal rounding, so the number you show someone is the number you calculated.

docs.title: Easy Numbers
docs.text: Working with numbers is central to most programs, checking if a value is even or odd, validating whether it's within range, calculating averages, or determining if a number is prime. Whether you're processing user input, analyzing data, or implementing business logic, easy_numbers provides beginner-friendly helpers that make numerical operations simple and readable.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're building a rating system for a mobile app. Users can rate items from 1 to 5, but due to a data sync issue, you've collected some ratings that might be negative or out of range. Before displaying the average rating, you need to validate the data, clamp ratings to the valid range, and calculate the mean.

from py_simple import clamp, average, is_positive

ratings = [-2, 4, 5, 3, 6, 4, 2]

# Clean up invalid ratings
cleaned_ratings = [clamp(r, 1, 5) for r in ratings]

# Verify all ratings are positive (they should be after clamping)
if all(is_positive(r) for r in cleaned_ratings):
    avg_rating = average(cleaned_ratings)
    print(f"Average rating: {avg_rating}")
else:
    print("Data validation failed.")

Note: This example uses Python's list comprehension syntax ([... for ... in ...]) to apply clamp() to every rating. If that's unfamiliar, you can write it as a regular loop instead. The result is the same!

# Alternative beginner-friendly way:
cleaned_ratings = []
for r in ratings:
    cleaned_ratings.append(clamp(r, 1, 5))

Example output:

Average rating: 3.43

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
clamp() constrains each rating to the 1–5 range, replacing out-of-bounds values with the nearest valid boundary. [-2, 4, 5, 3, 6, 4, 2] becomes [1, 4, 5, 3, 5, 4, 2].

is_positive() checks that each clamped rating is greater than zero, ensuring data integrity.

average() sums all cleaned ratings and divides by the count, returning the result rounded to 2 decimal places. The average of the cleaned data (1 + 4 + 5 + 3 + 5 + 4 + 2) ÷ 7 = 3.43.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of writing conditional logic for each validation step, manually calculating averages, or implementing range constraints yourself, you can simply write:

cleaned = [clamp(r, 1, 5) for r in ratings]
if all(is_positive(r) for r in cleaned):
    avg = average(cleaned)

These helpers keep numerical operations simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while providing essential tools for validation, normalization, mathematical calculations, and data quality checks across integers, floats, and real-world datasets.

docs.title: Easy Numbers
docs.text:
Working with numbers is something you'll often need in Python projects. Checking whether numbers are even, odd, positive, negative, or prime, as well as calculating averages, percentages, and common divisors, can require repetitive code.

The easy_numbers module provides simple helpers for common number operations, making them easier to use without writing the underlying logic yourself.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're processing a collection of numbers and need to check their properties and calculate some basic statistics.

from py_simple import is_even, is_prime, average, percentage_of

number = 90
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40]

print(is_even(number))
print(is_prime(number))
print(average(numbers))
print(percentage_of(number, 0.5))

Example output:

True
False
25.0
45.0

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
is_even() checks whether a number is even.

is_odd() checks whether a number is odd.

is_evenly_divisible() checks whether a number can be divided evenly by another number.

is_positive() and is_negative() check the sign of a number.

You can also calculate averages, percentages, rounding values, greatest common divisors, and check whether a number is prime.

from py_simple import is_odd, is_evenly_divisible, is_positive, is_negative, is_prime

print(is_odd(67))
# True

print(is_evenly_divisible(90, 9))
# True

print(is_positive(90))
# True

print(is_negative(-10))
# True

print(is_prime(97))
# True

docs.title: The Py_simple Way
docs.text:
from py_simple import (
    is_even,
    is_odd,
    is_evenly_divisible,
    is_positive,
    is_negative,
    average,
    is_prime,
    percentage_of,
    round_to_nearest,
    greatest_common_divisor,
    clamp,
)

print(is_even(90))
print(is_odd(67))
print(is_evenly_divisible(90, 9))
print(is_positive(90))
print(is_negative(-10))
print(average([1.5, 2, 3]))
print(is_prime(97))
print(percentage_of(100, 0.5))
print(round_to_nearest(23, 5))
print(greatest_common_divisor(12, 18))
print(clamp(15, 0, 10))

docs.title: The Traditional Way
docs.text:
Without py_simple, many of these operations require writing the comparisons or mathematical logic yourself:

import math

number = 90

# Even
even = number % 2 == 0

# Odd
odd = number % 2 == 1

# Evenly divisible
divisible = number % 9 == 0

# Positive
positive = number > 0

# Negative
negative = number < 0

# Average
numbers = [1.5, 2, 3]
average = round(sum(numbers) / len(numbers), 2)

# Percentage
percentage = round(100 * 0.5, 2)

# Greatest common divisor
gcd = math.gcd(12, 18)

# Clamp
clamped = max(0, min(15, 10))

For operations such as checking whether a number is prime, you would also need to implement the algorithm yourself.

The easy_numbers helpers package these common patterns into simple, reusable functions.

docs.title: Checking numbers
docs.text:
The module provides several helpers for checking the properties of a number:

from py_simple import is_even, is_odd, is_positive, is_negative

print(is_even(10))
# True

print(is_odd(7))
# True

print(is_positive(10))
# True

print(is_negative(-10))
# True

is_evenly_divisible() can check whether one number divides evenly into another:

from py_simple import is_evenly_divisible

print(is_evenly_divisible(90, 9))
# True
