print(is_evenly_divisible(10, 3))
# False

docs.title: Averages and percentages
docs.text:
average() calculates the average of a list of numbers and rounds the result to two decimal places:

from py_simple import average

print(average([1.5, 2, 3]))

Output:

2.17

percentage_of() calculates a percentage using a value between 0 and 1:

from py_simple import percentage_of

print(percentage_of(200, 0.25))

Output:

50.0

For example, 0.5 represents 50%, while 0.25 represents 25%.

docs.title: Prime numbers
docs.text:
is_prime() checks whether a number is prime:

from py_simple import is_prime

print(is_prime(2))
# True

print(is_prime(15))
# False

print(is_prime(97))
# True

A prime number is a number greater than 1 that can only be divided evenly by 1 and itself.

docs.title: Rounding and ranges
docs.text:
round_to_nearest() rounds a number to the nearest multiple you provide:

from py_simple import round_to_nearest

print(round_to_nearest(23, 5))

Output:

25

clamp() keeps a number inside a specified minimum and maximum range:

from py_simple import clamp

print(clamp(15, 0, 10))
# 10

print(clamp(-5, 0, 10))
# 0

print(clamp(5, 0, 10))
# 5

This can be useful when you need to make sure a value never goes outside an allowed range.

docs.title: Greatest common divisor
docs.text:
greatest_common_divisor() calculates the GCD of two numbers:

from py_simple import greatest_common_divisor

print(greatest_common_divisor(12, 18))

Output:

6

The GCD is the largest positive integer that divides both numbers without leaving a remainder.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
Some helpers validate their inputs and raise ValueError when they receive an invalid value.

For example, round_to_nearest() cannot use zero as the nearest multiple:

from py_simple import round_to_nearest

try:
    print(round_to_nearest(23, 0))
except ValueError as error:
    print(error)

Output:

'nearest' must not be zero.

Other functions perform similar validation when an operation requires a specific type or range of values.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of repeatedly writing mathematical comparisons and calculations, you can simply use:

is_even(number)
is_odd(number)
is_evenly_divisible(number, divisor)
is_positive(number)
is_negative(number)
average(numbers)
is_prime(number)
percentage_of(number, percentage)
round_to_nearest(number, nearest)
greatest_common_divisor(a, b)
clamp(number, minimum, maximum)

These helpers keep common number operations simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while handling the underlying comparisons, calculations, and algorithms for you.

docs.title: Easy Random
docs.text: Choosing random values is useful for games, raffles, quizzes, and small experiments. The easy_random module wraps Python's random module with beginner-friendly helpers for common tasks.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're drawing a winner from a short list of raffle entries. You can shuffle a copy of the entries and choose the first name without changing the original list.

import random
from py_simple import shuffle_list, pick_random_item

random.seed(7)  # Makes this example repeatable while you learn.
entries = ["Aiko", "Ben", "Chika"]
shuffled_entries = shuffle_list(entries)
winner = pick_random_item(shuffled_entries)

print(shuffled_entries)
print(winner)

Example output:

['Chika', 'Aiko', 'Ben']
Aiko

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
shuffle_list() returned a new list with the entries in random order, leaving entries unchanged.

pick_random_item() selected one item from the shuffled list. The module also includes roll_dice() for a random number from 1 to a chosen number of sides, flip_coin() for Heads or Tails, and random_int() for an integer between two inclusive limits, and random_date() for a date between two bounds.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text: Without these helpers, you would need to remember which random function fits each task and write the surrounding list-copying or validation code yourself. These small wrappers keep everyday random choices readable, while still letting Python handle the randomness.

docs.title: Building a Mystery Number Quest Game with Easy Random and Easy Game
docs.text: Combine Easy Random and Easy Game to build an interactive, beginner-friendly number guessing adventure in just a few lines of Python!

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you want to quickly spin up a fun command-line game where a player tries to guess a secret number within a limited number of tries, complete with colorful prompts and automated score tracking.

```python from py_simple import get_random_integer, start_game_loop

def play_quest(): secret_number = get_random_integer(1, 50) print("Welcome to the Mystery Number Quest! Guess a number between 1 and 50.")

# Run a simple game loop with 5 attempts
success = start_game_loop(secret_number, max_attempts=5)
if success:
    print("Congratulations, adventurer! You found the treasure!")
else:
    print("Oh no! You ran out of attempts. Better luck next time!")

if name == "main": play_quest()

docs.title: Easy Regex
docs.text: Working with text often requires extracting specific patterns like email addresses, websites, or numbers. Writing regular expressions from scratch can be tricky and frustrating, but the easy_regex module provides beginner-friendly helpers that make pattern extraction simple and readable.

docs.title: A Small Real-World Example
docs.text:
Imagine you're building a tool to parse a batch of user feedback messages or customer support logs. You want to extract all submitted email addresses and website links to build a quick contact list.

from py_simple import extract_emails, extract_urls

text = """
Please contact our support team at support@example.com or
sales@test.org. You can also visit our website at https://www.example.com
or check out our partner page www.test.org.
"""

emails = extract_emails(text)
urls = extract_urls(text)

print(emails)
print(urls)

docs.title: What Happened?
docs.text:
extract_emails() scans the text and returns a list of all valid email addresses found.

extract_urls() scans the text and identifies web addresses, including URLs that start with http://, https://, or www..

Instead of writing regular expressions manually, you can call these helpers directly with the text you want to search:

emails = extract_emails(text)
urls = extract_urls(text)

The results are returned as lists that are ready to use in your program.

docs.title: Why Use These Helpers?
docs.text:
Writing regular expressions from scratch can be difficult because you need to create, test, and maintain complex patterns. The easy_regex helpers handle this complexity for you.

Using these helpers makes your code:

  • Simple – No need to write complex regex patterns.
  • Readable – The function names clearly describe what they do.
  • Reusable – Use the same helpers whenever you need to extract emails or URLs.
  • Beginner-friendly – Focus on solving your problem instead of learning complicated regex syntax.

For example:

emails = extract_emails(text)
urls = extract_urls(text)

This is much easier to understand than writing and maintaining the regular expression patterns yourself.

docs.title: Extract Hashtag Names
docs.text:
Use extract_hashtag_names() when you want names without the leading #:

from py_simple.easy_regex import extract_hashtag_names

names = extract_hashtag_names("Hello #Python #hello_world #Python!")
# -> ['Python', 'hello_world', 'Python']

The helper preserves case, order, and duplicates. Names may contain Unicode alphanumeric characters and underscores, including digits at the start. Punctuation ends a name. Empty text or text without hashtags returns []. Hashes attached to a preceding word or another hash are ignored:

extract_hashtag_names("word#tag ##tag #valid")
# -> ['valid']

This helper follows Python's Unicode \w matching: combining marks are not included and no Unicode normalization is performed. It is not a validator for any particular social platform. The existing py_simple.easy_regex.extract_hashtags() continues to return tags with #.

docs.title: Extract Phone Numbers
docs.text:
Use extract_phone_numbers() to extract US/Canadian-style phone numbers from text:

from py_simple import extract_phone_numbers

numbers = extract_phone_numbers("Call us at (555) 123-4567 or 555-987-6543")
# -> ['(555) 123-4567', '555-987-6543']

The function supports standard North American Numbering Plan (US and Canadian) formats with optional country codes (+1 or 1), parentheses around area codes, and separators like dashes, dots, or spaces. It does not cover general international phone number formats.

docs.title: Easy SQL
docs.text: Working with a database often means managing connections, cursors, and repeated SQL statements. The easy_sql module provides beginner-friendly helpers around Python's built-in sqlite3 module so common database tasks are easier to read.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're planning a trip and want to keep a wishlist of destinations with an estimated budget for each one. You can save the destinations, then find the trips that fit within the amount you have available.

from py_simple import open_db, run_insert, conditional_run_select

connection, cursor = open_db(":memory:")

cursor.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE destinations (
        city TEXT,
        country TEXT,
        estimated_budget INTEGER
    )
""")

destinations = [
    ["Lisbon", "Portugal", 1500],
    ["Kyoto", "Japan", 1800],
    ["Reykjavik", "Iceland", 2600],
]

for destination in destinations:
    run_insert(
        connection,
        cursor,
        destination,
        "destinations",
        ["city", "country", "estimated_budget"],
    )

budget_limit = 2000
affordable_trips = conditional_run_select(
    connection,
    cursor,
    "destinations",
    "city, country, estimated_budget",
    "estimated_budget <= ?",
    (budget_limit,),
)

print(f"Trips within ${budget_limit:,}:")
for city, country, budget in affordable_trips:
    print(f"{city}, {country}: ${budget:,}")

connection.close()

Example output:

Trips within $2,000:
Lisbon, Portugal: $1,500
Kyoto, Japan: $1,800

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
open_db() opened an in-memory SQLite database and returned the connection and cursor needed for the other helpers. Using :memory: keeps the example temporary, so no database file is created on your computer.

run_insert() added each destination to the destinations table. It matched the values in each list to the city, country, and estimated_budget columns and saved the changes.

conditional_run_select() selected only destinations whose estimated budget was at or below the limit. The ? placeholder kept the budget value separate from the SQL condition, and (budget_limit,) supplied the value for that placeholder.

If you want every destination instead, use run_select(). The module also includes run_delete() for removing rows that match a condition and delete_all_from_table() for emptying a table while keeping the table itself.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text: Without easy_sql, you would need to build and execute each SQLite statement yourself, fetch the results, and remember when to commit changes. These helpers keep common database operations short and readable while still using familiar SQL concepts such as tables, columns, conditions, and parameter placeholders.

docs.title: Easy Stats
docs.text: Working with statistics is common when analyzing data, tracking performance, or making informed decisions. Whether you're finding the middle value of a dataset, understanding how spread out numbers are, or identifying percentile ranks, easy_stats provides beginner-friendly helpers that make statistical operations simple and readable.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're a teacher who just gave a quiz to your class. You want to quickly understand the overall performance: What's the typical score? How much do scores vary? What's the full range? Before uploading grades, you need a quick statistical summary.

from py_simple import median, standard_deviation, data_range

scores = [65, 72, 78, 81, 85, 88, 92]

# Get key statistics about the performance
middle_score = median(scores)
spread = standard_deviation(scores)
score_range = data_range(scores)

print(f"Median score: {middle_score}")
print(f"Standard deviation: {spread}")
print(f"Score range: {score_range}")

Example output:

Median score: 81
Standard deviation: 9.37
Score range: 27

Note: This example uses Python's list comprehension syntax ([... for ... in ...]) to apply functions to data. If that's unfamiliar, you can use the functions one at a time instead. The result is the same!

# Alternative beginner-friendly way:
scores = [65, 72, 78, 81, 85, 88, 92]
middle_score = median(scores)
spread = standard_deviation(scores)
score_range = data_range(scores)

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
median() finds the middle value when scores are arranged in order. With 7 scores, it returns the 4th value: 81.

standard_deviation() measures how spread out the scores are from the average. A value of 9.37 means scores typically vary by about 9 points from the mean. This helps you see if the class performed consistently or if there's a wide gap between top and bottom performers.

data_range() shows the difference between the highest and lowest scores: 92 - 65 = 27. This gives you the total span of performance at a glance.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of writing complex logic to sort data, calculate averages, or implement statistical formulas yourself, you can simply write:

middle = median(scores)
spread = standard_deviation(scores)
range_val = data_range(scores)

These helpers keep statistical analysis simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while providing essential tools for data summarization, performance tracking, and understanding data distributions without needing deep mathematical knowledge.

docs.title: Easy Strings
docs.text: Working with text is something you'll do in almost every Python project. Whether you're cleaning user input, creating filenames, or preparing text for URLs, easy_strings provides simple helpers that keep your code easy to read.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're collecting article titles from users. Before saving them, you want to:

  • remove extra spaces,
  • create a snake_case filename,
  • count how many words the title contains.
from py_simple import remove_extra_spaces, to_snake_case, count_words

title = "   My   First    Python Project!   "

clean_title = remove_extra_spaces(title)
filename = to_snake_case(clean_title)
words = count_words(clean_title)

print(clean_title)
# My First Python Project!

print(filename)
# my_first_python_project

print(words)
# 4

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
remove_extra_spaces() removes leading, trailing, and repeated spaces from the text.

to_snake_case() converts the cleaned text into snake_case, making it useful for filenames, variables, or URLs.

count_words() counts the number of words in the cleaned text without needing any extra logic.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of combining multiple string methods and regular expressions every time, you can write cleaner and more readable code:

clean_title = remove_extra_spaces(title)
filename = to_snake_case(clean_title)
words = count_words(clean_title)

These helpers keep your code simple, readable, and beginner-friendly.

docs.title: Easy Terminal
docs.text: Styling terminal output can make important messages easier to notice. easy_terminal provides a simple way to add colors and text styles without having to work directly with Rich style strings.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're running a build script and want successful builds to stand out clearly in the terminal.

from py_simple import EasyTerminal
EasyTerminal("Build complete").set_color("green").set_bold().show()

Example output:

Build complete

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
EasyTerminal() creates a terminal message that can be styled before it is printed.

set_color("green") changes the text color to green.

set_bold() makes the message bold.

Finally, show() prints the styled message to the terminal.

You can also use set_bg_color() to add a background color or set_light_weight() when you want dimmer text.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Without EasyTerminal, you would need to create a Rich console and manually build style strings such as "bold green".

With EasyTerminal, the same styling can be expressed by chaining readable methods together, which keeps terminal output code simple and beginner-friendly.

docs.title: Print styled text in a single call
docs.text:
If you prefer a single function call instead of chaining methods, use print_styled():

from py_simple import print_styled

print_styled("Build complete", color="green", bold=True)
print_styled("Warning note", color="yellow", bg_color="black", dim=True)

docs.title: Separate sections with a rule
docs.text:
Use print_rule() to separate parts of a report with a horizontal line:

from py_simple import print_rule

print_rule("Results")
print("3 checks passed")
print_rule()

The heading is centered in the divider; omitting it prints a plain line. Rich uses the current console width and fits or shortens long headings on narrow consoles, so the exact line length and characters depend on your console. The helper prints to standard output and returns None. Headings are literal text: print_rule("[red]") displays the brackets rather than treating them as a color instruction. Install the existing terminal extra with python -m pip install "py-simple-wrap[terminal]" if Rich is not already available.

docs.title: Easy Text
docs.text: Text appears everywhere in Python programs: user messages, passwords, titles, tags, and reports. The easy_text module provides beginner-friendly helpers for cleaning, formatting, analyzing, and transforming text without repeating the same string logic each time.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're preparing a social media post for a report. You want to clean the title, count its letters and digits, find its hashtags, and count the words that appear most often.

from py_simple import (
    remove_punctuation,
    count_letters,
    count_digits,
    extract_hashtags,
    word_frequency,
)

post = "Python 101: #coding makes text work! #coding"

clean_post = remove_punctuation(post)
letters = count_letters(post)
digits = count_digits(post)
hashtags = extract_hashtags(post)
frequencies = word_frequency(post)

print(clean_post)
# Python 101 coding makes text work coding

print(letters)
# 31

print(digits)
# 3

print(hashtags)
# ['coding', 'coding']

print(frequencies)
# {'python': 1, '101': 1, 'coding': 2, 'makes': 1, 'text': 1, 'work': 1}

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
remove_punctuation() removes punctuation while keeping letters, numbers, and spaces.

count_letters() counts alphabetic characters, and count_digits() counts numeric characters.

extract_hashtags() returns hashtag words without their # symbols.

word_frequency() ignores punctuation, converts words to lowercase, and returns a dictionary with the number of times each word appears.

docs.title: Truncating text
docs.text:
Use truncate() when you need to limit text to a maximum length. If the text is too long, an ellipsis is added.

from py_simple import truncate

print(truncate("A very long message", 10))
# A very lon…

print(truncate("Short", 10))
# Short

The traditional version uses slicing and a length check:

text = "A very long message"
length = 10
result = text[:length] + "…" if len(text) > length else text

docs.title: Reversing words and creating titles
docs.text:
reverse_words() reverses the order of words while keeping the words themselves unchanged. capitalize_title() capitalizes the first letter of every word.

from py_simple import capitalize_title, reverse_words

title = "the great gatsby"

print(capitalize_title(title))
# The Great Gatsby

print(reverse_words(title))
# gatsby great the

The traditional versions use Python's built-in string methods:

title = "the great gatsby"
capitalized = title.title()
reversed_words = " ".join(title.split()[::-1])

docs.title: Counting letters and digits
docs.text:
count_letters() and count_digits() are useful when checking or summarizing input. Spaces and punctuation are not counted.

from py_simple import count_digits, count_letters

text = "Order 123!"
print(count_letters(text))  # 5
print(count_digits(text))  # 3

docs.title: Masking sensitive text
docs.text:
Use mask_part() to hide part of a card number, account number, or other value. The first four characters remain visible by default.

from py_simple import mask_part

print(mask_part("1234567890"))
# 1234 ******

print(mask_part("1234567890", 2))
# 12 ********

The traditional version keeps the visible part and replaces the rest with asterisks:

text, visible = "1234567890", 4
result = text[:visible] + " " + "*" * len(text[visible:])

docs.title: Pluralizing a word
docs.text:
pluralize() returns the original word for a count of 1 and adds a plural ending for other counts. Words ending in s receive es.

from py_simple import pluralize

print(f"{pluralize('cat', 1)}")
# cat

print(f"{pluralize('cat', 3)}")
# cats

print(f"{pluralize('bus', 2)}")
# buses

docs.title: Extracting hashtags
docs.text:
extract_hashtags() finds hashtags made from word characters and returns them without the # symbol.

from py_simple import extract_hashtags

hashtags = extract_hashtags("Learning #Python with #py_simple!")
print(hashtags)
# ['Python', 'py_simple']

The traditional version uses a regular expression:

import re

text = "Learning #Python with #py_simple!"
hashtags = re.findall(r"#(\w+)", text)

docs.title: Counting word frequency
docs.text:
word_frequency() is useful for simple text analysis. It removes punctuation, treats uppercase and lowercase words as the same, and counts each word.

from py_simple import word_frequency

print(word_frequency("Hello, hello! Welcome."))
# {'hello': 2, 'welcome': 1}

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of repeatedly writing slicing expressions, character checks, regular expressions, and word-counting loops, you can use clear, reusable functions:

summary = {
    "title": capitalize_title("my text report"),
    "tags": extract_hashtags("#python #text"),
    "words": word_frequency("Text text tools"),
}

These helpers keep common text operations simple, readable, and beginner-friendly.

docs.title: Easy URL
docs.text: Links show up in bookmarks, club pages, and search results. Pulling out the site name, checking HTTPS, or adding ?page=2 usually means importing four names from urllib.parse. easy_url keeps each of those jobs as one function.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine a club page that should only link to secure sites, and the "next page" button needs a page number on the link.

from py_simple import add_query_param, get_domain, is_https

link = "https://school.example/clubs"
print(get_domain(link))
print(is_https(link))
print(add_query_param(link, "page", "2"))

Example output:

school.example
True
https://school.example/clubs?page=2

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
get_domain() returns the host name and leaves off the path.

is_https() is True only when the link starts with https.

add_query_param() adds page=2. Call it again with the same name and the old value is replaced instead of duplicated.

docs.title: Read every value for a query parameter
docs.text:
Links can use the same query name more than once. get_query_values() keeps those values in order, including blanks:

from py_simple import get_query_values

link = "https://school.example/clubs?tag=python&tag=&tag=art+club#list"
print(get_query_values(link, "tag"))
print(get_query_values(link, "missing"))

Example output:

['python', '', 'art club']
[]

Pass the decoded, case-sensitive name. Percent escapes are decoded and + becomes a space; a bare tag also produces an empty string. The fragment is ignored, and the input link is not changed. This uses the module's existing full-link validation rather than checking whether a link is safe to visit.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text: A link without https:// is rejected with a clear error, so a bare school.example does not quietly become an empty host. The query helper keeps any parameters that were already on the link.

docs.title: Easy Validator
docs.text:
Validating user input is something you'll often need in Python projects. Checking emails, usernames, URLs, ZIP codes, and passwords can require repetitive regular expressions and validation logic.

The easy_validator module provides simple helpers for common validation tasks, allowing you to check whether values follow expected formats without writing the underlying validation logic yourself.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you're creating a registration form where users need to provide an email address, username, and password.

```python id="h4x8sd" from py_simple import is_valid_email, is_valid_username, is_password_secure

email = "hello@example.com" username = "user_name" password = "1andkrf!AG5"

print(is_valid_email(email)) print(is_valid_username(username)) print(is_password_secure(password)) 

Example output:

```text id="t2k6pf"
True
True
True

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
is_valid_email() checks whether a string follows a valid email format.

is_valid_username() checks whether a username contains only letters, numbers, and underscores.

is_valid_zipcode() checks whether a value is a valid five-digit US ZIP code.

is_valid_url() checks whether a string follows a supported URL format.

is_password_secure() checks a password against several security requirements.

For example:

```python id="s7n3qm" from py_simple import is_valid_url, is_valid_zipcode

print(is_valid_url("https://example.com"))

docs.title: True
docs.text: print(is_valid_zipcode(12345))

docs.title: True
docs.text:
## The Py_simple Way

```python id="j8v2nc"
from py_simple import (
    is_valid_email,
    is_valid_username,
    is_valid_zipcode,
    is_valid_url,
    is_password_secure,
)

print(is_valid_email("hello@example.com"))
print(is_valid_username("user_name"))
print(is_valid_zipcode(12345))
print(is_valid_url("www.google.com"))
print(is_password_secure("1andkrf!AG5"))

docs.title: The Traditional Way
docs.text:
Without py_simple, you would normally need to write the appropriate regular expressions and validation logic yourself:

```python id="r5k1zp" import re

email_pattern = r"[a-zA-Z_.%+-]+@[a-zA-Z0-9-]+.[a-zA-Z]+" username_pattern = r"^[a-zA-Z0-9_]+" zipcode_pattern = r"^[0-9]{5}$"

email_valid = bool(re.fullmatch(email_pattern, "hello@example.com"))

username_valid = bool(re.fullmatch(username_pattern, "user_name"))

zipcode_valid = bool(re.fullmatch(zipcode_pattern, str(12345))) 

For password validation, you would additionally need to manually count characters, check their types, and make sure characters aren't repeated.

The `easy_validator` helpers package these common validation patterns into simple, reusable functions.

## Validating emails and usernames

`is_valid_email()` checks whether an email follows the expected format:

```python id="c3n7vw"
from py_simple import is_valid_email

print(is_valid_email("hello@example.com"))
# True

print(is_valid_email("not-an-email"))
# False

is_valid_username() accepts usernames containing letters, numbers, and underscores:

```python id="x9q4mk" from py_simple import is_valid_username

print(is_valid_username("user_name"))

docs.title: True
docs.text: print(is_valid_username("user-name"))

docs.title: False
docs.text:
## Validating URLs and ZIP codes

`is_valid_url()` checks common URLs:

```python id="p6d2fz"
from py_simple import is_valid_url

print(is_valid_url("www.google.com"))
# True

print(is_valid_url("https://example.com"))
# True

is_valid_zipcode() checks for a five-digit US ZIP code:

```python id="m8r5yx" from py_simple import is_valid_zipcode

print(is_valid_zipcode(12345))

docs.title: True
docs.text: print(is_valid_zipcode(1234))

docs.title: False
docs.text:
## Checking password security

`is_password_secure()` checks that a password meets several requirements.

A password must have:

* At least 9 characters.
* At least 1 uppercase letter.
* At least 2 lowercase letters.
* At least 2 digits.
* At least 1 special character.
* No consecutive repeated characters.

For example:

```python id="f7c2ka"
from py_simple import is_password_secure

password = "1andkrf!AG5"

print(is_password_secure(password))

Output:

```text id="b9w4qt" True 

A password that doesn't meet the requirements returns `False`:

```python id="v3m8sx"
print(is_password_secure("password"))
# False

docs.title: Validating credit card numbers
docs.text:
is_valid_creditcard() checks that a credit card number meets some basic requirements (which doesn't necessarily mean that it's a real credit card number).

A valid credit card number is 13 to 19 digits long with optional dashes or spaces for formatting. Additionally, numbers meeting those requirements are checked against the Luhn algorithm, a type of checksum designed to detect errors when relaying or transcribing credit card numbers.

For example:

from py_simple import is_valid_creditcard

# Valid test numbers provided by Stripe
# https://docs.stripe.com/testing?testing-method=card-numbers#cards
visa = "4242-4242-4242-4242"
visa_error = "4242-4242-4242-4241"  # last digit changed!

print(is_valid_creditcard(visa))
print(is_valid_creditcard(visa_error))

Output:

True
False

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Instead of repeatedly writing regular expressions, character counters, and validation conditions, you can simply use:

python id="n2x6pk" is_valid_email(email) is_valid_username(username) is_valid_zipcode(zipcode) is_valid_url(url) is_password_secure(password) is_valid_creditcard(card_num)

These helpers keep common validation tasks simple, readable, and beginner-friendly while handling the underlying regular expressions and validation logic for you.

docs.title: Easy Web
docs.text: Working with websites often involves several steps before you can extract useful information. The easy_web module provides beginner-friendly helpers that make common web tasks simple and easy to read.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Imagine you want to check whether a website is available before collecting some basic information about it.

from py_simple import is_page_up, get_page_title, count_links

url = "https://github.com"

if is_page_up(url):
    print("The website is online!")

    print(get_page_title(url))
    print(count_links(url))
else:
    print("The website is unavailable.")

Example output:

The website is online!
GitHub · Build and ship software on a single, collaborative platform · GitHub
144

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
is_page_up() checks whether the website is available before doing anything else.

get_page_title() retrieves the title of the page, making it easy to identify the website you're working with.

count_links() counts all the links on the page without requiring you to parse the HTML yourself.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
These helpers let you focus on the information you want instead of writing the same networking and HTML parsing code every time.

if is_page_up(url):
    print(get_page_title(url))
    print(count_links(url))

This keeps your code simple, readable, and beginner-friendly.

docs.title: Build a Game Asset Packager with Easy Archive and Easy Bytes
docs.text: Combine Easy Archive and Easy Bytes to bundle game files into a ZIP archive, inspect the contents, and calculate storage savings in readable units.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Game developers and mod creators often need to package dialogue files, maps, and textures into compressed bundles for players to download. This example uses a temporary folder to create sample assets, bundle them into a ZIP archive, and measure how much bandwidth and disk space the compressed pack saves. The temporary directory and its files are automatically removed when the script finishes.

Install the package:

python -m pip install py-simple-wrap

Save this as game_asset_packager.py:

from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

from py_simple import (
    add_bytes,
    bytes_to_human,
    get_zip_file_count,
    is_smaller,
    list_zip_contents,
    percent_used,
    remaining_bytes,
    zip_files,
)

with TemporaryDirectory() as workspace:
    folder = Path(workspace)

    # 1. Prepare sample game asset files
    dialogue = folder / "quest_dialogue.txt"
    map_data = folder / "dungeon_layout.json"

    dialogue.write_text("Hero: Halt! Who goes there?\n" * 200, encoding="utf-8", newline="")
    map_data.write_text('{"tile": "stone", "walkable": true}\n' * 150, encoding="utf-8", newline="")

    asset_files = [str(dialogue), str(map_data)]
    total_uncompressed = add_bytes([dialogue.stat().st_size, map_data.stat().st_size])

    # 2. Package the files into a compressed ZIP bundle
    bundle_path = str(folder / "dungeon_pack.zip")
    zip_files(asset_files, bundle_path)

    # 3. Inspect archive contents and calculate storage savings
    file_count = get_zip_file_count(bundle_path)
    members = list_zip_contents(bundle_path)
    bundle_size = Path(bundle_path).stat().st_size
    saved_bytes = remaining_bytes(bundle_size, total_uncompressed)
    compression_ratio = percent_used(bundle_size, total_uncompressed)

    print("--- Game Asset Bundle Report ---")
    print(f"Files packed: {file_count}")
    print(f"Archive contents: {members}")
    print(f"Original size: {bytes_to_human(total_uncompressed)}")
    print(f"Compressed size: {bytes_to_human(bundle_size)} ({compression_ratio:.1f}% of original)")
    print(f"Space saved: {bytes_to_human(saved_bytes)}")
    print(f"Is bundle smaller: {is_smaller(bundle_size, total_uncompressed)}")

Run the script from your terminal:

python game_asset_packager.py

Example output:

--- Game Asset Bundle Report ---
Files packed: 2
Archive contents: ['quest_dialogue.txt', 'dungeon_layout.json']
Original size: 10.7 KB
Compressed size: 383 B (3.5% of original)
Space saved: 10.4 KB
Is bundle smaller: True

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
add_bytes() sums up the sizes of the raw asset files from a list of byte counts, returning the uncompressed total without manual integer math.

zip_files() packages the list of file paths into a single compressed ZIP archive at the destination path, storing files using their clean file names.

get_zip_file_count() opens the generated archive and reports how many files it contains.

list_zip_contents() inspects the archive structure and returns a list containing the names of each bundled file.

remaining_bytes() computes how many bytes of disk space were freed up by taking the compressed archive size and the original uncompressed total.

percent_used() calculates what percentage of the original footprint the compressed file occupies (in this case, shrinking the assets down to just 3.5% of their original size).

bytes_to_human() converts raw integer byte numbers (like 11000 and 383) into friendly, human-readable strings like 10.7 KB and 383 B.

is_smaller() compares the archive size against the original total to confirm that compression reduced the overall file footprint.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
• Add an audio asset: Add a third file (like music_theme.ogg or sound effect text) to asset_files and re-run to see how the file count and saved space adjust.
  • Extract a single file: Use extract_file_from_zip(bundle_path, "quest_dialogue.txt", str(folder / "unpacked")) to pull out only the dialogue file from the pack.
  • Check decimal units: Pass decimal=True to bytes_to_human() to format sizes using 1000-byte decimal kilobyte units (KB) instead of binary kibibytes (KiB).

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Without py-simple-wrap, achieving this with Python's standard library requires importing both zipfile and math while writing manual helper functions: - Setting up a zipfile.ZipFile context manager with zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED, iterating over files, and extracting relative names with os.path.basename to avoid storing deep directory trees. - Manually reading infolist() or namelist() to count and inspect members. - Writing custom formatting functions to calculate logarithms or unit division loops (size / 1024 ** power) just to print human-friendly file sizes like "10.7 KB".

Combining easy_archive and easy_bytes replaces archive plumbing and byte math with concise, descriptive functions.

For more examples and detailed function references, see Easy Archive and Easy Bytes.

docs.title: Building a Homework Log with Easy Date Formatter and Easy Logging
docs.text: Combine Easy Date Formatter and Easy Logging to keep a plain-text log of finished homework, dated in a way you can read later.

docs.title: What we are building
docs.text:
Each time a task is done, the script writes one line with today's date and a short note. The file is homework.log.

from py_simple import get_pretty_date, log_to_file

today = get_pretty_date()
log_to_file("homework.log", f"{today} | math worksheet finished")

Example line in homework.log:

Saturday, October 10, 2026 | math worksheet finished

The weekday and date follow the day you run the script.

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
1. get_pretty_date() returns today as words, such as Saturday, October 10, 2026, so you do not have to remember a strftime pattern.
  2. log_to_file() creates homework.log if needed and appends the message as one line. Call it again with a different subject and the new line sits under the first.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text: The usual version imports datetime, picks a format string, then opens the log in append mode. Here the date is already readable and the log write is one call, which is enough for a homework list you check at the end of the week.

docs.title: Building a Lunch Picker with Easy CSV and Easy Random
docs.text: Combine Easy CSV and Easy Random to keep a short lunch menu in a spreadsheet and pick one meal without staring at the list.

docs.title: What we are building
docs.text:
A class list of lunches is easier to edit in a CSV than inside the program. This small script writes that menu, reads it back, and chooses one row at random.

from py_simple import pick_random_item, read_csv_to_list, write_csv_from_list

lunches = [
    {"meal": "Pasta", "side": "Apple"},
    {"meal": "Rice bowl", "side": "Carrots"},
    {"meal": "Sandwich", "side": "Yogurt"},
]

write_csv_from_list("lunches.csv", lunches)
rows = read_csv_to_list("lunches.csv")
choice = pick_random_item(rows)

print(f"{choice['meal']} with {choice['side']}")

Example output (one of the three meals):

Rice bowl with Carrots

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
1. write_csv_from_list() saves the menu as lunches.csv, using the dictionary keys as column names.
  2. read_csv_to_list() loads that file back into a list of dictionaries, so each lunch still has a meal and a side.
  3. pick_random_item() chooses one of those dictionaries. Run the script again and you may get a different lunch.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text: Writing and reading CSV usually means opening the file, creating a DictWriter, and remembering newline="". Picking a random row means importing random and calling choice. Here the script stays on the task: save the menu, read it, pick one.

docs.title: Build a Message Capsule with Easy Base64 and Easy JSON
docs.text:
Write a note to your future self, store it as a shareable code in a JSON file, then open it in a later run. Combine Easy Base64 for the text encoding with Easy JSON for saving and loading the capsule.

Base64 is reversible encoding, not encryption or a time lock. Anyone who has the file can read the message, so use a fun note rather than a secret.

docs.title: The build
docs.text:
Install the package:

python -m pip install py-simple-wrap

Save the following as message_capsule.py. This project uses the existing text and JSON helpers and needs no optional extras.

import argparse

from py_simple import (
    EasyBase64Error,
    decode_text,
    encode_text,
    open_json,
    save_json_data,
)
from py_simple.easy_json import EasyJsonError


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Save or open a message capsule")
    parser.add_argument("action", choices=["create", "open"])
    parser.add_argument("file", help="Path to the capsule JSON file")
    parser.add_argument("--message", help="Your note, required when creating")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    if args.action == "create" and args.message is None:
        parser.error("create requires --message")
    if args.action == "open" and args.message is not None:
        parser.error("--message is only used with create")

    try:
        if args.action == "create":
            capsule = {
                "format": "message-capsule-v1",
                "message": encode_text(args.message),
            }
            save_json_data(args.file, capsule)
            print(f"Saved capsule: {args.file}")
        else:
            capsule = open_json(args.file)
            if (
                not isinstance(capsule, dict)
                or capsule.get("format") != "message-capsule-v1"
                or not isinstance(capsule.get("message"), str)
            ):
                parser.exit(1, "This file is not a message capsule.\n")
            print("Your message:", decode_text(capsule["message"]))
    except (EasyBase64Error, EasyJsonError) as error:
        parser.exit(1, f"Could not {args.action} capsule: {str(error).strip()}\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Save it, then come back later
docs.text:
Run these commands in the folder containing your script:

python message_capsule.py create capsule.json --message "You finished your first Python project!"
python message_capsule.py open capsule.json

Output:

Saved capsule: capsule.json
Your message: You finished your first Python project!

These are separate program runs: the second command gets the message from the file, not from a variable left over from the first run. You can close the terminal and run the open command tomorrow, or send the JSON file to a friend who has the same script.

Unicode works too. Try a new file with --message "Hello, future me! 🎉".

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
encode_text() converts your note to UTF-8 and then Base64. The JSON object stores that code alongside a small format label, so the script can recognize its own files.

save_json_data() writes the object to the chosen filename. It refuses to replace an existing file. If you repeat the create command with the same filename, the program reports an error and leaves your original capsule alone. Pick a new filename for your next note.

open_json() loads the saved object. The script checks its format and message field before calling decode_text() to restore the original note. An invalid JSON file, missing file, or malformed Base64 message produces a short error and a nonzero exit status.

Python's argparse handles the two commands and required arguments. Run python message_capsule.py --help to see them. The two py-simple-wrap modules handle the encoding and file operations.

docs.title: Make it your own
docs.text:
• Write a capsule for each finished project, using a different filename.
  • Add a title field and show it above the decoded message. Update the reader's field checks if you make the title required.
  • Add a suggested opening date as a label. It is a reminder, not protection against someone opening the file early.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
With the standard library, you would convert between text and bytes, validate Base64 while decoding, open files with the right encoding, and serialize or parse JSON. These helpers keep those steps behind named operations while the project code focuses on creating and opening a note.

See Easy Base64 and Easy JSON for the individual modules. For a different in-memory game involving a checksum, try Message Detective.

docs.title: Build a Message Detective with Easy Base64 and Easy Hash
docs.text: Combine Easy Base64 and Easy Hash in a tiny clue-solving game: decode a message, then spot a changed clue using its original checksum.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
Your detective club has a meeting place hidden in a Base64 clue. Someone has changed the destination! Keep a checksum of the original message so you can check which version matches.

Base64 is an encoding anyone can reverse, not encryption. This is a learning game, so use a fictional message rather than a real secret.

Install the package with python -m pip install py-simple-wrap, then save this as message_detective.py and run python message_detective.py. It works entirely in memory and does not create files or contact a service.

from py_simple import decode_text, encode_text, hash_text, hashes_match

original_clue = "Meet at the moon garden."
original_checksum = hash_text(original_clue)
encoded_clue = encode_text(original_clue)

decoded_clue = decode_text(encoded_clue)
print("Encoded clue:", encoded_clue)
print("Decoded clue:", decoded_clue)
print("Original clue matches:", hashes_match(decoded_clue, original_checksum))

# Change the clue, but keep the checksum from before the edit.
changed_clue = decoded_clue.replace("moon", "star")
print("Changed clue:", changed_clue)
print("Changed clue matches:", hashes_match(changed_clue, original_checksum))

Example output:

Encoded clue: TWVldCBhdCB0aGUgbW9vbiBnYXJkZW4u
Decoded clue: Meet at the moon garden.
Original clue matches: True
Changed clue: Meet at the star garden.
Changed clue matches: False

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
hash_text() records a SHA-256 checksum, a fingerprint of the original text. Keep that value: making a new checksum after editing the clue would replace the baseline you are trying to compare against.

encode_text() turns the clue into Base64 text. decode_text() reverses that encoding, giving back the original sentence. Both helpers handle UTF-8, so clues can contain accented letters and other Unicode characters.

hashes_match() compares the text with the saved checksum. The decoded clue matches; replacing moon with star makes the second check return False. Spaces, punctuation and letter case also affect the checksum.

A plain checksum alone does not prove who sent a message. If someone replaces both the message and the expected checksum, they can make the check pass. This example detects a change against a baseline you already trust; it does not authenticate a sender or keep the clue private.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Change original_clue to "Meet at the moon café." and run it again. The decoded text should keep the accent, and the changed destination should still fail the checksum check.

Next, replace the changed_clue = ... line with changed_clue = decoded_clue.replace(".", "!"). Changing only punctuation should also give False. Keep using the original checksum for each comparison.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text: With Python's base64 and hashlib modules, you would convert text to bytes, encode or hash it, and convert the results back to strings. These helpers handle those steps so you can focus on the game: prepare a clue, decode it, and check for changes. See Easy Base64 and Easy Hash for more examples.

docs.title: Building a Palette Journal with Easy Colors and Easy File Manager
docs.text: Combine Easy Colors and Easy File Manager to collect random colors in a text file you can open later.

docs.title: What we are building
docs.text:
A small journal that picks a color, says whether it is light or dark, and appends that note to palette.txt. Run it once for each new swatch.

from py_simple import add_a_line, hex_to_rgb, is_light_color, random_hex_color

color = random_hex_color()
kind = "light" if is_light_color(color) else "dark"
red, green, blue = hex_to_rgb(color)

add_a_line(
    "palette.txt",
    f"{color} is {kind} (rgb {red}, {green}, {blue})",
)

Example line appended to palette.txt:

#A1B2C3 is light (rgb 161, 178, 195)

The hex value changes every run. The shape of the line stays the same.

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
1. random_hex_color() returns a color such as #A1B2C3.
  2. is_light_color() decides whether text on that color should be dark or light, which is handy when you paint a button.
  3. hex_to_rgb() turns the same color into red, green, and blue numbers.
  4. add_a_line() creates palette.txt if it is missing and adds one line. The next run adds another line under the first.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text: A random hex color, a lightness check, and an RGB conversion are three separate recipes if you write them yourself. Appending a line also means opening a file in append mode and adding a newline. These helpers keep the journal script focused on the color you want to remember.

docs.title: Building a Pizza Party Bill Splitter with Easy Money and Easy CSV
docs.text: Combine Easy Money and Easy CSV to calculate discounts, tax, and split costs among friends, then save an itemized summary to a spreadsheet.

docs.title: What we are building
docs.text:
When ordering food for a group, calculating each person's share after coupons and tax usually requires multiple calculations. This example calculates the total, divides it evenly among four friends, and writes a clean summary to a CSV file that can be read back and shared.

from py_simple import (
    add_tax,
    calculate_discount,
    format_money,
    read_csv_to_list,
    split_bill,
    write_csv_from_list,
)

items = [
    {"item": "Pizza Party Pack", "price": 60.0},
    {"item": "Garlic Bread", "price": 12.0},
    {"item": "Soda Pitcher", "price": 8.0},
]

subtotal = sum(item["price"] for item in items)
discounted = calculate_discount(subtotal, 10.0)
with_tax = add_tax(discounted, 8.0)
per_person = split_bill(with_tax, 4)

summary_rows = [
    {"description": "Subtotal", "amount": format_money(subtotal)},
    {"description": "After 10% coupon", "amount": format_money(discounted)},
    {"description": "Total with 8% tax", "amount": format_money(with_tax)},
    {"description": "Per person (4 friends)", "amount": format_money(per_person)},
]

write_csv_from_list("pizza_party.csv", summary_rows)
saved = read_csv_to_list("pizza_party.csv")
for row in saved:
    print(f"{row['description']}: {row['amount']}")

Example output:

Subtotal: $80.00
After 10% coupon: $72.00
Total with 8% tax: $77.76
Per person (4 friends): $19.44

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
1. calculate_discount(subtotal, 10.0) applies a 10% discount to the initial sum and returns the discounted total.
  2. add_tax(discounted, 8.0) computes the total after applying an 8% sales tax rate.
  3. split_bill(with_tax, 4) divides the bill evenly among 4 people.
  4. format_money() converts numbers and decimals into formatted currency strings with two decimal places.
  5. write_csv_from_list() saves the rows to pizza_party.csv, using dictionary keys as header columns.
  6. read_csv_to_list() reads the saved spreadsheet back into a list of row dictionaries so values can be displayed.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text: Calculating currency with floating-point math often introduces rounding errors. easy_money handles exact decimal values under the hood and formats them cleanly. Paired with easy_csv, you can save and load tabular records without writing boilerplate file-opening and CSV writer code.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: Get up and running with py-simple-wrap in under a minute.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install py-simple-wrap

This installs the lightweight core — most modules (easy_math, easy_strings, easy_validator, and 15 others) work right away with nothing else to install. A few need extra packages:

Extra Unlocks [ai] easy_ai [game] easy_game [viz] easy_data_visualization [images] easy_images, and easy_generator's generate_qr_code [web] easy_web [config] easy_config's gh_workflow_config(at_root=False) [json] easy_json's flatten_json

Install everything at once:

pip install py-simple-wrap[all]

Or install just what you need, e.g.:

pip install py-simple-wrap[game]

Note: The PyPI package is named py-simple-wrap (the name py-simple was already taken), but you still import it as py_simple in your code.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
Every function is available directly from the top-level package — no need to dig into submodules:

from py_simple import make_blank_file, miles_to_km, is_valid_email

# Create a new file in one line
make_blank_file("notes.txt")

# Convert units without memorizing formulas
distance_km = miles_to_km(26.2)
print(distance_km)  # 42.16...

# Validate common input formats
print(is_valid_email("hello@example.com"))  # True

docs.title: 📂 File handling — easy_file_manager
docs.text:
from py_simple import make_blank_file, add_a_line, read_file_to_list

make_blank_file("todo.txt")
add_a_line("todo.txt", "Buy groceries")
print(read_file_to_list("todo.txt"))

docs.title: 🕰️ Dates — easy_date_formatter
docs.text:
from py_simple import get_pretty_date, dd_mm_yyyy

print(get_pretty_date())  # e.g. "July 31, 2026"
print(dd_mm_yyyy())  # e.g. "31-07-2026"

docs.title: 🔄 Unit conversion — easy_converter
docs.text:
from py_simple import celsius_to_fahrenheit, kg_to_lb

print(celsius_to_fahrenheit(20))  # 68.0
print(kg_to_lb(70))  # 154.32...

docs.title: 🔢 Numbers — easy_numbers
docs.text:
from py_simple import is_prime, average

print(is_prime(17))  # True
print(average([4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42]))

docs.title: ✅ Validation — easy_validator
docs.text:
from py_simple import is_password_secure, is_valid_url

print(is_password_secure("hunter2"))  # False
print(is_valid_url("https://example.com"))  # True

docs.title: 🌐 Web — easy_web
docs.text:
Needs the [web] extra: pip install py-simple-wrap[web]

from py_simple import is_page_up, get_page_content

print(is_page_up("https://python.org"))  # True

docs.title: 🔤 Strings — easy_strings
docs.text:
from py_simple import to_snake_case, is_palindrome

print(to_snake_case("Hello World"))  # "hello_world"
print(is_palindrome("racecar"))  # True
