docs.title: Building a Screen Time Detective with Easy CSV and Easy Data Visualization
docs.text: Combine Easy CSV and Easy Data Visualization to turn a week of phone usage data into charts in just a few lines of Python.

docs.title: What we are building
docs.text:
Ever wondered how much time you actually spend on your phone? We'll log a week of screen time in a spreadsheet, then let Python read it and draw charts showing which day was the worst and which app wins most often.

First, save this as screen_time.csv in the same folder as your script:

day,hours,top_app
Mon,3.5,TikTok
Tue,2.0,YouTube
Wed,4.5,TikTok
Thu,1.5,Spotify
Fri,5.0,YouTube
Sat,6.5,TikTok
Sun,4.0,Instagram

Then create detective.py:

from py_simple import read_csv_to_list, plot_data

# 1. Read the spreadsheet into a list of rows
rows = read_csv_to_list("screen_time.csv")

# 2. Pull out each column we care about
days = [row["day"] for row in rows]
hours = [float(row["hours"]) for row in rows]
apps = [row["top_app"] for row in rows]

# 3. Print the week's total
print(f"Total screen time this week: {sum(hours)} hours")

# 4. Chart hours per day, then which app was the top app most often
plot_data(days, hours)
plot_data(apps)

Run it and you'll see your weekly total, a bar chart of hours per day, and then a bar chart and pie chart of your top apps.

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
1. read_csv_to_list("screen_time.csv") opens the file and returns every row as a dictionary, so you can grab values by column name like row["hours"].
  2. The list comprehensions pull each column into its own list. CSV values come in as text, so float() turns the hours into numbers.
  3. sum(hours) adds up the whole week.
  4. plot_data(days, hours) notices that days are labels and hours are numbers, so it automatically picks a bar chart.
  5. plot_data(apps) sees a single list of labels, so it counts them and shows a bar chart and a pie chart side by side.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Doing this with raw Python and matplotlib usually means: - Importing the csv module, opening the file with with open(...), and wrapping it in a csv.DictReader. - Counting how often each app appears yourself before you can chart it. - Creating figures and axes, choosing the right chart type, and calling plt.show().

By combining easy_csv and easy_data_visualization, reading the data and picking the right chart each take one line, so you can focus on the fun part: finding out Saturday was a 6.5-hour day.

docs.title: Building a Secret Message Vault with Easy Base64 and Easy Hash
docs.text: Combine Easy Base64 and Easy Hash to disguise notes from casual reading and verify message integrity using digital fingerprints in just a few lines of Python.

docs.title: What we are building
docs.text:
Imagine you and a friend want to pass secret dispatches back and forth—such as game clues, mission briefings, or club codes. You want to disguise the text from casual eyes so someone glancing over your shoulder cannot immediately read it, while generating a digital fingerprint to verify that the message has not been altered or corrupted by comparing it against a trusted original checksum.

Base64 is an encoding format, not encryption—it obscures text from casual viewing but provides no confidentiality, as anyone can easily reverse it. Similarly, a regular hash allows a recipient to detect changes against a trusted original baseline, but cannot prevent an active attacker from modifying both the message and the hash if both are transmitted together over an untrusted channel.

Install the package:

python -m pip install py-simple-wrap

Save the following as secret_vault.py:

from py_simple import (
    decode_text,
    encode_text,
    hash_text,
    hashes_match,
    is_base64,
)

# 1. Write the secret dispatch
secret_message = "Meet at midnight by the old oak tree. The password is: BLUEBERRY."

# 2. Scramble the message into Base64 and record a SHA-256 digital fingerprint
# Note: Base64 disguises text from casual glance, but provides no encryption/confidentiality.
vault_payload = encode_text(secret_message)
fingerprint = hash_text(vault_payload)

print("--- Outgoing Dispatch ---")
print(f"Scrambled: {vault_payload}")
print(f"SHA-256 fingerprint: {fingerprint}")

# 3. Simulate receiving and verifying the payload against the trusted original fingerprint
# Hashes verify data integrity by comparing against a known baseline.
print("\n--- Incoming Delivery ---")
if is_base64(vault_payload) and hashes_match(vault_payload, fingerprint):
    print("Integrity check: VERIFIED (Payload matches trusted fingerprint)")
    revealed = decode_text(vault_payload)
    print(f"Decoded message: {revealed}")
else:
    print("Integrity check: WARNING (Payload does not match expected fingerprint)")

# 4. What happens if the payload is altered in transit?
# If the payload is modified without the trusted original fingerprint matching, it alerts us.
tampered_payload = vault_payload[:-4] + "AAAA"
print("\n--- Tamper Test ---")
if not hashes_match(tampered_payload, fingerprint):
    print("Tampering alert: The payload does not match the trusted fingerprint!")

Run the script from your terminal:

python secret_vault.py

Example output:

--- Outgoing Dispatch ---
Scrambled: TWVldCBhdCBtaWRuaWdodCBieSB0aGUgb2xkIG9hayB0cmVlLiBUaGUgcGFzc3dvcmQgaXM6IEJMVUVCRVJSWS4=
SHA-256 fingerprint: ae35c0900d3181cf57b07c0b7a7235eff5dbe756bafe99e97779697994134c18

--- Incoming Delivery ---
Integrity check: VERIFIED (Payload matches trusted fingerprint)
Decoded message: Meet at midnight by the old oak tree. The password is: BLUEBERRY.

--- Tamper Test ---
Tampering alert: The payload does not match the trusted fingerprint!

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
1. encode_text(secret_message) converts the plaintext string into a Base64-encoded ASCII string. Base64 is an encoding format, not encryption. While it obscures text from a casual glance and makes binary or formatted strings safe for storage and transmission, it provides no confidentiality—anyone who sees the encoded string can immediately decode it back to the original text.
  2. hash_text(vault_payload) calculates a cryptographic SHA-256 checksum of the scrambled payload. Even if a single character is changed later, the hash will produce a completely different result.
  3. is_base64(vault_payload) checks that the payload format is valid Base64 before attempting to decode it.
  4. hashes_match(vault_payload, fingerprint) verifies that the payload still matches the trusted original checksum. Because the checksum matches our known baseline, we can verify that the text was not accidentally modified or corrupted in transit.
  5. decode_text(vault_payload) converts the Base64 string back into readable plaintext.
  6. In the tamper test, changing even a few characters in tampered_payload causes hashes_match() to return False, alerting the recipient that the payload differs from the original baseline.

docs.title: Understanding Security: Integrity vs. Confidentiality
docs.text:
When working with Base64 and hashes, it is essential to understand what these tools do—and what they do not do:

  • Base64 disguises, but does not encrypt: Base64 is an encoding scheme, not encryption. It prevents someone glancing at a screen from immediately reading the text, but provides no actual confidentiality. Anyone with access to the encoded text can decode it with decode_text(). Never rely on Base64 alone to protect sensitive data or real secrets.
  • Hashes detect alterations against a trusted baseline: A SHA-256 hash acts as a digital fingerprint used to verify data integrity. When compared against a trusted original fingerprint (such as one saved beforehand or shared across a secure channel), you can detect if the message was altered or corrupted.
  • Hashes alone are not "tamper-proof": A regular hash does not prevent an active attacker from modifying the message if both the message and the hash are transmitted over the same untrusted channel. An attacker could alter the message, compute a brand new SHA-256 hash for the altered text, and replace both. To guard against an active attacker modifying both data and checksum in real-world systems, cryptographic tools like Hash-based Message Authentication Codes (HMAC) or digital signatures with private keys are used.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
• Save to disk: Use encode_file() and decode_to_file() to disguise and save an entire secret file or clue sheet to disk.
  • Switch algorithms: Pass algorithm="md5" or algorithm="sha1" to hash_text() and hashes_match() to see how different checksum algorithms look.
  • Interactive decipher tool: Wrap the receiving step with Python's input() prompt so users can paste in scrambled dispatches and security keys to unlock them interactively.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Without py-simple-wrap, achieving this with Python's standard library requires several boilerplate steps: - Converting strings back and forth to bytes using .encode("utf-8") and .decode("ascii") for base64.b64encode() and base64.b64decode(). - Setting up hashlib.sha256(), feeding bytes to the hasher, and calling .hexdigest(). - Handling decoding errors and validating strings manually with try/except blocks.

Combining easy_base64 and easy_hash replaces repetitive byte conversions and hashing plumbing with intuitive, single-line functions.

For more examples and detailed function references, see Easy Base64 and Easy Hash.

docs.title: Build a Signup Validation Check
docs.text: When people create an account, a program needs to check their details before accepting them. This small command-line example combines the email, username, and password helpers from py_simple into one clear signup check.

docs.title: What we are building
docs.text:
Imagine a community site where a new member enters an email address, a public username, and a password. We will keep the checks together, then tell the member whether their details can be accepted.

from py_simple import is_password_secure, is_valid_email, is_valid_username


applicant = {
    "email": "maya@example.com",
    "username": "maya_dev",
    "password": "River!27Map",
}

checks = {
    "email": is_valid_email(applicant["email"]),
    "username": is_valid_username(applicant["username"]),
    "password": is_password_secure(applicant["password"]),
}

if all(checks.values()):
    print("Account details accepted")
else:
    for field, accepted in checks.items():
        if not accepted:
            print(f"Please update the {field}.")

Example output:

Account details accepted

docs.title: Try an invalid detail
docs.text:
Changing a detail shows which part needs attention. Here the username contains a hyphen, while is_valid_username() accepts letters, numbers, and underscores.

applicant["username"] = "maya-dev"

checks["username"] = is_valid_username(applicant["username"])

for field, accepted in checks.items():
    if not accepted:
        print(f"Please update the {field}.")

Example output:

Please update the username.

docs.title: How the checks work
docs.text:
is_valid_email() confirms that the email has the expected address format. is_valid_username() keeps usernames simple and predictable by allowing letters, numbers, and underscores. is_password_secure() checks that a password is long enough and includes uppercase letters, lowercase letters, digits, and a special character without repeating adjacent characters.

Putting the results in a dictionary lets all() decide whether every check passed, while the final loop can point to the exact detail that needs changing. This keeps a beginner-friendly program readable without writing regular expressions or password-counting logic by hand.

docs.title: Building a Smart Contact Extractor
docs.text: Combine Easy Web, Easy Regex, Easy Lists, and Easy Strings to build a tool that fetches a webpage, extracts contact emails, and outputs a clean, deduplicated list in just a few lines of Python.

docs.title: What we are building
docs.text:
Imagine you are organizing a local tech meetup and want to reach out to the organizers of similar events. Instead of manually visiting their "About Us" pages and copying emails one by one, we can write a short script to fetch the webpage, extract the emails, and clean them up automatically.

```python from py_simple import get_page_content, extract_emails, unique_items, to_title_case

docs.title: 1. The URL of the page we want to scan
docs.text: target_url = "https://example.com"

docs.title: 2. Fetch the raw HTML content of the page
docs.text:
page_html = get_page_content(target_url)

if page_html: # 3. Extract all email addresses from the HTML text raw_emails = extract_emails(page_html)

# 4. Clean up: make them lowercase and remove duplicates while keeping order
clean_emails = unique_items([email.lower().strip() for email in raw_emails])

print(f"Found {len(clean_emails)} unique contacts on {target_url}:\n")
for email in clean_emails:
    # Bonus: Generate a friendly name label from the email prefix
    name_part = email.split("@")[0].replace("_", " ").replace(".", " ")
    formatted_name = to_title_case(name_part)
    print(f"{formatted_name} <{email}>")

else: print("Could not fetch the webpage. Check the URL.")

docs.title: Build a Story Prompt Jar
docs.text: Stuck staring at a blank page? Combine Easy Random and Easy JSON to pick a character, a setting and a challenge for a short story. Save the idea so you can come back to it instead of losing it when the program closes.

docs.title: Set up the project
docs.text:
Use Python 3.11 or later. In a new project folder, install the package:

python -m pip install py-simple-wrap

The helpers used here are available in version 0.9.0. They use Python's standard library, so this example does not need any optional extras or an internet connection after installation.

docs.title: Build the jar
docs.text:
Save this as story_jar.py in your project folder:

from pathlib import Path

from py_simple import open_json, pick_random_item, save_json_data

characters = ["curious robot", "sleepy dragon", "tiny detective"]
places = ["a floating library", "a moon garden", "an underwater bakery"]
challenges = [
    "find a missing key",
    "deliver a mysterious parcel",
    "stop a clock running backwards",
]

prompt_file = Path(__file__).resolve().with_name("story_prompt.json")

if prompt_file.exists():
    prompt = open_json(str(prompt_file))
    print("Back to your saved idea:")
else:
    prompt = {
        "character": pick_random_item(characters),
        "place": pick_random_item(places),
        "challenge": pick_random_item(challenges),
    }
    save_json_data(str(prompt_file), prompt)
    print("A new idea for your jar:")

print(f"A {prompt['character']} in {prompt['place']} must {prompt['challenge']}.")

Run it from that folder:

python story_jar.py

One first run produced this output. Your choices may be different:

A new idea for your jar:
A tiny detective in an underwater bakery must deliver a mysterious parcel.

Run the script again and it loads the same idea from story_prompt.json. The first line becomes Back to your saved idea:; the story starter stays the same. Write a few sentences about what happens next!

To draw a new idea, delete only this example's story_prompt.json file and run the script again. A new draw can still choose the same combination.

docs.title: Drawing three ingredients
docs.text: pick_random_item() chooses one item from each list. The dictionary keeps the three ingredients under descriptive keys, ready to save together. Try adding your own characters and places, but keep each list nonempty: choosing from an empty list raises ValueError.

docs.title: Keeping the idea
docs.text:
save_json_data() creates the JSON file beside story_jar.py, even if you run the script from another directory. Its keys and string values are the same ones in the prompt dictionary.

This helper refuses to overwrite an existing file. The exists() check therefore sends later runs to open_json(), which reads the saved data instead of drawing and saving another prompt. The example assumes the saved file still has the three keys written by the script.

JSON stores data between runs; it does not run Python code. If you edit the file, keep it valid JSON. Invalid JSON or a file that cannot be read raises EasyJsonError from py_simple.easy_json. A failed save also raises that error. The script lets these errors surface rather than replacing a saved idea. Keep any writing you want to preserve somewhere safe before deleting this example's file.

docs.title: Turning data into a story starter
docs.text: The final f-string reads the dictionary's three keys to assemble one sentence. On the first run it uses the newly generated dictionary; on later runs it uses the dictionary loaded from disk.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
• Add a new ingredient, such as a surprising object. Give it a list, a dictionary key and a place in the printed sentence. Delete the old example JSON before running your changed version so its saved keys match.
  • Include characters or places in another language. JSON preserves the strings when they are loaded again, even if the file shows Unicode escapes.
  • Write a different ending for the same saved prompt each time you return.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Without these helpers, you would call random.choice() and write the JSON file-opening, encoding and serialization code yourself. Here you can focus on the little creative loop: draw an idea, keep it, and return to write.

For more examples, see Easy Random and Easy JSON.

docs.title: Building a Study Habit Tracker with Easy Date Formatter, Easy Stats, and Easy Data Visualization
docs.text: Combine Easy Date Formatter, Easy Stats, and Easy Data Visualization to track daily study sessions, analyze study consistency, and visualize your progress across the week.

docs.title: What we are building
docs.text:
Whether you are preparing for exams or building a daily coding habit, seeing your study patterns helps you stay consistent. In this project, we track daily study sessions, calculate your weekly average and variability with easy_stats, format report timestamps with easy_date_formatter, and render a clean progress line chart with easy_data_visualization.

Create study_tracker.py:

from py_simple import (
    data_range,
    get_pretty_date,
    mean,
    median,
    plot_line_chart,
)

# 1. Study time recorded across the week (in minutes)
study_sessions = [
    {"day": "Mon", "minutes": 45},
    {"day": "Tue", "minutes": 60},
    {"day": "Wed", "minutes": 30},
    {"day": "Thu", "minutes": 90},
    {"day": "Fri", "minutes": 50},
    {"day": "Sat", "minutes": 120},
    {"day": "Sun", "minutes": 75},
]

days = [entry["day"] for entry in study_sessions]
minutes = [entry["minutes"] for entry in study_sessions]

# 2. Analyze the week's study stats
avg_minutes = mean(minutes)
median_minutes = median(minutes)
spread = data_range(minutes)
total_hours = sum(minutes) / 60

# 3. Print the weekly summary with a formatted date
report_date = get_pretty_date()
print(f"=== Study Habit Report ({report_date}) ===")
print(f"Total time studied: {total_hours:.1f} hours ({sum(minutes)} mins)")
print(f"Daily average:      {avg_minutes:.1f} mins/day")
print(f"Median session:     {median_minutes:.1f} mins")
print(f"Session spread:     {spread:.1f} mins (difference between shortest and longest)")

# 4. Plot the study trend over the week
plot_line_chart(
    labels=days,
    values=minutes,
    title="Weekly Study Trend",
    x_label="Day of Week",
    y_label="Minutes Studied",
)

Run the script to see your formatted habit summary in the terminal (note that the exact date in the header will depend on the day you run the script) and a clean line chart showing your daily progress:

=== Study Habit Report (Saturday, October 24, 2026) ===
Total time studied: 7.8 hours (470 mins)
Daily average:      67.1 mins/day
Median session:     60.0 mins
Session spread:     90.0 mins (difference between shortest and longest)

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
1. get_pretty_date() generates a human-friendly date string including the weekday (such as "Saturday, October 24, 2026") for your report without needing complex strftime directives (the exact date and weekday will reflect when the script runs).
  2. mean(minutes) computes your average daily study time, while median(minutes) gives the middle session length, showing your true typical study effort even when a weekend study marathon spikes the average.
  3. data_range(minutes) calculates the difference between your highest (120 mins) and lowest (30 mins) days to show habit variance.
  4. plot_line_chart(days, minutes, ...) draws a clean line chart with marked data points and labels the axes without raw Matplotlib boilerplate.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
Building this analysis from scratch in Python usually requires: - Importing datetime and looking up formatting codes (%B %d, %Y) just to print the current date cleanly. - Importing the statistics module or writing manual loops for sums, means, medians, and ranges. - Writing several lines of matplotlib.pyplot code to initialize subplots, draw plots, configure titles, remove unnecessary frame borders, and call plt.show().

By combining easy_date_formatter, easy_stats, and easy_data_visualization, you get a complete personal analytics tool in under 30 readable lines of code.

docs.title: Build a Website Health Monitor
docs.text:
Combine Easy Web, Easy CSV, and Easy Terminal to build a command-line application that monitors health of websites and saves a report.

You will read website addresses from a CSV file, check the health of each address, pretty-print the results, and also save a report to another CSV file. You should be comfortable with Python loops, dictionaries, and functions before starting.

docs.title: Set up the project
docs.text:
Use Python 3.11 or later and install the package with its web and terminal extras:

python -m pip install "py-simple-wrap[web,terminal]"

Create a folder containing two files:

website-monitor/
    websites.csv
    monitor.py

Add these addresses to websites.csv:

url
https://www.google.com
https://github.com
https://offline.invalid
https://www.python.org
https://youtube.com

The first row is the column name, url. Be sure to include https:// or http:// in each address. The offline.invalid address is deliberately invalid so you can see how the monitor handles a failed request.

docs.title: Build the monitor
docs.text:
Copy and paste the example below into monitor.py:

from pathlib import Path

from py_simple import (
    EasyTerminal,
    get_page_title,
    get_csv_columns,
    is_page_up,
    read_csv_to_list,
    write_csv_from_list,
)
from py_simple.easy_web import SomethingWentWrongError


def check_website(url: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Check a URL and return its status, title, and any error details."""
    result = {"url": url, "status": "OFFLINE", "title": "", "error": ""}

    try:
        online = is_page_up(url)
    except SomethingWentWrongError as error:
        result["error"] = str(error).strip()
        return result

    if not online:
        result["error"] = "The response did not have HTTP status 200."
        return result

    result["status"] = "ONLINE"

    try:
        result["title"] = get_page_title(url) or ""
    except SomethingWentWrongError as error:
        result["error"] = f"Title unavailable: {str(error).strip()}"

    return result


def main() -> None:
    """Read website addresses, display their health, and save a CSV report."""
    folder = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
    input_file = folder / "websites.csv"
    report_file = folder / "website_health.csv"

    print("─" * 60)
    EasyTerminal("WEBSITE HEALTH MONITOR").set_bold().show()
    print("─" * 60)
    # 1. Read list of websites from websites.csv.
    try:
        columns = get_csv_columns(str(input_file))
        websites = read_csv_to_list(str(input_file))
    except (OSError, ValueError) as error:
        EasyTerminal(f"Cannot read websites.csv: {error}").set_color("red").show()
        return

    if "url" not in columns:
        print("websites.csv must have a column named url.")
        return

    urls = [row.get("url", "").strip() for row in websites]
    urls = [url for url in urls if url]

    if not urls:
        print("No websites to check. Add addresses below the url header.")
        return

    print(f"\nChecking {len(urls)} websites...\n")
    results = []
    # 2. For each website address check its online status.
    for url in urls:
        result = check_website(url)
        results.append(result)

        online = result["status"] == "ONLINE"
        symbol = "✓" if online else "✗"
        color = "green" if online else "red"
        message = f"[{symbol}] {url:<36} {result['status']}"
        EasyTerminal(message).set_color(color).show()

    # 3. Compute statistics and display results in terminal.
    total = len(results)
    online_count = sum(result["status"] == "ONLINE" for result in results)
    offline_count = total - online_count
    availability = online_count / total * 100

    print()
    print(" SUMMARY ".center(60, "─"))
    print(f"Total Websites: {total}")
    print(f"Online:         {online_count}")
    print(f"Offline:        {offline_count}")
    print(f"Availability:   {availability:.0f}%")
    print()

    # 4. Save results to a csv file.
    write_csv_from_list(str(report_file), results)
    print(f"Report saved: {report_file.name}")

### Entry point of script ###
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Open a terminal in your project folder and run:

python monitor.py

Example output (results will depend on your connection and the websites):

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
WEBSITE HEALTH MONITOR
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Checking 5 websites...

[✓] https://www.google.com               ONLINE
[✓] https://github.com                   ONLINE
[✗] https://offline.invalid              OFFLINE
[✓] https://www.python.org               ONLINE
[✓] https://youtube.com                  ONLINE

───────────────────────── SUMMARY ──────────────────────────
Total Websites: 5
Online:         4
Offline:        1
Availability:   80%

Report saved: website_health.csv

docs.title: Reading the website list
docs.text:
read_csv_to_list() uses the first CSV row as column names and returns a list of dictionaries. Each website becomes a row such as {"url": "https://github.com"}.

get_csv_columns() reads the actual header so an empty first data row does not hide a valid url column. The script checks that header, strips surrounding whitespace from addresses, and skips empty addresses. If there are no addresses, it stops before calculating a percentage or trying to write an empty report.

docs.title: Checking each website
docs.text:
is_page_up() returns True when the final HTTP response has status 200.

HTTP errors, connection problems, and timeouts raise SomethingWentWrongError. The try/except inside check_website() records the error and lets the loop continue to the next website. Other responses that return False also count as offline in this example.

Here, OFFLINE means the check did not pass. It does not prove the website is unavailable to everyone: a website might block automated requests, or your connection might have a problem. The report's error column gives more detail.

After a successful health check, get_page_title() makes another request to retrieve the HTML title. Wrapping it in its own try/except keeps a title retrieval failure from changing an ONLINE result to OFFLINE. For example, a page might respond successfully but have no title element.

docs.title: Styling the terminal output
docs.text: EasyTerminal() holds the text you want to display. set_color() selects its color, set_bold() emphasizes the heading, and show() prints it. print() repeats the ─ character to separate the heading and summary from the results.

docs.title: Calculating the summary and saving the report
docs.text:
The script counts the ONLINE results and subtracts that number from the total to get the offline count. Availability is calculated as:

online websites / total websites × 100

Four passing checks out of five give 80%. This is the percentage of websites that passed this run and not a measurement of uptime over a period of time.

write_csv_from_list() writes the result dictionaries to website_health.csv, using their keys as the header: url,status,title,error. Each checked address has one report row, including failed checks. The final save message on the terminal appears only after the file is written; a file-writing failure raises an error instead.

docs.title: Challenge to try yourself
docs.text:
• Add a timestamp column to show when each check ran.
  • Run checks every 30 seconds using time.sleep(). Keep an accumulated history to measure availability over time.
  • Highlight title retrieval errors in yellow while keeping the health status green when the initial check passed.

docs.title: Helpers in this project
docs.text:
These are the helpers used in this project:

Module Helpers Easy Web is_page_up(), get_page_title() Easy CSV get_csv_columns(), read_csv_to_list(), write_csv_from_list() Easy Terminal EasyTerminal, set_color(), set_bold(), show()

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text:
The helpers help you handle HTTP requests, CSV parsing and writing, and terminal styling in the simple and easy way. This health monitor connects those pieces into a workflow: read, check, display, summarize, and save.

For more examples, see Easy Web, Easy CSV, and Easy Terminal.

docs.title: Build a Word Detective with Easy Text and Easy CSV
docs.text: Combine Easy Text and Easy CSV to find repeated words in a short story and save a ranked table you can open in a spreadsheet.

docs.title: A small real-world example
docs.text:
You are writing a story about a moon garden and want to spot words you keep reusing. Install the package with python -m pip install py-simple-wrap, then run this in a practice folder. It creates or replaces word-counts.csv in that folder.

from py_simple import word_frequency, write_csv_from_list

story = "Moon gardens glow. Moon flowers glow, and moon paths sparkle!"
counts = word_frequency(story)

# Put the most frequent words first; sort ties alphabetically.
ranked_words = sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda item: (-item[1], item[0]))
rows = [{"word": word, "count": count} for word, count in ranked_words]

if rows:
    write_csv_from_list("word-counts.csv", rows)
    for row in rows:
        print(f"{row['word']}: {row['count']}")
    print("Saved word-counts.csv")
else:
    print("No words to count; no CSV was written.")

Example output:

moon: 3
glow: 2
and: 1
flowers: 1
gardens: 1
paths: 1
sparkle: 1
Saved word-counts.csv

The CSV starts with:

word,count
moon,3
glow,2
and,1

docs.title: What happened?
docs.text:
word_frequency() removes punctuation, lowercases the text, and counts words separated by whitespace. That makes Moon and moon share one entry, and glow. and glow, share another.

The sorting key uses a negative count to put larger counts first. Its second value is the word itself, so equal counts appear alphabetically. We then turn the pairs into dictionaries with word and count keys.

write_csv_from_list() uses those keys as column headers and writes one dictionary per row. It opens the output file for writing, so running the example again replaces the previous report. The if rows check avoids passing an empty list, which the helper rejects. An empty story leaves any existing report untouched.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text: Replace story with your own paragraph, then try an empty string to see the no-words message. Remember that punctuation is removed rather than replaced with spaces: moon-garden becomes moongarden. This is a simple word counter, so review the results before using them to edit a story.

docs.title: Why use these helpers?
docs.text: You can concentrate on the report: count the words, rank them, and save the results. The helpers handle the character cleanup and CSV headers, encoding, and row writing. See Easy Text and Easy CSV for more ways to work with the same data.
